FRIGHTENED. "Last night I played at hide and seek Till I was most too tired to speak, And, hungry as a little bear— I couldn't find you anywhere, „ And so I went all by myself For cookies on the pantry shelf. But, mamma dear, I was afraid,l It was so dark—" "Why, little maid, You sui ely do not mean you fear The darkness; what could harm you here?" "I wanted you to go with me And take a light, so I could see. I was afraid, if I should go Without you, that I shouldn't know—" "But you have often heard me say The darkness is as safe as day. 'Tis very wrong, and foolish, too, ' For such a great big girl as you To fear to go in it alone— . . Afraid of what, my little one?" "Why, just afraid at first, because I couldn't find the jar—l was, Dear me !--most dreadfully afraid There were not any cookies made." ,

Ajust economy is not niggardliness; one need not be a miser in avoiding the extravagance of a spendthrift. A Nebraska editor, named Ladd, was struck by light- ning last week, and effectually shocked. He likens his experience to that produced by a subscriber paying cash in advance. . .

A man in a Western town hanged himself to a bedpost by his sumenders. The coroner's jury, which was com- posed o-Mthers, decided that " The-deceased came to his death by coming home drunk and mistaking himself for his pants." Ray and Ernest were playing together, and oc- casionally quarrelled. Their mother told them that if they were naughty egain she should separate them. In a little while Ernest called out, "Mamma, please come and separate Ray, he's naughty." • ABOUT ADEUSEMENT.—Never seek for amusement, but be always ready to be amused. The least thing has play in it, the slightest word wit, when your hands are busy and your heart is free. But if you make the aim of your life amusement, the day will come when all the agonies of Fa pantomime will not bring yoU an honest laugh.— . Ruskin. . . .

Two men were discussing the burial question. One of them was of an i&moclastic turn of mind, the other a bumptious aspirant to the pulpit. Iconoclast: "What rest hes the parson te charge extra for burying folks in the consecrated side?" Embryo Parson: " Yo'r rang thor. It's not mair for the consecrated, but less for the unconsecrated side!" . . .

A rough-looking man got into an American train, took a seat, dropped his head on his hands, and sobbed like a babe. "What's the trouble, friend?" said a man in a neighbouring seat. " Wal, you see, stranger, my ole chum is dead, and I'm a-carryin' his corpse home ter his de mother. It makes me sad; you oughter know'd I shall never get another like him. He was 18-carat, fine." "Was he sick long?" "Naw; he died kinder sudden." "Fever?" " New ; he—he" (and here a suffocating sob choked his voice) "he committed suicide, stranger." "Shot himself, eh ?" " Wel, no-o, but it 'mounted tá 'bout that." " How ?" "Wal, you see, he , called me a liar." , One morning, when:Dr. von Laver called to see" the late German Emperor, the latter remained standing at the window, as though:absorbed in thought, and without returning his salutation. The physician, surprised at this, waited forean explanation, when suddenly the monarch turned round, and,beckoning Dr. Lauer to ap- proach, said to him, in his most affable manner, "Excuse my apparent want of attention, but on looking out into the street, I noticed a peasart, who must have come a long way to see thet Emperor: he was holding up his litt;e boy, to let him have a good look. 1, therefore, was compelled to stay a little longer at the window, so as not to spoil the pleasure of the good folks." CAN HENS TALK ?—A gentleman had among his Spanisb hens a mother with nine chickens. This hen at length sickened and died with the comb disease. Her chicks were only about four weeks old, and could scratch but little for themselves. The weak mother would go round with them, putting down her bill to indicatel where they were to scratch. She soon became too weak for this, and the gentleman says :—Soon after we noticed all of her chicks standing around her in a sort of half circle, with their eyes looking piteously toward her, " peeping " mournfully, she in turn, giving faint "chirps." At this all the other fowls came around her, and each seemed to have something to say. After about fifteen minutes had been spent in this manner, a healthy young dominick hen that was laving eggs every day, and had shown no'signs of even desiring to set, stepped out from among the rest, and took her position by the side of the sick hen. Upon this, the mother hen gave a few faint chirps, which all the chicks answered with a chirp. Then the mother looked toward the dominick, and gave two or three "clucks," to which the dominick responded for the first time with "Cluck! cluck!" and the chickens answered with " Peep ! peep!" in concert, and all rushed up to the dominick. The mother hen gave two or three farewell chirps, and the new mother walked off with the brood, clucking and scratching as vigorously for them as though she had herself hatched the brood. The dominick and brood never went near the mother again. She died the next day, and dominick protected and faithfully raised the chicks committed to her care Whatever others may think of this, it seemed to the writer, and those who witnessed the transaction, as genuine a case of giving away children before death as we witness among human kind. These creatures must have had communication with each other respect. lug the matter, at least judging from their actions, and the old saying that "Actions speak louder than words" was literally true in this case. Sins REEVES.—I was born October 21, 1821, at Shooter's Hill, in Bent. My father was a musician, and it was said that at an early age I used my voice with no little skill. When 14 years old I performed the duties of organist of North Cray Church, where I likewise had charge of the lycal choir. "Doctors differ," it is said; so, too, do singing masters. The professor under whom I studied treated me as a baritone; yes, and as a baritone I came upon the stage and succeeded. While studying harmony and counterpoint under Mr. H. Calcott, I practised the piano with John Cramer. I also learned to play more than one musical instrument, including the violin, violoncello, oboe, and bassoon; in fact, so proficient did I become as .a violinist that at the beginning of my career I not seldom undertook the duties of orchestral leader. In 1839, being then in my 18th year, I made my debut at• the Newcastle-on-Tyne theatre as the Gipsy Boy in "Guy Mannering," for the benefit of the late tenor, George Barker. This was followed by my appearance as Count , Rodolfo, the travelling nobleman in "La Sontuunbula." Some years afterwards I earned enthusiastic applause for singing and acting the tenor part in this same de- lightful pastorale of Bellini's. There have been instances of singers coming out as tenors, and finding afterwards that they had baritone voices: Lablache, for example, is said to have played the part of Count Almayiya in -" The Barber of Seville" before relinquishing it for that of Figaro—which he in turn gave up for that of Dr. Bar- tolo, thus descending from tenor to baritone, from bari- tone to bass. But other than myself lam not aware of a vocalist commencing as a baritone, then rising to the rank of tenor, and holding a foremost position as such for upwards of forty years. Subsequent to my engage- ment at Newcastle, Isang et the Grecian Theatre under the nom de theatre of "Mr. Johnson." I likewise under- went a course of training at the hands of Mr. Hobbs and Mr. I. Cook as a tenor—and appeared at Drury Lane, then under the direction of Macready.—Sints Reeves's Life and Recollections.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

TEMPERATURE AND PLANTS.—Every plant must have a certain degree of heat in order to prosper, and it pros- pers in accordance with the amount received until this gets to the maximum, when it grows sickly in propor- tion as the amount is exceeded, until finally it dies. The amount required differs for every plant. Some at the freezing-point suspend all development, and others— especially in cold or temperate countries—will bear many degrees below....zero. One would think that this low temperature, by freezing the juices of the plant, would tear the cells asunder, and so destroy the organi- sation; but this cannot be, for often plants will be seen quite stiff with frost, and grow again as well as ever after being thawed, while others will be " nipped " when it was impossible that the juices could have been frozen. The "zero" of life in different plants is very different, and, in general terms, it .may be said to be sooner reached in plants of warm than of cold or Alpine countries or situations. Martin tells us that he ob- served Soldanella flowering under the snow, and in Arctic countries it is not uncommon in late spring to see saxifrages and other plants in bloom while their stems are covered with snow. Snow, however, keeps plants warib, and this fact ought always to be taken into ac- count in calculating the cold which plants endure in certain countries. Excess of temperature acts in much the same way as cold, and acts more from the injurious effects of the dryness which it induces than from the mere heat. The open woods of the Highland slopes called Catingas in Brazil cast their leaves during the warm and dry season, just as other trees do in the cold season. For plants, there is accordingly (I) a useful temperature, comprising all degrees between the mini- mum and maximum required or endured by that plant; (2) a useless temperature, below the minimum and above the maximum, ending in either direction in a noxious one. It is plain, therefore, that there exists a relation between the temperature and the life of the plant, and that "each plant is a kind of thermometer whichi has its own zero.—Fronz "Our Earth and its Story." for October.

Fa= GAynnatNo.—Apples and pears mast be fre- quently examined in order to ascertain if they are fit for picking, as dates are very misleading. Fruits that have been gathered other years a fortnight or three weeks before this are still on the trees in many a :'garden, though it is feared the frost we have been having will be the means of causing the fruit to part sooner from the trees than it would have done. When apples or pears begin to fall from the trees, it is one of the signs of maturity, unless caused by a maggot, which can be readily ascertained by cutting a fruit or two in halves, when traces of the maggot will be seen, more particu- larly in the core ot the fruit. The colour of some varieties gives some clue as to their ripeness. Taking hold of the fruit and gently raising it up, and if it parts readily from the tree, is another indication that the fruit is fit for gathering; so is falling fruit if a tree receives a smart shake, and, if fruit will not bear this, it is pretty certain that it will not stand the force of winds which we may expect any time, which, fortunately for our scanty ;fruit crops, have done us no harm hitherto. The best articles to place the fruit in as it is gathered are a boat-shaped basket made of thin pieces of wood, with a handle across, known to gardeners as " trugs ;" a light-made box with a handle, and a light zinc pail. All kinds of wicker work articles must be avoided, as all the fruit that will be nearest the sides still receive impres- sions from the willow or cane. For the same reason, baskets should not be used to convey the fruit to the store-room, nor vet to market; boxes such as those that oranges are peeked in being much better. We wonder what would be the state of the American apples upon their arrival in this Country if sent over in baskets, the same as the English grower -transports his fruit in. Fruit intended to, keep must be carefully handled, and not hurled from one vessel to another as is usually done. The fruit at the time may not show any indications of this rough treatment beyond a few depressions over its surface, but if in a few days the skin is raised covering the depressed part, the flesh will be rusty and in an in- cipient stage of decay. Select dry weather to gather the fruit, and lay it in store in as thin a layer as space will allow, so that it may be readily inspected, and bruised or bird-pecked fruit, which so soon decay, may be moved to prevent them affecting fruit that is sound. A dry, airy room is a good place in which to keep fruit; and after it has passed through its first sweating, it may be packed in boxes, and then piled one upon another. THE Fnorr GARDEN.—Thotigh the tops of dahlias are completely destroyed, we consider the roots to be much better in the ground than lifted for two or three weeks yet, but the tops may be cut and taken away for appear- ance sake. All other plants that have been destroyed by the frost should be moved and the ground raked over or forked to give it a fresh appearance. Cuttings may still be taken from such hardy plants as Centranthes, rubra and alba, Phloxes Penstemons, Antirrhinum and Rudbeckias. Of Phloxes it may be said that they are more easily propagated by division of the roots, and cuttings are only resorted to when a variety is scarce or the grower intends exhibiting cut blooms, which are always larger and in every way superior to those from old plants or divisions. THE GREENHOUSE.—The Hyacinth: The culture of these plants it appears differs but little at the present time from what it did fifty years ago, if at that date the instructions of an old writer were followed, whose writings have been kindly submitted for our perusal. "To grow Hyacinths properly," he says, "the soil should be composed of one-half turfy loam Of mellow texture, one-fourth old cow dung or cow dung mixed with leaf mould, one-fourth clean but coarse sand. Deep pots, four inches in diameter, should be used." These deep pots are seldom used now. ",The soil made firm beneath the bulb and the top of the bulb about level with the surface. The medium-sized, plump-looking bulbs should be chosen and potted in October. After potting plunge the pots in old tan or coal ashes so as to cover them over tvio or three inches. They are to remain until removed in succession to a warm room or house to forward the blooms." Even their culture in glasses was not unknown in those days for the same writer says :—" When grown in.glasses Of water dark-colourediglasses-should be pre- ferred and the more opaque the better. November is soon enough to put the bulbs in the glasses. First keep them a week or so in damp moss or sand, then put them in the hollow top of the glass, and at first allow the water to just touch their base. Rain water, quite clean, should be used, and this changed once a week. The glasses should be set in the dark until the roots have grown an inch or two in length. When the flower stem is ad- vancing two drops oh spirits of hartshorn may be put in the water each time it is changed with advantage. Ityacinths will grow in wet sand, and where it is covered with moss the plants look pretty." Further comments and instructions will tee given next week.

. RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. TH' "HOLEY CORNER" LOT. When bod a lad, aw often went To t' play-heawse, up i' th' "gods," An' thripenny bits aw sometimes spent To ged th' pit at th' " Odd's." Wod gain ther wur among thad rook, As never cared a jot Wod end coons fost, if they geet th',nook— 'Twur th' "holey corner" lot ! I' th' reight-hand corner, next to t' stage, They allus took ther shop; An' spent wed brass wur left fro' t' wage I' Eccles cakes an' pop. Or, if a mate wur eawt o' wark, They'd gather "turn" on t' spot; They acted fair, an' up to t' mark— Thad "holey corner" lot! A rougher Set one cuddn'd find Than them o th' district reawnd, But mooast, at heart, wur true an' kind Wi feelin's reight an' seawnd. They'd laff, an' jooak—or feight—wi' glee, An wodn'd stan' no " ret ;' An' wise foak allus leet 'on be— Thad "holey corner" lot! If singers coom as cuddn'd sing, By gum! they bed to dert ; Forth' lads wod hey ther bit o' t' fling, An' wodn'd let 'em stert. ; But if one suited wee!—" Encore!" • They'd bellow like a Scot: Id meant "success" dud th' welcome rooar , Fro' th' "holey corner" lot! They claimed th' owd corner for thersels, • An' kept id' mony a year. 'Twur seldom onnybody else Could ged to peeark deawn theer. Wodever artiste geet th' fawt, They'd co him" Tommy Rot," . An' tell him he vrorn'd woth his sawt,— Thad " holey corner "lot. Time's flown a tidy space sin th'" Odds" Wur gooin' i' full blow • An some o' t' lads aro under t' sods 0 th' graveyard, buried low. Some's rnannin' British Ironclads ; On th' desert some's bin shot: For England geet some gallant lads Fro' th' " holey corner "lot. Some's doin' weel ; some's gooan to t' bad, - An' plenty's getten wed; An' mony a fayther tells his lad O'er th' gain as he once hed. Its a long while sin th' " Odds " shut up, An' th' owd spooart went to pot; But mony a tooast owd cronies sup, Toth' "holey corner 'lot.. • Time changes t' world, an' o at's in't, As Progress hurries en; Fresh ways, like hawp'nies new fro' t' mint, Come every day wi' th' Sun. But one thing changes nooan wi' me, That's t' wish, as nowt con blot, . Good luck an' health, so wheer they be, To th' '6 bolo, corner" lot! JACK o' AA.

to feet nes pulses stirred by want isomer calls the sweetest and most perfect of human enjoyments." The music was divine, the parquet floors charming. Hundreds of artistically tinted wax candles, or shaded electric lamps, s'hed a light which was soft and pleasing, on decorated walls; or on plush draperies which instead of gilt framework, hung in folds on either side of mirrors. Flowers were every- where. She did not know the exorbitant sums of money which were lavished on these flowers, but there was a subtle intoxication for the senses in the perfume of the Stephanotis or the Gloire de Dijon and Marechal Neil roses which hung in festoons from the walls of the larger rooms in which they danced, whilst the ante-rooms adjoining were some- times filled with wild flowers, and sometimes with fair palm trees, luxuriant ferns, or grotto-like arrange- ments of running water and Virginian cork. She ehjoyed such scenes all the more from the fact that she had never been able to secure such pleasures for herself in her stinted and hardworking life abroad, and Miss Wilson, astonished, wrote • another letter to the Havards, in which she declared that Ursula was becoming quite dissipated. It was a mild form of pleasure compared with the more active dissipation which was going on in the heart of the season in London. Yet Ursula ac- cepted several invitations, and felt' more than ever as if she were .in dreamland when in one of these balls, she came again across the face of' the young man who had helped to rescue her in the boat catas- trophe at Abbeyford. She was angry with herself for starting as if in astonishment. Why should she imagine that this stranger with the powerful face ansi the somewhat roughly-cut features, which had imilressed her in a way she found it difficult to explain, should be superior to the frivolity of an ordinary ballroom? It -was true that he -did not seem to dance much, and that, when her eyes just encountered his, he was looking at her with a keen scrutiny which ca.used her to lower hers. True also that he seemedlo have an unusual and intense en- joyment in the pleasure of others. She took herself to task for feeling a sort of excitement when he was introduced to her. What should he be to her more thaw the others whom she niet—it was absurd that she who prided herself on her absence of sentiment should exaggerate the small service he would doubt- less have rendered to anyone! • She mastered the inclination to feel a ridiculous agitation -when they' fell into conversation after being introduced. "Mr. 'Wilfrid Fielding." The name did ' not convey anything to her, and she was inclined to' resent an aside of the good-natured friend who introduced them, and who told her that he was a man who had taken his first class et Oxford, and of whom great things were prophesied. "Not that I think the great things will be realised, for he is a ' fellow who invariably stands in his own light ! " added the friend with a meaning smile, as Wilfrid Fielding stood looking at her with that scrutinising look which she could not tell to be one of amused surprise. ' The well-dressed figure with the hair coiled round the shapely head, the clear brown eyes,and the grace- ful pose was so like and yet so unlike the same figute when he had last seen it, with dripping garments, and disordered locks, that his first words came slowly, "I think, Miss Campion, we haVe met before ? " She was ashamed of herself for answering with a quick blush. "I beg your pardon," as if she did not remember. i When n fact she remembered well enough, and prided herself on her direct truthfulness. But she had the excuse of being slightly confused. Her pretty white throat was coloured With her blush. "I don't know what we should have done if you had not come to our assistance," she said with a quick correction of her hist hesitation. "I should thank you for my brother's sake if-tot for my own." And then the recollection of the last time they had met was so eminentlyridiculous that she laughed—an infectious laugh—in which he joined. The laugh set them both at their ease, and in a short time they were talking as if they had known each other, all their lives. Ought Ito apologise for this unconventional Ursula if I admit that an hour afterwards she had "cut all her dances," asshe herself would have expressed it, and WM sitting in one of the flower-decorated antechambers, so commonly near these ballrooms, in close conversation with Fielding. A well-hrought•up girl would never have done so, but then I lat ver pretended that Ursula Iva§ awell brought' up girl. The need for a "bon camarade " had been heavy upon her of late; perhaps it accounted for the light way in which she played at shuttlecock with hearts. None of the Abbeyford men had been "bong camarades," and these London ones who laughed at her sallies and coveted her money bags,were another step removed from the free and easy ideal. She did not believe in any Damon or Pythias among women. The women she had met seemed to her constrained, narrow, and self-conscious, Sometimes in her dreams she had thought there might be one woman in the world with whont she Could form a close friendship =scarcely two—and that woman it had never hitherto been her fate to meet. The _conjunction of tuo girls. hanging on each other's arms made a pretty picture; asMissHavard had once told her, but Ursula prided herself on never going in for pretty pictures. She would have been half offended if some one had told her what a picture she made herself beneath the fan palms in the shaded light, with the blue-green foliage contrasting with the tints of her russet hair. She was dressed in gauzy black, it being one of her latest "fads," as Margret said not to spend much money on her own adornment, and black, which brought out the ivory whiteness of an unusually fair shin—was, as she declared, less menotonous than white.
"Isn't that orchid a thing to dream of ?" she asked, pointing to a wonderful-looking flower with two long slendeilcreamy wings, and a faint flush of crimson at its centre.

"Yes," he answered, with gravity, which she did not understand ; "the florist who produced it must bo little short of a genius. It has been all the rage this last six months with people of fashion—the crowning beautyof decorations—oh, yes; it ha.s"been a hit I"

"How coldly you speak of it." " Well,if you were to know the prices paid for such things you would excuse me for -thinking them not only fabulous but almost scandalous! in Loncloti we are always wanting something new. To keep in favour with the luxurious classes the growers must constantly produce fresh colours. The last rage in roses is for the Catherine Veimet which has held its own in New York, but the Safrano is now becoming a rival—fifteen guineas for a bouquet is nothing.' . _

"Aid why not? If people have money to pay for such floral aristocracy ? " she answered a little de- fiantly—the lavish abundance of tropical climes being very pleasant to her senses at that moment. "Why not ?" he asked, speaking as if to himself, "Why should we not surround ourselves with every blessing of refinemmet and culture—except that there are thOusands of children, aye, and men and women in our back yards, who have never seen a cowslip growing, and cotild not tell you the shape of roses; sooner or later we shall see that we are responsible ourselves for the sorrows and crimes of other, and for their deprivations, too ! But," a little abruptly, "I ought not to speak so to you, who no doubt have your .dresses from Worth." " Whilst other women are in rags. Indeed you are quite mistaken," she rejoined, with that sudden vibration in,her voice,which struck a stranger who heard it first.

. Again his eyes met hers. A shadow had fallen on her face. There was a sudden dilation of the pupils of thebrown orbs whichstruck him as also uncommon, and he said with quick sympathy. " Ah, vote are not one of the women who spend thousands on their own, luxuries, and then think they can heal broken hearts by dealing out flannel as Kingsley said, I little below cost price.' might have known you were not. But there are hundreds of them in London."

"I have no right to pride myself on my Arcadian simplicity," she answered with that shadow still on her face—the chesnut eyebrows knotted till they almost met. "But you would hate to have your gowns described in the society papers." • "Unless I went in for the divided skirt society— what society do you call,it?" They laughed again, and her eyebrows unknotted. She had not been used to such a perfectly natural give and take in conversation since she had discussed many things—social problems among the rest—with her "bons camarades" in the old days at Paris. Did she not know the deeps and shallows of this hmiy hive of life far better, most likely, than he who had only a theoretic acquaintance with it. "I ought to apologise for speaking to you in this way—trotting out a skeleton at the feast," he said when the laugh was over, and she looked her merry sell again. "But how could I tell that you were different from the rest I and one gets a little sick sometimes of pretty pictures, pretty pageants, fresh things to tickle the palate, longing hands stretched out to the future, denianding more and more:" . " And you think that the majority of women must be like that," she said, with a sort of pout (they would have called it a moue in Paris): I assure you you are quite mistaken. I have thought of all these things hundred times before, and I have a belief" with a little toss of her head " that sooner or later Nature will right herself. We must do what we can. but blight and disease and misery

div.head: CHAPTER
div.p: CHAPTER
A CHANCE MEETING.

It was May again in-England. The people were coming hack who had shirked th London fogs, the Yorkshire snowstorms, the biting winds of the East coast, or the Devonshire moisture. The swallows of society were flitting home who had been disporting themselves in the sunshine on the other side of the Alps, in sight of the blue Mediter- ranean.

And at the season when country cousins throng the streets of the West-cad of Londoia and may be easily recognised from the initiated by their unsophisticated manners, their absence of fashionable languor, their insatiable curiosity, and a tendency to get enjoyment out of trifles quite unknown to the habitues of Belgravia—Ursula Campion was devoting herself to the , pursuit of sightseeing with an eagerness of interest rarely equalled b' the greenest of provincials. Miss Havard did not think it • was keeping up pearaztces, and wrote to remonstrate with Ursula for shewing her usual want 4 appreciation of the fitnegs of things. The girl was 'so indefatigable that. good Mrs: Wilson was worn.to a shadow. Not that Urkula tried her as yet with rushing about to the inevitable luncheons, races, dinners, and, balls which people who are not "out of it" are supposed to share in. Such engagements had hardly commenced. And before she paid her toll to "society," Ursula Campion made a point of going to hear all the best singers, and seeing all the best pictures. She fagged through the Academy and Grosvenor bravely with her cata- logues, marking everything that was good. She dragged her poor old companion, not only to St. James's Hall on Satnrclay afternoons or Monday evenings, but insisted on contemning the reserved seats as commonplace, and on squeezing up the narrow staircase into the orchestra where she could watch the working of the "rushing bow" in the hands of Joachim or Madame Neruda, the nimbi( play of the fingers up and down the necks of their instruments, where her eager eyes could .semetimes catch a glimpse of the luminous transparent varnish on its back, which is the glory of an old "Strad," or note the many movements by which an eminent pianist would express his emotions in his face or in his back, all Of which could be studied with great accuracy by those who were ambitions of acquinng a professional style. , "I am afraid I am naturally vulgar," she would say, with a sigh; "but, it is not only that you can get all these 'blessings for a shilling, but you can watch the three or four hundred others who are waiting till the music begins, and that is such fun." This study of life was an endless feast to Ursula. She was Very far indeed from being like the orthodox young lady, and manifesting, blase indifference to everything that was, beautiful. Her ecstacy of de- light in tremulous sound would bring the tears into her eyes with pleasure akin to pain, and perhaps that was one reason why she liked to hide herself m the orchestra, and abstain even from good words till the music was over.

Owing to the simple life she had led in Paris she was unsophisticated enough to be astonished at the magnificence of the bill of fare which those who cater for the public taste can supply in London. Plays so magnificent with their brie 4 brae, marqueterie, . minted scenery, and lavish surroundings that the hero's heroism seemed in danger of being merged in the splendour of the accessories, as if those who pandered to the public taste had forgotten that the background should be' subordinate to the actors; and concerts in Which all grief and passion, all joy and delight seemed te, .oe concentrated .into ,a few half hours of such marvellous sound that Ursula could not criticise, but wonld draw a deep breath, or lean forward in an excited way, unconscious oi the amused expressions of those about her. "I'm so frightened to think of taking care oi her in that great Babylon all alone. Isn't it like going into the very jaws of the lion?' Mrs. Wilson had protested when it was first of all pro- posed that she and Ursula should settle themselves for a time in handsome .lodgings in one of the streets near Piccadilly. . . . . . . .

But she soon found that she had no reason for her vague alarms, and began to adopt a different tone of regret. "She doesn't seem to care for dinners or dances. She has no right to hate society at her age, has she?' lamented the old lady in a different tone to Dr. Howard. "She is really most impracticable, and lived such a free and easy life in Paris that now she wants to go back to all her old ways, and asks me why she should bother herself by going through the pretence of saying what-isn't true for the mere sake of being polite.' "And quite right, too," said the doctor, as he put down theletter. "We should treat Society as we treat a spoilt child, and never let it get the upper hand of us. ' So treated, Society may be scornful at first, but will at last learn to respect those who have a higher ideal than itself." "But it does not do for a girl like Ursula to make herself ridiculous," protested Margaret, shaking her head. "Depend upon it we shall soon hear of her doing some queer things." Mrs. WilSon's next letter lamented the fact that when Ursula did go out she would insist on neglect- ing the friends belonging to her own position, and talking to the professionals—musicians, artists, and such people. It was useless for Ursula to urge her sympathy for those whose traditional reputations had to stand a fresh test every year with new com- petitors, and a fresh " Velungencht." There were surely as she said as many artists in London who had their pictures untrung as there were briefless barristers, and as many disappointed musicians as there were crossing-sweepers. She herself had once found it difficult to get enough to eat, and was now beginning to think a good deal about others who lived by their with, and Who were slighted by those who possessed another kind of capital. Ah, I thought she'd soon begin about reforming something," grumbled Sir Thomas m hen UrsufVs opinion was repeated to him. "These sort of women don't know where to stop—they'd reform the sun and moon and, make them rise and set in different , ways if they could." , But as time went on awl the doctor wrote cheery letters telling her how Raymond was really thriving at Heidelberg, and how the friend who had accompanied him declared he was buckling to his work, Ursula proved to be not so averse to enioyin,,c herself as they had imagined. With that fresh and healthy delight in everything which was a part of her nature, she threw off the burden of care which had lately oppressed her. Margaret Havard—comingnp to town fora day— was surprised to find the tvio ladies preparing for a ball.
_ "You must let me see you in all your war paint," said Margaret jokingly. • "Well, it is a relic of savagery." "What is ?"

"Why that.women should adorn themselves in this way for men—it is giving in—a sort of survival of slavery." " Oh, don't let us begin all that I". said Margaret, diplomatically, inspecting the girl's dress to see that the trimmings were satisfactory: Once before she had been startled by Ursula 's quotations from Rousseau and George Sand, and ever after" had thought it wise to keep off her favourite subject of marriage. It had been enough to make the hair stand up on her head to hear the girl say to her brother, "Pont you think it a, mistake for people to tie themselves by vows for life? Doesn't it seem to you that the lin- possibility of breaking such a tie must lead to a cer- tain amount of tyranny and dulness" she added, puckering up her pretty brow. • "My dear child, when you are a little older you will not talk like pat," the doctor had , said good- naturedly, and iVfargn.ret,perha,ps did wisely in keep- ing off the subject. • , 'ATter all Ursula had made no confidence about the sort of understanding which she still had with Louis Grandet. With her tendency for putting off disagree- able things, she had decided that it would be time enough to tell the Havards when Louis appeared in person upon the scene. "Why should my life be lonely andunlovely—why shouldn't I share it With other people? If lam en- gaged to be married, that doesn't prevent me from havingfriends!" said Ursula to herself, forgetting, all her fine ideals whenever -the surging motion of the , waltz carried her away.

The Abbeyford folk, with their elaborate ritual of minor observances—their "you roust not know this person," and "you must not speak to that " had counterbalanced the pleasure of dancing for her by all sorts of drawbacks. Nor could she be ignorant of the fact that the amusement itself was not regarded with favour by mony of 'Margaret Havard's friends who belonged to the Stricter set 1y what was called in Abbeyford the religious world. Here in London it was different. Dancing, apartfrom local associations, was athoroughly invigorating exer- cise, and Ursula was too high-spirited and natural, too fond of music and the.rhythm of movement not

't)/ • all kmas are simply the nonquittiment or tne conditions of health. As the race makes progress there will be nothing abnormal." It was now his turn to look astonished. He did not know that she was- simply retailing the philo- sophy with which good Desnoyers used to soothe inmself when his philanthropic Soul was moved with" any form Of distress. Ursula had been a good listener, and had listened to some purpose. . "The more you learn to think of the Uniyerse as [do," she continued, still retailing her old ruapteea, .opinions, nothing disconcerted, "the more you will see that there is no real blot or lack of harmony in man or anything else—it is simply our limited hornan sight; and our want of cultivatiOn which makes us think.so."

She was fairly taking away his breath. ITo was too polite to laugh again, arid only said quietly— " Take away their hopes about the future from the people and it will be. all the more incumbent on you to make them hapPyin the present." But Ursula was not again Ap he stalled out of her comfortable view of things,. 'Since her efforts to help the poor people of S. Xga.tha's had not turned out so well as she expected, she had been more inclined to take an optimistic view. . "Depend upon it," she said with perfect serenity, "it is men who. have wanted to enslave women here and keep them down, who have invented that theor; about Another life, to make them more subniis..L.- in this. I doubt if you really believe in it selves."

He looked at her again, too surprised, to speak for a minute or two. ," Utilitarianism and materialism, these be thy. gods, 0 Israel," he was saying to himself. What hope of calling into play those spiritual forces which were to help in the material difficulties of the life he had chosen for himself, if even a woman —an unselfish and, fascinating girl—could reason with perfect satisfaction in this way? . . .

Than he'answered, but he never knew what he said. So little was she aware that anything had happened to chill the pleasant sense of friendship which had warmed her heart that eveninf ,hat she lay awake that night speculating for the first time on the nature of the tie which hound her to Grandet. How was it that that night she felt for the first time her need for slaking her thirst with a full draught of the rich wine of life such as is offered to other• women? Her lips were not yet parched, and she could enjoy herself as few enjoyed, now that her anxiety about Raymond had in some measure ceased. But the veil seemed to be lifted which hid from her the solemn mystery of life. What had she done in the thoughtlessness Of her youth? • Was Louis Grandet the enly man for whom she could really care? It would be bad enough to be tied to the routine of fashionable life—the most irksome of all bondages when the sands of time -began ,to run out of the inevitable hour glass —to be weariedby.its monotony when one began to recognise the limitations of human existence, or when repletion in pleasures might be followed by dissatisfaction. This at least she should be saved from. • There was always St. Agatha's —always the fragrant breath of the sweet country life But to be tied to a man for whom she could not really care! Why had she made such a hasty promise ; It had been a thought stifled till now in the depths of her heart. _ _ .

div.p: (To be continued.)
NOTES AND QUERIES ON SOME OBJEC-
TIONS TO HOME RULE. BY "HoME BULB."

In an article which appeared in the " Examiner ", of September 22nd, wu showed, or at least, attempted to show:- I.—That hitherto, and up to the present moment, Ireland has been governed not according to, but generally without due regard for, or rather, in defiance of Irish opinion. The Liberal party, in spite of strenuous Conserliative opposition and a reactionary and infatuated House of Lords, has passed some important and much- needed measures. The Conservatives also have been 'compelled to do something; but legislation has only been the result of great pressure, and has almost always, through being "too late," proved a partial or total failure. Something, it is true, has been done, but that '-does not alter'the fact stated in this first proposition., 2,—That the Libel-al party now propose to alter this state of affairs by making the Government of Ireland representative, not in name only, but in fact. This to be effected by the creation of a separate Parliament in Dublin for the management of all affairs which exclu- sively concern Ireland, as distinguished from those which concern the Empire. 3.—That this policy is opposed by moderate men, not because they approve of and support the present state of things, for that state is insupportable; nor because there is any alternative policy which they can agree to adopt; —for middle courses they now consider to be outside the range of practical politics—but because of the objections and difficulties which Home Rule presents to their minds.' Taking up the threads of argument where last dropped some five weeks since, we now proceed at once to con- sider some of these objections. I.—Let us commence with the most proverbial—that Henze Rule will lead to separation. This assertion is based partly upon the present state of feeling in Ireland, but chiefly upon the declarations made in former years by the leaders of public opinion in that country. It is some- times said that the policy is sufficiently condemned by the admissions of Home Rulers themselves. The latter admit, and not only admit but vigorously assert, the reality of Irish National Aspirations—the phrase is hackneyed but correct—and hope to see them realized. Therefore it is said they must be prepared for the dis- memberment of the Empire. This does not follow nor are they prepared for anything of the kind. What the Irish ask, is a separate Parliament in which they may manage in their own way, their own affairs. This, if it led to the pacification of the country will certainly be preferable to the present paper union and will strengthen iastead of weakening and disintegrating the Empire. This constitutes the Irish demand; this satisfies the national aspirations of all reasonable Irishmen, and this is what we are prepared to grant. But what about the speeches made eight or ten years, and more, since; what about Mr. VarnelPs statement in America that he would not be satisfied until the last link in the chain which bound England to Ireland was severed? It is deperate statements of this kind that form the most important part of the stock in trade of the unionist press. How often must it be reminded of the circumstances under which they were made? Not many months since, Mr. Parnell, in the House of Commons, said:—" It is now 12 years since r first entered political life. At that time, very few people in Ireland—not one in ten—believed in the efficacy, of Parliamentary action. The idea widely. prevailed that revolution was the only means of securing justice to Ireland. All that is changed. I ask my constituents to trust to Parliamentary action. The people have given us a trial, the proportions are reversed, and now 9 persons out of 10 in Ireland believe in Parliamentary and Constitutional action." Surely this is a change which a patriotic party should foster, and (far from scouting) welcome. The popular expectation was that their deliverance from thraldom would come in the shape of what was vaguely thought of all thrOugh the country, as" the big war. Bound by the spell of traditional prejudice, ignorant of the rights and wrongs of the case—for here comprehension has proved to be more than half way to sympathy— Englishmen shut their eyes, and turned deaf ears to Irish grievances. These no doubt came in time to be taken more or less indifferently, as a matter of course; very much, if we may borrow the simile ,as seaboard dwellers become accustomed to the natural natirmureof agitated waters, of which a certain amount of disturb- ance they know to be only the natural condition. But it is not surprising that the bulk of the Irish were, in these dark periods of their history, unsettled, resorting to methods of violence and rebellion. Nor is it surprising that since the great change which has taken place dur- ing the last few years lathe attitude of the English to- wards them , their feelings towards us should have changed also—while hope gradually inspires the hearts so long filled With desperation. But for the writings of the "Times," the London Tory press and its satellites, unhealthy stimulants of an unhealthy mental disposition—but for these it should hardly be necessary to observe that there usually is a very wide difference between the language of hope and the language of despair; or between that of gratitude and cordiality on the one side and hatred, bred of tyrannous injustice, on the other. Unfortunately there are a large, happily a decreasing, but still a large number of people who will not believe in any such cordiality of feeling on the part of the Irish towards England, or that great portion of the English from' which the hand of good fellowship is ' held out towards them. All this, in their opinion, is sentimental rubbish. Confirmed believers in the theory that Ireland received a double dose of original sin they laugh to scorn the idea of their being capable of gratitude. Yet, in 1782, Mr. Fox, the father of English Liberalism, as he has been called, expressed himself as follows upon this point :—" I love the Irish nation. They may have their faults like other nations. They may have a quick feeling of injury, and notbe very patient under it. But I do affirm," said Mr. Fox, "That of all their characteristics, there is not one feature more prominent in every class of the conntry— from the highest to the lowest order—than gratitude for benefactions and sensibility to kindness."*

, Those who have,as our American friends say, read any br travelled any (wemean,of course, in Ireland) and kept their eyes open, will be able, unhesitatingly to endorse this important and eloquent testimony to one of the most conspicuous virtues of a much-maligned people. Yet, exactly the opposite is assUmed by that consider- able portion of the community •to whom we have just referred. And politicians who really do believe in the
* Quoted last spring by Mr. Morley, in one of his Lancashire speeches.
•„,vator-

separation cry, assume a good deal more. The Nationa- lists in Parliament, have declared that they will accept a large and liberal measure of Home Rule as a finality. They repudiate the insinuation that entire separa- tion, and not legislative, and, so to speak, naional free- dom is their object It is assumed that ' they, or at least the majority of them, deliberately intend to per- jure themselves. This In itself, is a pretty considerable assumption. Without professing to give an opinion upon the Irish members as a whole, or to criticise them individually, to do which, we are not qualified, we must say that of those we have seen and listened to, men like Mr. Mahoney or Mr. Sullivan, strike us as quite incapable of such treachery and such dishonesty. But supposing it to be true that this intention does lurk in the corners of their minds, would it receive the sanc- tion of the Irish? We venture to say it would not. We deny that there is amongst them a feeling of empittered. hatred towards Englishmen. We believe the chders with whrch English Home Rulers are received, with Which the statements where Separation is disavowed, are received, —such as those made by Lord Rip)on to the masses in Dublin—we believe these cheers to be not artificial but spontaneous and genuine. We believe that if there were in Ireland any real and wide spread desire for separa- tion, it would find for itself articulate utterance, and that when Mr. O'Brien ridicules the idea' of there being such a desire, he would be hooted. But he is only cheered! What does it mean? Can it be assumed that the whole of the nation's real feelings, not merely those of accomplished and, as is implied, dishonourable politi- cians, can be consoled? Apparently yes.

- - ,It is assumed that the Irish are our natural enemies, to be ruled only as a good many people undoubtedly think, like conquered colonies of old. That we have already given them a good deal of this necessary and wholesome, but severe government, and that the people will never forget or forgive it ; that they are utterly implacable and that their object is not a lust and reasonable settlement at all, but revenge. That they are, therefore, from top to bottom, acting a part of finished duplicity—and this is considered possible of a nation whom even Mr: Disraelli called a "high minded and generous people." Is the assumption reasonable? Shall we not rather in this case, say with Burke "Nobody shall persuade me, where a whole people are concerned, that acts of lenity are not means of concilia- tion"; and refuse, as some would have us do, to treat them as incorrigibles and thus renouncing all hope of these centuries of bitterness arid strife being terminated by an amicable settlement, recklessly, to fling the helve after the hatchet? It might be argued with some show, at least, of reason that the Irish being no more deficient in imagination than in generosity, would not, of their own free will,—after such reparation for and redress of long standing treubles as can be made—seek to disasso- ciate themselves from that portion of past history in which they in common with other Britons, have some natural interest and pride. There are some bright spots in that history even for Ireland. Triumphs in art, in poetry, in eloquence, in science, the works of wisdom and of cour- age, of the geniuses of the heroes, not a few of whom ha.ve hailed from the Sister Isle. There have been great military feats of valour and some national reverses too, in which she' has shewn her willingness to forget what is best forgotten when the need for its rememberance is past, and hi which Irishmen have made common cause with us. The Duke of Wellington said that, without them, he could not have won his victories in the Peninsular war. They fought by the side of the English there as they have done elsewhere. Is it likely that, after having done their share, in the making of the Empire, they will, when times of peace between them and we arrive, disclaim all coffnection mirth it ? Inextin- guishable hatred alone could lead them to attempt to sacrifice their position' as part of the most important Empire in the world for one wherein they would figure among those lowest in the scale of nations. Ireland has neither the numbers, the arms, nor the money, to give her the least chance of succeeding in an attempt at Separation, and even had she a chance, we can- not, in view of the above considerations, admit the assumption that she would be willing for it to be made. It is as little like the return which, for -air treatment, might be expected from a " highminded and generous people" as is the fear with which we are now coming to close quarters worthy of those who, belonging to the almost infinitely strongersidedndulge in it. One more assumption we have to consider,stilllarger, still less allowable. Nine-tenths or thereabouts of Ireland's trade in exports, and imports, is with England. It is assumed that her spirit of hostility will be , so ,extreme, so insane that, in utter disregard of her own interests, she will force on a war with the country upon a trade with which hervery existence at present, almost depends. And for what are such sa,crifices to.be made? That she may have the right to establish a system of coinage different from eurs, gather no more with the English Scotch and Welsh under the Union Jack, and have the ' priviledge, after exhausting herself in warfare with us, of supporting a separate army and navy of her own instead of contribeting her quota to the Imperial Exche- quer. We wonder that this assumption has not been too much for even the truest of those True Blues who still deem us infatuated and gullible Separatists. Truly the receptive capacity for this kind of political food displayed by some of our friends (especially at Primrose League meetings) is marvellous. But We would not be under- stood to imply' that they are insincere. On the contrary, those who are afflicted with "separation on the brain" are only too sincere,—like a good many others, who, if we may be permitted to say so, ought, on this question, to be wise enough to know better than to continue fighting against fact. We know well, that they arc sincere in their apprehensions, and that there are amongst them leaders with shields as bright and with voices that have a ring as true as those of the best in our own party; aye, and thousands of followers with an integrity of motive, worthy of such leaders. But we believe that this great company of our opponents was justly described bp&-Mr. Gladstone in a passage, the latter Part of which, goes straight to the root of the whole ' question 'and in which, they, are referred to as those—.. who in mood faith call themselves Unionists but who, in my 'firm conviction, are themselves the greatest enemies of the Union. For it is impossible to have any true Unionism between England and Ireland except one which is founded upon a genuine and large equality of treatment, applied to each country according to its history, its traditions and its needs and legislative provisions, of which it is found by the permanent con- , victions of its people to stand in need.

II —lt has been argued by some Unionists—we don't say all; different people have different ideas—that the Irish demand springs from illegitimate Catholic ambi- tion; that the result of granting Horne Rule will be tyrannical treatment of Protestants by Catholics. The same thing was said at the time of the disestablishrnent of the Irish Church, with how much justification experience has shown. If this were a question of Catholic supremacy, is it probable that the recent differ- ence between Ireland and the Pope would have occurred? The Pope admits the reality of Irish Nationalism; does not disapprove of it, but disapproves Of the methods, or some of the methods, adopted in this political warfare. The Irish party disagree with him, recognising. only his right to decide u pon questions of morality as distinct from policy. They dispute this right which the Pope would arrogate, and with such determination that even the " Times " remarked, only the other day: " The attitude of the Irish clergy towards the Pope shows that opposi- tion to the rescript condemning the plan of campaign, threatens to reach the proportions of a schism." Can it be contended, in the face of this, that theirs is not a national and political but a large sectarian object? The movement in Ireland never has had her its object Catholic supremacy. That has net been the question there; on the contrary, as far as religion was concerned, it has always been a question of extreme Protestantism, embodied in Ulster Orangemen, fighting for supremacy and for the privileges by which the English Government i has enabled Protestants n Ireland to figure a§ altogether superior to the rest of the population. Whilespeaking of this northern part of Ireland, it may be as well to clear up a not unfrequent misapprehension as to its political opinions taken as a whole. Ulster is often referred to as if an enormous majority of its inhabitants were opposed to, or rather filled naturally with, a just and deep-seated hatred of the Nationalists. But , when we come to facts, we find tkat out of 33 members returned by Ulster to Parliament 17 are Nationalists, and if the decision rested with it, there is little doubt that a plebiscite taken now in Ulster, would by a much larger majority than ode in 33 affirm the principle of Home Rule. That principal is opposed, not by Ulster, but by parts of Ulster, more especially that quarter of which Belfast is the centre. There, and • in a few other places the majority are, we know, against it,; but is Belfast to overrule the rest of Ireland. Unionists are given to praising the loyalty of the people there. Too often their loyalty means only hatred of the Catholics. They are the descendants of the privileged garrison of Protestants, aniong,whom an Anti-Catholic feeling at the titne, and for a long while after the times of the planta- tions, was, owing to the prevailing feeling amongst Protestants towards Catholics, the manner in which the plantations were carried out, and to other circumstances, • now become matters of history—a fealing not to be wondered at. Prejudices usually die hard. They are not yet dead in the north-east of Ireland. But it can scarcely do much good to fanthem into a flame. Mr. Cham- berlain has done his best to encourage them, and to prevent their becoming less bitter or possibly, in time, dying a natural death. Liberals may be allowed to remind those of the Unionist persuasion who approved, if any of them did apprev,e of his inflammatory speeches in Ulster, that there wea time when Mr. Bright condemned the extreme Orangemen as a violent and factious party of bigoted and intolerant spirit. But we should be very sorry to run down the inlportant body of Protestants in Ireland, or to create the Impressions that they are as a whole— either outside or • inside Ulster—united in a feeing of aversion towards the notion of home rule. Far from this being the case, one of the strongest. answers that can be made to those who fancy this to be an agitation for Catholic supremacy, is to point to the- great le.aders of the People, past and present, who have been, the majority of them, Protestants. For if the Irish Catholics, predominating in the country, were endeavour- ing to persuade the Protestants, to help them in a falsely called national movement, • intending all the while to afterwards turn round upon and arrest them, we may be quite sure that the Protestants would neither be So stupid or so blind as to be unable to get an inkling of what the otherside were driving at. We should not find Protestants among the most ardent and energetic propagators of the

Home Rule cause, nor the head of the whole Nationalls party with several of his most able lieutenants, himself a Protestant. Protestants would not help to further their own ruin, or if they did, they would be even more unnatural than the impulsive Irish in accepting them as leaders. But these fears for Irish Protestants, for those, at least, who are content to dwell peaceably on equal terms with their Catholic neighbours, are quite uncalled for. As Mr. Mahoney told Us in Warrington, speaking of himself and his family living in the midst of Catholics (if we remember rightly, six miles from any other Protestant or actually from any Police Station!) Protestants are by no means living in daily terror of our lives; we are .quite capable ef taking care of ourselves and supporting our own religion: And if we were not, if Protestantism could only be sustained in Ireland through the bolstering up of an English Government, then it must indeed have become a poor and lifeless creed, not worthy of being supported at all." In England there is still a good deal of strong Anti - popery' feeling left which many of our opponents have not failed to work upon and turn to account. It is to be hoped that the Cause of Ireland will not again suffer from mistaken' if conscientious religious prejudices. lII.—It will be said no doubt, that this reasoning '5 plausible enough but overdone; that these objections are very real, or they would not have influenced the numbers of able men in the Unionist party who, to 3 greater or less extent, are affected by them. Put briefly, something like this, no doubt, passes in the' minds of many.who understand men better. than measures. This, of course, is 'a kind of error to which' Home Rulers and Unionists are equally liable, nor do we for one moment stiggest that the character and knowledge •of the mOr prominent supporters and opponents of a movement should be ignored when thinking out its probable denier its or merits. We merely remark that Politicians, the ablest amongst them, with the widest knowledge and experience, are still, by no means infal- lible : and for the benefit of any who are inclined t. think that some men are too wise to be mistaken on this question, those, for instance, who have been accustomed to take Lord Hartington for their guide, or those who, all their lives, have looked to John Bright as almost the incarnation of political wisdom---for their benefit, we give the following extracts from the Hand Book of Florae Rule. • Mr, Dicey himself tells us " that the wisest thinkers of the eighteenth century, (including Burke) held that the inch.dence of the American Colonies meant the irreparable Great Britain, There were apparently solid reasons for belief: experience has proved it to be without foundath The various changes in our own constitution, and eve: our crimiaal code, were believed by "men of light and 11 log" at the time to portend national ruin. All the ju In the land, all the bankers, and the _professions 'goner petitioned against alteration in the law which sent childr ten to the gallows for the theft of a pocket-handkerchief. great Lord Eilenborough declared in the House of Lords the learned judges were unanimonsly agreed" that mitigation in that law, would imperil "the public securit "My Lords," he exclaimed, "If we suffer this to 'pass, we shall not know where we stand; shall not know whether we are on our heads or our feet." Mr. Percival, when leader of the House of ( mons in 1807, declared that "he could not conceive'a or change of circumstances which would render further cessions to the Catholics .consistent with the safety of State." (Croker Papers 1. 12). Croker was a very man; but here is his forecast of the Reform Act of 1832: kings, no lords, no inequalities in the social system • all be levelled to the plane of the petty shopkeepers and, ea. farmers this, perhaps, not without bloodshed, but certal by confiscations and persecutions." There can be no lot any doubt that the Reform Bill is a stepping stone in Ent to a Repoblic, and in Ireland, to separation." Croker the Queen in 1832, considered her very good looking, thought it not unlikely that "she may live to be plain Guelph." Even Sir' Robert Peel wrote If lam ts believed, I foresee revolution as the consequence of Bill " ; and he "felt that it had ceased to be an objec ambition to any man of equable and consistent mind to el into the service of the Crown." IV.—There are a good many people who oppose IT, Rule because they hate the Irish; and not a few • we are mistaken, because they hate the radicals. have not been unknown in earlier periods of this tury's history. Whenever and wherever there has a question of " Reform" so surely has there sprui a section, greater or smaller according to circumsta of politicians of this genus. Whether it will in become extinct, we are not prepared to say, but if should ever come to pass, we fear it will only be in dun and distant future to which (to quote a favou expression of the" Times ") the lass " robust" of 1 party relegate the large and liberal measure of government for Ireland which they are weak ere to suggest. For the present they continue, and doubt in the future, will continue to raise their baselt fabrics of baleful vaticinations ' • and still decry a measures and movements radical,—as is their nature• We may pass them by, and with them, another close to be found amongst the less robust of their confreres. For among those who do not think, that this old sore, so often irritated and reopened, could be cured by send' ing over a regiment of soldiers and blowing the neople to pieces (a remedy not unfrequently recommended) there are a certain number of Conservatives v/h° object to this reform in the Government of Ireland, b; causeit is a yielding to democracy. Anything which ten to strengthen democracy and democratic govern_lnlevv.. they dislike. Perhaps they are not so important a Duz ' as once tHey were, but still a body not to be ignored generally to be• found amongst those who, having tlo'.- Well under existing circumstances, think that tho' circumstances, good enough for thentnlferentr Wa"l'Y others without considering how those others have really fared under them, and why they at times, So urgently demand a change. These forlunate ones are not inter- ested in the change, ,anci conceive themselves to be interested in opposing it. This; at least, we take to be their view, but must confess ourselves unable to follow,: always the process of reason (assuming the existence 01 such process) by , which a good many of he opponents referred to under this 4th heading, arrive at their con- clusions, . A SHEPHERD FOR FORTY YEARS. From The Chelmsford News. While on the subject we may mention the case of krs. Mary Ann Halls, of Wardley, Uppingham, whose husband has been a resident of Rutland County for over forty years. His calling is that of shepherd, and it is safe to say that no one is better known in all the country about Wardley than John Halls. In reciting the particulars of the case, we can do no better than use Mr. Halls' own statement made to our reporter. He says : "Por over eighteen years my wife was an intense suf- ferer from rheumatism. Much of the time her hands, elbows, knees, and feet were swollen, to two or three times their natural size, so that she was unable to walk or dress herself. She was in fact absolutely helpless. Tier joints became so stiff at times that she could not move them. During these periods she suffered the most intense agony, and in all these long years she was never entirely free from pain, either day or night. Different remedies were recommended to her, all of which Ole used, but got no relief, Our family doctor said that her case was incurable. ,We had given up all hope. She bad suffered so long that she had become thoroughly disheartened. Just before last Christmas we reap in a newspaper an article copied from the London 3 agpzine of Chemistry and Medicine, which gave parthodars of the wonderful cure, by St. Jacobs Oil, of Edward Evans, whose case was similar to my wife's. We concluded to try this remedy The Oil was first applied to her hands which had for many years been so fearfully deformed as to be almost Without shape. Before she had used the contents of one bottle, to our arriazement and joy the swelling dis- appeared, and her crippled hands once more assumed their natural shape. "She then applied the remedy to the joints of her limbs and feet, and marvellous as it may seem, the swelling and pain, which had withstood all treatment, began to disappear, and before the contents of this one bottle had been used, the swelling, stiffness, and pain with which she had been afflicted for nearly twenty years, vanished as if by magic. She recovered the full use of her limbs, hands, and feet. She can walk as well as ever she could in her life, attends to her householdtuties, and sleeps soundly at night, while for years she, had not known what it was to have a mood aig,lit's rest. She is free from pain and complerely eured, and all this was brought about by arsingle bottle of St. Jacobs Oil. I tell you frankly that I believe this remedy has no equal inthe world. It has brought com- fort and happiness to my home, and I advise everyone suffering from pain to try it. The 2s. 6d. I spent fora bottle was the best investment I ever made in my life." Mrs. Halls personally confirmed everything that her husband had said, and could scarcely say enough in praise of this remarkable agency which had rescued her from her sufferings.

_ FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN. Canctrrre, SUNIAY.—The details received of the battle fought at Tashkurgan between the Ameer's troops and tllose of Ishak Khan prove how perilously near the ' Ineer's general was to a disastrous defeat. The crown- nig suCC69B was almost entirely due to the deadly effect of the Martini rifle. The battle commenced on The 29th, when a division commanded by Abdullah Khan Go- vernor of Badakshan, was utterly routed by Ishak's general. Gholam flaidar, nothing daunted, then de- livered a determined attack on the enemy's main body, and after overcoming a desperate resistance, completely defeated them, with a loss of 1,600 killed, their artillery, baggage, and camp being captured. He then attacked and captured Mahomed Flosain's victorious division, and on the 30th occupied Mazer' Sherif, where Ishak's gene- ral, Mabomed Hosain, was brought in a prisoner. THE COLONIES AND THE MOTHER COUNTRY.
M

Addressing a large meeting at the end of last week tha Premier df Nev; South Wales, Sir Harry Parkes, said that the Ministry had succeeded in reducing the annual expenditure of government by £1,000,000, and their future policy would be to further remodel taxation in the direction of free trade. The Premier contended that, to be permanent the Imperial Constitution must be recast. In uniting the outlying colonies to the Mother Country England must present an object for love and loyalty, and for the young passion for national authority in Australia, which would be more attractive than any elsewhere to be found. THE STANLEY EXPEDITION.

Dr. Peters, who is promoting the new German expe- dition for the relief of Emin Pasha, has admitted in an interview that the German Government were not favourably disposed towards the enterprise. Dr. Peters attributed the murder of Major Barttelot to the ma- chinations of Tippo 'rib, and expressed the opinion that Stanley had been dead for-a considerable time. INCOME TAX IN FRANCE. MONMY NIGHT.—The new Income Tax Bill discussed at the Council of Ministers held to-day. Ina bill is absolutely independent of existing taxes, and It therefore bnrthens the ratepayers in a way unknown in England, seeing that the octroi and other phases of indirect taxation are in nowise modified. A distinction is, however, made between income resulting from labour and that derived from settled revenue, the first being taxed at the rate of i• per cent, and the second at 1 per cent. All annual incomes below 2,000 trance re- ; main untaxed, while false declarations will bring about an increase in the tax. The State, the communes, and • charitable institutions are exempt from the proposed tax, as also are ambassadors: but foreigners residing m France will be under the same obligations as French subjects. Even temporary residents will not be quite exempt, as they will be taxed in proportion to their stay MOVEMENTS OF RUSSIAN TROOPS. BERLIN, TORSDAY.—The Post to-day endeavours to allay apprehensions regarding the movements of Russian troops towards the Austro-German frontier, declaring the movellents referred to were announced by the Russian Government last spring. VIENNA, TIIRSDAY.—An article. on the movemonts ol Russians on the frontier is believed to be a warning to Public opinion.

div.head: LONDON MURDERS.
div.p: THE LONDON MURDERS.

A man was arrested near the Tower of London, on Tues- day, on suspicion of being concerned in the East End murders. His appearance tallied with the published de- scription. The inquest on the remains of a woman found in'a vault at the new police offices: Whitehall, was resumed on Monday, before Mr.. Troutbeek, coroner for West- rninster.—Geo. Grant, clerk of works, deposed that he was in the vault on the Friday preceding the Monday on which the remains were found. He save nothing then, but a few rags, which the men had used on the brickwork. --Mr. Jasper Waring. journalist, stated that he Visited the vaults on the /.7th init. witti Mr. angle. Witness had a small dog with him. The dog attracted attention to the mound of earth from which a portion of a leg was found.—Mr. William A nszle., journalist, corroborated the last witness, and said the limb was not more than five inches below the surface.—Dr. Bond, divisional police surgeon, said the leg had been skilfully severed, and he believed it belonged to the bony found in the same place previously. Death must have occurred seven or eight weeks ago.—Dr. Bibbed haying given corroborative evidence, the jury returned an open verdict—found dead. The inquest on the b 0,137 of ..Elizabeth Stride, who was murdered in Berner-street, was resumed on Tuesday, before Mr. Wynne Bai-ter, coroner for East Middlesex.— Inspector Reid said he had examined the books . of the Stepney and Poplar Sick Alsylum (Bromley), and found an entry of the death of John Thomas Stride, a carpenter, on 24th Oct., 1884.—Walter Stride, a police constable, deposed that he 110 seen the photograph of deceased, and reeognised it as that of the woman who married his uncle, John Thomas Stride, in, 1872 or 1873. Elizabeth Stokes VMS called,.and eaid her first husband's name was Watts. He was a wino merchant at Bath. Mrs. Malcolm was her sister, blit she had not seen her for years. She wanted to clear her character from her sister's state- usents.—The Coroner proceeded to sum up; dwelling on the fact that the ordinary motives of murder—revenge, jealousy, theft, and passion--appeared to be absent from the case; and that. the same skill had been ex- hibited in the way in which the victim had been en- trapped as in the other cases in the noighbourhood.—The jury returned a verdict of " Wilful murder against some Person or persons unknown."

SHOmING TRAGEDY IN MONTOOMERYSHIRIL—A tragic occurrence took place at a small farm called Rendre Mochtre, near Newtown, Montgomeryshire, on Tuesday ewning. The tenant of the farm, a man named Abraham Morris, with his son Edward, twenty-five Years of age, had been drinking together at a public- 'louse a short distance from their house. On their way home, abdut eleven o'clock, a quarrel arose between them, and on arriving at Hendre the son challenged the father to fight. The latter refused, whereupon the son said, "One of us must die," and immediately took up a loaded gun which stood near at hand, and, resting the toek on the groufid, with .the barrel pointing to his iflead, he pulled the trigger. A farm servant rushed orward, but it was too late to prevent the gun going Off. Death was instantane;ous.
