PAR,NELLISM AND CRIME.-OPENING
OF THE COIiMiSSION.

The business proper of the Special Commission appointed to inquire and report upon the charges and allegations made against certain members of the Irish Parliamentary party, in the case of the action by Mr. Hugh O'Donnell v. The 7imes, commenced in the Probate Court of the Royal Courts of Justice, at 11 a.m. on Monday, before Mr. Justice Hannen, Mr. Justice Day, and Mr. Justice Smith. Intense interest was manifested in the proceedings, as was evidenced by the strenuous efforts of the public to obtain tickets of admission. These tickets were, however, necessarily limited in number, in spite of the special accommodation provided. In fact, all the extra accommodation was practically taken up by those actually engaged in the Commission, and mem- bers of Parliament. As early as ten o'clock in the morning, those people fortunate enough to obtain the necessary permits were in waiting at the various en- trances; but no one was allowed admission until a quarter past the hour. The body of the court was mainly devoted to counsel engaged in the proceedings, and a large body of Pressmen, belonging both to London and the pre- vious. In the gallery were members of Parliament and others who had succeeded in making good their claims to be present. Amon.. those to arrive early were Mr. Justin Mc.Carthy, Mr'. Baumann, Dr. Robertson. Mr. J. Rowlands, Mr. T. D. Sullivan, and Mr. Arthur O'Connor —the last named of whom, in wig and gown, took his seat among the counsel. Mr. Michael Davitt was also present, and both he and Mr. Callan, ex-member for Louth, were armed with witness tickets. Sir Richard Webster, the leading counsel for The Times, and Sir Charles Russell, counsel for Mr. Parnell, entered the court almost simultaneously, shook hands, and took their seats. Mr. Parnell, in whom the chief interest in the case centres, arrived at five minutes to eleven. Sir Henry James, Mr. Murphy, Q.C., and other leading counsel on The Times' side; and Mr. Asquith, M.P., the second counsel for Mr. Parnell, also appeared at the same time, and took their seats. Sir Charles Russell and Mr. Asquith were also the leading counsel for other) members of the Irish party mentioned in The Times charges; and Mr. Lock- wood appeared on the same side. By the time the Judges took their seats the gallery was nearly filled with Irish members, who naturally seemed deeply interested in all that transpired. Sir Charles Russell, who was the first counsel to rise, made an application that Mr. William Redmond might be released from prison, so as to enable him to attend the inquiry. Sir James Hannen said a similar application was made on behalf of Mr. Dillon; and the Court granted it upon easy condition. Sir Richard Webster then commenced his opening speech for The Times. He said his clients were there to give their lordships the fullest information in theit power. They accepted at once the duty indicated at the previous sitting of proving as well as they could the charges which had been made. At the same time his clients were not the persons who had to inquire into the truth, the responsibility of *which rested with their lord- ships. But if The Times received any further information during the progress of the case they would feel it their duty to tender it to their lordships. Continuing, Sit Richard Webster said they were not there to inquire, into the rights or wrongs of Home Rule, but to inquire into specific allegations in the proceedings of O'Donnell v. Walter. Be should feel it his duty to show that the individuals referred to were directly, or by clear impli- cation, included in those named in the original charges first promulgated in the articles called u Parnellism and crime," which commenced on the 7th of March. 1887. These were a repetition of the charges made in 1882 and 1884. He would not say they were in possession of legal proof of every assertion made when the articles were written, because, they were made on infor- mation conimunicated, and from extracts from news- papers such as the Irish World, United Ireland, and Freeman's Journal. No notice was taken of the publica- tion of these articles until April, 1887, when The Times published a letter. Purporting to be signed by Mr. Par- nell, and dated 15th. May, 1882, and the circumstaices surrounding which ought to be examined by their lord- ships thoroughly. The writing of n. particularietter would not,however,enab le their lordships to judge the main proof of the allegations, which were directed, not against Mr. Parnell alone, but also againSt all his associates. His clients would allege that all the acts that were done were in furtherance of a coiscerted conspiracy, with definite objects, and that those objects could not be effected without the commission of crime. In other words, "Parnellism and Crime" was a correct paraphrase of the history, in three words, of what the organisation was. Mr. Parnell was the leader of this organisation, and was supported by men of great energ,v and ability. He dealt. at length with the objects of the Land League, which was started in 1879, under the presidency of Mr. Parnell, and read the names of ten gen- tlemen who were paid organisers of the Land League to stir up agitation among the tenantry, and who had no interest in land at all. He also remarked that the secretaries of the League were Messrs. Kettle, Davitt. and Brennand ; with Messrs. Biggar, O'Sullivan, and Patrick Egan, as treasurers. The effect of the agitation was that the landlords could not get their rents. In 1880 Mr. Parnell and Mr. Dillon went to organise the League in America, and in 1881 Mr. Egan proceeded to Paris, there to organise the League in greater safety than in Ireland. While there, he was visited by Mr. Parnell and others.. At this point the Court adjourned for luncheon. -

Upon the Court resuming, the Attorney-General put in a number of letters in reference to the presence of Mr. Parnell and Mr. Egan in Paris, and alluded to the connection of the Irish party with the United Ireland newsnaner. started in August. 1681. Mr. Parnelj being one of the principal shareholders. Passing ater the arrest of Mr. Parnell in October of the same year, the learned gentleman referred to the effect of the speeches delivered in Galway, Mayo, Clare, Kerry, and Cork, and said the ordinary relations between the authorities and those who lived in those counties were abscdutely uprooted.

div.head: SECOND DAY.
div.p: SECOND DAY.
The Commission resuinell its sittings at half-past ten on Tuesday morning.
The Attorney-Ge-neral at once appealed tor a day's delay in answering an affidavit, handed him on Monday, as to the "particulars." _

Mr. Lockwood said be did not appear for Mr. Biggar, who represented himself; and Mr. Biggar asked The Times counsel for a copy of the 'Teethes referring to him, as he was not in a position to get a verbatim report. The President said that Mr. Biggar should have the same facilities as the counsel for his colleagues. • The Attornev-OPneral said that, when possible, copies should be banded over to him. Sir Charles Russell said that as the reports of the speeches relied on by the Attorney-General were taken by constables, on Government instruction, it was neces- sary he should have full reports. and not extracts. The Attorney-General said that the speeches were obtained by the solictors for The Tithes in the ordinary way, and netlltrougl___l the Government. Sir Trecnarct webster sairequently reautnea ore on behalf of The 7'ime.4, and said he should later on deal with the "no rent" manifesto, which purported to be issued by Mr. Parnell, from Kilmainham, in 1881, and was signed by Mr. Parnell and others. He then pro- ceeded to deal with speeches delivered by the Irish members in the county of Kerry, in the same way as he yesterday dealt with Galway; first calling attention to a. speech made made by Mr. Parnell in May. 1880, at Beavemont. Mr. Parnell's remarks on that occasion were violent, and he said. that if the Legislature did not interfere to prevent people being evicted, the agitation must go on. This and other speeches were reported, and United Ireland and the Freeman's Journal spoke of murder and incendiarism as incidents in the warfare between the League and the landlords. The learned gentleman next alluded to speeches by Mr. Biggar and Mr. A. O'Connor at Castleisland, and to one made by Mr. T. Harrington at 13osna, one result of the last-named gentleman's speech being. that a tenant alluded to had his house burnt. Then Mr. Flarrington was on the plat- form at Barradough, when a Mr. Boyton advised the tenants to put an end to landlords. In fact, the Land I,eague, of which Mr. Parnell was the head, was power- less without tyranny and intimidation. The Attorney - General then dealt with a number of speeches delivered in Cork—a county in which many 'steeple bravely resisted the orders of theaLeague. After quoting from numerous speeches, the Attorney-General said he should, at a later sage, call their lordships' attention to ether speeches delivered in 1885 and 1888, under the auspices of the National League, which was the direct successor of the Land League—having the same objects and the same sources of income; and, in this case also, the same re- sults 'followed the delivery of League speeches. Indeed, no Parnellite member had ever suggested that there was any difference between the two organisations. He had in this county to report a large number of outrages—some of them fatal. In one case the wrong man was killed; in another a man had his right ear cut with scissors, because he had paid his rent; a man, named Leary, was shot for giving information to the police; and a" land grabber" was shot through the right thigh, after a meeting at which land grabbers were denounced. It would be his duty to lay before the Commission many other speeches, and many subsequent outrages, but now he would pass to the last of the counties he intended to deal with, viz., the county of Clare. At a meeting at Ennis, Mr. Parnell told his hearers that farmers could do no good by attending to give evidence before a Land Commission, and he sueeested that men who took evicted farms should be sent to "moral Coventry." and isolated as the leers of old ; and the only inference the court could draw from that advice was that any steps were to be taken which were necessary to compel land grabbers to give up the farms. Other speeches, similar in tone, and often more violent, were delivered. What was the result? From January to July, 1882, there were six murders and 12 attempts at assassination; from January, 1882, to November, 1883, there were six attempts at assassination. There were also numerous cases of boycotting, and of houses being fired into.
' THIRD DAY. On Wednesday, the proceedings of the Parnell Com- mission yielded little excitement. Sir Charles Russell,

div.head: -EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888. GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: THE -EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888. GENERAL NEWS.

soon after their Lordships entered, applied for the dis- closure of important documents. He read an affidavit from Mr. Lewis, in which it was alleged that the " Times " were in possession of original letters written by Mr. Parnell. Mr. Dillon, and other members of Parlia- ment. The "Times," it was stated, had a bundle of documents in a box which they had obtained since the O'Donnell action, and it was necessary for the purposes of the inquiry that copies of them should be furnished to the defendants. Sir Charles also read extracts from the affidavit of Mr. Soames, the solicitor for the "Times," in which it was asserted that certain documents received from America were not genuine and for the purposes of the inquiry were worthless. He said he should call Captain O'Shea to show that Mr. Parnell was intimately connected with Sheridan, Boyton, and Egan while outrages were going on, and that he signed tke manifesto after the Phoenix Park murders against his will. He did not accuse Mr. Parnell of active complicity with crime, but said the Irish leader had certainly made speeches the direct outcome of 'which was crime. Counsel produced the original manuscript of the letter attributed to Mr. Parnell dated May 15, 1882, in which Lord Frederick Cavendish's,peath is spoken of as an accident. It was decided that the letter should be photographed. The Attorney General. went on to maintain that Mr. Parnell had been closely associ- ated with Frank Byrne and had countenanced outrage, and said he should prove beyond doubt that concurr- ently with the strength of the Land League organisation crime was found to exist, and that without the organis- ation and the speeches there would be no such'crime. FOURTH DAY. On Thursday the fourth day's proceedings were rather more interesting than in the earlier stages of the Attorney General's opening statement. There was al skirmish between counsel, and towards the end of thei sitting a gleam of humour—in fact, it may be said that the Court rose in a broad grin at the remembrance of Sir Richard Webster's quotations from Dr. Tanner's speeches. The Attorney General had altogether a trying day. Though he endeavoured to infuse some enthusiasm into his interminable speech, he was scarcely successful in concealing his own weariness; aad Mr. Michael Davitt .greatly disturbed Sir Richard's imperturbability by quietly pointing out his errors, and raising a laugh against the Times counsel by showing that he could not have been in Paris at the time the Attorney General averred, inasmuch as he was in Portland prison. The Attor- ney General resumed his speech with a refer- ence to the connection between the persons charged in the particulars and the American Nationalists. He said the Land League was a conspiracy plotted and carried out by means of American money, and -that Mr. Michael Davitt was• the link by which the American dynamitards were paid. The whole connection of Mr. Parnell and his party with conspirators in America, he affirmed, proved the allegations in " Parnellism and Crime." He traced Mr. Davitt's action from the time he was introduced to Ford in America to the formation of the Land League, saying, however, that the programme of the League came from the American section, and not in any way from the Nationalists on this side of the Atlantic. Mr. Parnell did not, he said, really wish to be pushed forward in movement which at last, landed the Nationalist party in a "slough of despond." A special correspondent states that Sir Richard's speech will ,soon conclude that Sir Charles Russell will then raise important objections, and that the Times witnesses are not likely to be called before Tuesday.

At the Old Bailey, on Monday, Alf. Milligan, 25, letter sorter, was sentenced to six years' penal servitude for stealing letters containing money. William Russell, whp accused himself. at Maidenhead, of murdering a woman in London, has been committed for trial. The doctors think be is not responsible for his actions. . . .

Pomona Palace, Manchester, which has been the scene of many great political gatherings, has been demolished to make way for a portion of the Ship Canal under- taking. Stamm DBATH OF A FOOTBALL PLAYEEL-011 Satur- day afternoon, during the progress of a match between the second teams of the Ardwick and Levenshulme Football Clubs, a young player named Spearmint, a member of the Ardwick team, was seized with a fit, and died before medical assistance could be procured. A lad of sixteen, named Chadwick, has been charged at Daleton, London, with stabbing his father. The pri- soner having used abusive and threatening language towards his father, the latter took up a poker, where- upon his son stabbed him in the arm, exclaiming, "You will have it in your heart next time." The prisoner was remanded.

SIR MORELL MACKENZIE'S LIBELLERS.—Sit Morel! Mackenzie's solicitors have by letter warned a firm of Liverpool publishers of the fact that they have received instructions to institute proceedings for libel and claim damages against any publishers or persons who sell or circulate a copy of the pamphlet issued by the German doctors upon the illness of bite late Emperor Frederick.

There vras an exciting scene id the aty (London) on Monday morning, when a man suddenly rose from his seat on the top of an omnibus and shouted out at the top of his voice that he was a murderer, but the police should not take him; and then jumped into the street. Re retained his feet on reaching the ground, and was at once given into custody. Inquiries proved that be was a vianderbag lunatic. -

A sad accident occurred at the Bolton Goods Station of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Co., on Satur- day, by which a checker, named F. Simister, aged 60, lost his life. ' Be was walking down the line, with the object of checking some waggons, when he was knocked down by a heavy goods train, which was being shunted, and was run over. ,His bbdy was terribly mangled, and death was instantaneous. -

The London police are investigating a robbery of precitillis stones from a diamond merchant in Hatton-garden, the value of the missing property 'being about £6,000 or £7OOO. A warrant was yesterday issued by the Clerkenwell magistrate against Michael Eisenberg, a Roumanian. He opened an office about two months ago, and, by means of letters of introduc- tion, obtained, it is said, precious stones to the amount named, ostensibly to show customers. He then dis- appeared. DESTRUCTIVE MILL FIRE IN YORKSHIRE : DAMAOF £lo,ooo,—On Monday, a fire broke out at Field Mill, Ossett, belonging to Mr. Abraham Pollard, woollen manufac- turer,.while the people were on the premises. An alarm was at once raised, and several fire brigades attended; but, despite their strenuous efforts, the mill was gutted. The roof fell in an hour after the fire was discovered. The damage is estimated at over £lO,OOO, none of which, it is stated, is covered by insurance. The mill was only purchased by Mr. Pollard three months ago.

A Frmatir "JACK TR;K RIFPER."—EXTRAORDINARI FRE.AK.—The Bradford police, on Saturday, apprehended a young woman named Maria Coroner, on the charge of sending letters signed "Jack the Ripper" to the local press and the Chief Constable. The girl is good looking, respectably dressed, and in regular work at one of the leading drapery establishments in Bradford. Several written references to Jackson, the Manchester murderer, and the card of Berry, the hangman, carefully wrapped in silk paper, were found in her possession. She was remanded on the charge of inciting to a breach of the peace. SUICIDE OF A 13ELITISE NAVAL OFFICER.—A letter from the North American squadron records a sad event on board H.M.S. Emerald. While at Hall's Bay, on the 24th September, First Lieutenant Sidney Barnes Thompson committed suicide by blowing his brains out with a rifle. tie had suffered from melancholia, but none of his mess- mates feared such a tragic ending. An inquiry was held at Twillingate, Newfoundland, by a magistrate, and a verdict of suicide while temporarily insane was returned. Deceased aartntried in the Church of England cemetery, the body being followed to the grave byCaptain Hamond and the ship's Company. For the first time in the annals of the London Uni- versity College,'s lady is putting up as candidate for a nrofbssorial chair. The Chair of Archeology, vacant by the retirement of Sir Charles .Newton, will be contested by Miss Jane Harrison, whose lectures in Greek art have won for her a high place among the lecturers of the day. This lady, a gradua‘e of Newnham College, is recognised by scholars as holding an almost unique place among them for her knowledge especially of the popular form of Greek art expressed on vase paintings. 'She has been several times in Greece, where every sort of honour has been paid to her by the King, by professors, and by officials. A TERRIBLE RAILWAY Rrns..—On the antral of a Mid- land London express at Bradford, on Monday night, the .-lothes of a woman were noticed dangling on the guard's van. Examination disclosed a woman, seriously injured, and it was elicited that she had ridden in this manner from Frizinghall—over two miles outside Bradford,—at which station she had, in a fog, stepped off the platform on to the line. The driver of' the engine stated that he ;lid not slacken speed in the smallest degree in passing through this station; and it is evident that having fallen on the line, the woman's clothes were caught by he depending fittings of the van, and she was carried on. When the poor woman was found her feet were touching the ground, and they had evidently dragged the greater part of the distance. Strange to say she recovering from her injuries. - - -

SNORT 'ENTENCES A; DETERRENTS TO CRIME.—MT. C H. Hopwood, Q.C., Recorder of LiVerpool, in charging the Grand Jury at the opening of the City Sessions, on Monday, referred at some length to the question of short sentences, in reference to which he has been the subject recently of considerable public criticism. He defended the principle of short sentences for trivial offences, and said that since he had been appointed to the recorder- ship, the records of the court showed a steady decrease of crime. He quoted the opinions of the Lord Chief Justice and Mr. Justice Matthew in favour of short sen- tences, and of the importance of helping prisoners, after they were discharged, to get back into honest courses, and expressed the hope that all thoughtful and philan- thropic men in the country would give him their support MURDER IN MANCRESTER.—A murder was committed at Pendlebury on Saturday night. Pendlebtn:y is a coi,- liery district, and on Saturday a number of miners went ;tithe Albion Inn. At eleven o'clock they were turned out. ' Among them were two colliers named Samuel Tudor and William Montague Lernm, who got into a quarrel about card playing and pigeon flying. Accord- ing to the police report, fiador was heard to call Lemm a "red thief," and was seen to strike the man twice. Lemm struck back, and the men fell to the ground, but after walking two or three yards Tudor staggered, fell on his back, and never spoke again. Dr. Herbert, of Fondlenury, was sent for, and in the meantime Tudor was conveyed to his own house. When the doctor arrived be pronounced the man dead, but declined to say the exact cause of death till after the post mortem. Lemm has been apprehended on a charge of murder. ARREST OF A SUSPECTED BUROLAR.—At the Liverpool County Magistrates' Court, on Monday, John Foster, a jobbing watchmaker, was charged with having, on the 13th September, broken into the dwelling-house of Mr. Arthur Cross, Crosby, near Liverpool, and stolen £.5 and a quantity of jewelry. After the burglary no clue was obtained until the 11th instant, when the prisoner was • arrested in Belfast on suspicion of being "Jack the Ripper," and of being concerned in the being murders. After a remand on that charge, no evidence was found against him, and he was discharged; but as the result of inquiries he was handed over to the Crosby police. Several articles of jewelry and abont 0.9 in money were found upon him, amongst the jewelry being a locket bearing the initials of Mrs. Cress. He now stated that lie picked up the jewelry on the shore at Southport, and that he could satisfactorily account for the posses- sion of the money. He was remanded.

DISASTROUS FIRE us LONDON.—A DOZEN BUILDINGS AT- TACICED.—A warehouse, occupied by Mn J. Harvey, office-fitter, Red Cross-street, London, took fire on Tuesday, and the flames spread so rapidly that ten steam fire engines were urgently summoned. The buildings, 40 yards long, speedily became involved, and surrounding property was threatened. Two buildings in Wiiitecross-streetmccupied hyn wire manufacturer and a dairyman respectively, were gutted, and nearly a dozen other buildings were attacked, including a number of tenements in Herring-court. the occupants of which had to retreat hurriedly, with their effects. After two hours hard work,. the flames were checked. Mr. Harvey's workshops were burnt out, and partly fell, and the buildings used as offices were badly damaged. • The two buildings before named were gutted, and twelve other houses and shops partially destroyed. The amount of the loss is unknown, but most of the property was insured,

SENSATIONAL LEAP FRODI THE CLOODS.—On Satur- day, many thousands of spectators assembled at the Alexandra Palace, London, to witness the closing performances of some of the principal attractions which have ensured such success for this place of amusement during the season. Shortly after half-past four o'clock Professor Baldwin ascended from the North Park with nig new balloon, the " Alexandra," after informing the unrnense concourse of Spectators that this was the last of his series of performances at the Palace for this year, and that he was going to try to 'reach the highest alti- tude ever yet attained by a mirach attn." The balloon rapidly rose high in the air, travelling in a north'-westerly direction, and when at an altitude of 8,800 ft., as registered by his pocket aneroid 'barometer, Baldwin dropped away from the balloon with his parachute, which slowly but surely became fully inflated, and he safely descended, landing at a spot two or three miles away from the palade in the neighbourhood of FinchleV. Subsequently he appeared before a vast audience in the central hall, and gave an account of his parachute ex. periences. or all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley and Wright a cotton is the best.—ittivr.
IRELA,'.\ D.
The Parnell indemnity fund exceeds £lO,OOO. The Land Sub-Commissioners have reduced rents in South Tippemry by about 30 per cent.

_ Lord Dufferin is expected in Dublin next week, and will, it is hoped, preside at the conferring of the degrees in the Royal University of Ireland, of which he is Chan- cellor. A fatal wager was reported from Newry on Monday. A man named Neill, who had been drinking, accepted a wager in a public-house that he could not drink a half- pint of whisky off. He won, and then went home and slept. He died in his sleep.

Ellen Shirin, 30, was brought to Mercer's Hospital, Dublin, on Sunday morning, suffering from wounds in the head and a fractured skulL A hatchet, stained with blood, was found beside her on the floor of her house ift Bishop-street. She is not expected to recover. Her husband and his brother have been arrested.

It is proposed to hold an International Exhibition in Dublin in 1890. A deputation representing an influen- tial body of manufacturers and employers waited upon the Lord Mayor on Saturday to obtain his advice and assistance, and it was arranged to hold a meeting for the purpose of discussing the scheme broadly, and ascer- taining what proportions a guarantee fund might be ex- pected to reach. Count Moore, who owns a fine estate at Mooreefort, Tipperary, and who formerly sat for Tipperary in Par- liament as a Home Ruler, is about to quit Ireland and take up his residence permanently abroad. The Count, who is greatly irritated at the action taken by some of his tenants, is reported to entertain the idea of turning his estate into a bullock run for the supply of cattle to the London market.

At the Queen's County Quarter Sessions, on Saturday. Lord Lansdowne obtained ejectment decrees against 40 of his Luggacurran tenants. From two to four years' rents were Claimed to March 25th last. Judge Demolyns said it was the saddest spectacle he had been caned upon to witness, and remarked on the fact that not one of the tenants appeared to claim the benefits which the Act of 1887 allowed County Court judges to exercise. The trial of Robert Dunlop and James Speers Orr, on charges of conspiracy and fraud in connection with the Equitable Insurance Company, concluded at Wicklow Assizes on Saturday. Both prisoners were found guilty on the charge relating to the issue of the policy on the life of Joseph Wilson upon a fraudulent misrepresenta- tion. Dunlop was sentenced to nine months' and Orr to six months' hard labour. There are other cases to be tried against several prisoners in connection with the frauds.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SITURDAY.—Before Alderman ..Burgess and Mr. R. Garnett.

--Ditrmt.—Patrick Moore was finellOs. and costs for having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on the previous evening. "JACK THE RrPPEn."—Ambrose Foden, labourer, Fillings- court, was brought up on warrant charged with having assaulted his wife on the 18th.—Domplainant said her hus- band on that day mune home drunk, and made a great noise, calling out that he was "Jack the Ripper," He attempted to put out the fire with a tub of water and finally ended by assaulting her violently. Prisoner was ordered to find two sureties of £5, and to be bound over himself In £lO, to keen the peace for six months. MONna.V.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alderman Harrison, and Councillors John Pierpoint and Greening. DRUNKENNESS.—The following fines were imposed for drunkenness :—John Mullen, ss. and costs; Mary Ann Fudge, be. and costs ; Mary Ana Tarpley. 10s. and costs; John Hoban (90th appearance) 58. and costs ; Mary McLough- lin, be. and coats; Daniel O'Loughlin, ss. and costs; James Briers, 55. OnsTnuerrokr.—William Jackson, carter, was fined 10s. and costs for having obstructed Buttermarket-street, by allowing a horse and cart to stand there an unreasonable time, and also for having allowed offensive matter to run therefrom. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.— Michael 0' Shaugnessv, 18 Dial-street, was fined Is. for this offence against the bye-laws. FIREWORKS IN THE STREET.—Thomas bakin, Joseph Day, and Joseph Whittaker, lads, for having set off fireworks in Greenall-street, on the night of the 15th inst., were fined 3s. each. _ _

UNREGISTERED LODGING HOUSE.—David Jones, Knutsford- rd., was fined 2s. 6d., including costs, for keeping lodgers without having his house registered. ASSAULTING A LA.NDLADT.—Annie Quinn, wife of Thomas Quinn, tanner's labourer, 3 Hill-st., was chargied with having assaulted Zilpah Darbyshlre. wife Of the landlord of the Boar's Headbeerheuse, Town Hill, on Saturday, an(d alsowith having stolen a small basket of the value of 2s. 6d. Prisoner committed the assault in the beerhouse, and snatching the basket, took it outside and kicked it to pieces. For the assault she was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment HI default. The charge of theft was dismissed. CRUELTY CASE.—Lawrenee Baldwin was summoned for having worked a pony that was not in a fit state for working, and Nancy Hill, the owner, was summoned for having caused it to be so worked. The case-was dismissed.

Assl.l7LT.—Thomas Clynes was charged with having assaulted Margaret Boyle, of Dial-st., an elderly woman, and he was fined 20s. and costs, or in default of payment, im- prisonment for one month, with hard labour, TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Francomb and Mr. E. J. Guest. DRUNKENNESS...I9'Or this offence the following were fined the amounts stated ;—William Bamford, ss. including costs; John Maddon, ss. and costs ; Michael McNicoll, be. and costs; John Welsh, ss. and costs. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.—Ames Hansbury was charged with having been drunk on the licensed premises of John Marsh, Scotland-road, with refusing to quit the same, and with having been drunk in Horsemarket-street, on the evening before. It was proved that the prisoner went into the house the "Theatre " Tavern, and made a disturbance, so that he had to be rather roughly handred. Prisoner was ordered to pay 20s. and costs, or in dgfault go to prison for a month. ' . _ .

WRANGLE.—Charlatte Plunkett was charged on warrant with baying assaulted Alice Dolfier, on the 20th inst. It was shown that the women had a quarrel, which ended in the assault complained of. Defendant was fined ss, including costs, or in default seven days. WEDNESDAY,—Before Messrs. J. Patrelough, R. Garnett; and Alderman Chandley. DRITNTARTESS.—Ann Mullen was fined 5e., including costs, for this offence.,

BEGGING.—Thomas Cunningham, for asking alms in Wilderspool-road, the same morning, was sent ti prison for a fortnight. WIFE NEGLEGT.—John Ford, carter, was eommitted to prison for thirty days, with hard labour, for having disobeyed an order of the magistrates calling upon him to pay 26. 6d. a week towards the maintenance of his wife, from whom he Is separated. The arrears amounted to £1 7s. 6d. Mr. Hides' appeared for the complainant. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton and Councillor Greening. A DESEETER.—Thomas Gilbert, last from Liverpool, was charged with being a deserter from H.M. Connaught Rangers, stationed at Portsmouth. He was remanded to Walton Prison to await escort.
FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall.
MAINI'MNANCE ORDER.—Michael Coffey was ordered to pay is. a week towards the maintenance of his son in an Indus- trial School at Liverpool. . .
LIt—UNICENNESS.—Mary Ann McClew, Preston, was brought up for this offence, and was discharged on promising to leave the town.

AN ABSCONDER.—TiIomas Nally, who admitted having absconded from the St. George's Industrial Scilly', Liverpool, was ordered to be handed over to the School authorities. NEGLECT or WORK.—Mary Ireland, 7, Edward-st., an apprentice to Ellen Oakes, fustian-cutter, 101 Orford-lane, was summoned for disobeying an order of the magistrates requiring her to fulfil her contract. Defendant attributed her absence from work to illness, and handed in a medical certifi- cate in support of her statement. The case was, adjourned for two months en the defendant undertaking to return to her ezi,ployment.
, RUNCORN POLICE COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hule. hurst. _

DRUNK AND DISORDEILLY.—Jaraes Hayes and Peter Carter, 'were each fined 108. and costs 7s. 4d. tor being drunk and disorderly on the previous night.—Samh Alice Clark. and Elizabeth Barker, women of bad character, were charged with being guilty of riotous behaviour, in Church-st. on the previous afternoon. Clark was sentenced to a month and Barker to a fortnight's hard labour.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT PRESTON ]ROOK. On Saturday afternoon there was a shocking occurrence at the railway station at Preston Brook. A timber merchant named Thomas Wood, who was 76 years of age, and who was in business at Burs- lem. Staffordshire, had during the afternoon been round the Norton estate, belonging to Sir Richard Brook, in company with one of the woodmen, inspecting timber with a view to making a pur- chase. At about five o'clock he returned to the station, for the purpose of proceeding home by rail. He had obtained his ticket at the booking-office, and as he had a few minutes to spare he was passing them in the waiting-room. Whilst there he heard a train approaching the station, and, thinking it was the one by which he had to travel he ran along the level cross- ing to get to the other platform, but when only part war across an express camerushing by, and he was caught on the buffers of the engine and carried nearly 80 yards along the line, his body being literally cut to pieces. The coroner, Mr. J. E. Worsley, held an inquest regarding the death at the Red Lion Hotel, Pres on Brook, on Tuesday. Mr. Charles Ferrand was present to watch the proceedings on behalf of the London and North- Western Railway Company. Evidence of identification having given by Ralph Bloor, a nephew of the deceased, John Pekeman, woodman of the Norton estate, deposed that he was in company with the deceased on Saturday afternoon. They reached the station shortly after five o'clock, and he saw the deceased get his ticket. Hearing a train coming deceased ran out from the waiting-room across the platform, and on to the level crossing.—Arthur Webb (12), said that at about half- past five on Saturday afternoon he was at Preston Brook station, and saw the deceased attempt to cross the line. Befcre he reached the other side a train came up, and he was carried along for Eome distance in front of the engine. It was getting dark at that time.—P.C. Jenkins/ deposed that he received information of the accident very shortly after it had occurred. He found ' the remains of the deceased about 80 yards from the Ilevel crossing. The legs had been cutoff; both hands land one arm had been severed; and the bowels 'were protruding. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, writing with reference to a statement made at Birmingham Liberal meeting that he had refused to drink the Queen's health, says Allow me at once to nail this lie to the counter. There is abso- lutely not the slightest foundation for it so far as I am concerned. I have never refused to drink the Queen's health, or to stand when it was proposed, and should re- gard Such a refusal as an act of stupid discourtesy." Great preparations are being made by the Black Country Liberals for Mr. Gladstone's drive from Bir- mingham to Wolverhampton. now definitely fixed tor November Bth. Mr. Gladstone will be accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone. and demonstrations and addresses are expected nearly all along the route. The population a the district numbers half a million, and the bulk of these are Gladstonian Liberals. The reception of this mass of toilers is likely to be one of the most enthusiastic and unanimous that has ever taken place in South Stafford- shire.

div.head: PARNELL v. THE TIMES.
div.p: PARNELL v. THE TIMES.

In Edinburgh Court of Session. onTuesday, the action by Mr. Parnell against The Times was brought before Lord Kinnear for final adjustment of the record. After hearing Mr. Strachan, for the plaintiff, and Mr. Graham Murray, for the defendants, his lordship adjourned the further hearing of the case till Saturday, in order that the plaintiff might afford the defendants some necessary information.

div.head: MR. lIORLEY IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: MR. lIORLEY IN SCOTLAND.

A great Liberal demonstration was held in the County Hall, Perth, on Monday, the chief speaker being Mr. John Morley. Sir John G. S. Kinloch,, Bart., presided. Mr. Morley was presented with about fifty addresses from the Liberal Associations of Perthshire, Forfarshire, Fife- shire, and Stirlingshire. , Mr. Montar haying acknowledged the warmth of his reception, and spoken of his loyalty to their prand Old Chief. declared that the Liberal party was never better disciplined, more full of vigour. and under better self- command than now. He ridiculed the declaration of the Liberal Unionists that Seotland was only waiting for a chance to follow the example of Ireland in launching a policy of violence, robbery, and confiscation. He declared the Liberal Unionists to be a party of fear; and said that if he were a Conservative he would say, in the interests of the most Jaw-abiding Scotchmen, settle this Irish question. He criticised Lord Hartington's declarations and policy, and expressed an opinion that the Liberal Unionist leaders had gone back from their former proposals, and they were not in agreenient as to what should be done in respect of Ireland. A de- fensive contest was Lord Hartington's phrase for the position in which he and his friends declined to move one step out of the policy of pure coercion and mere repression. The Irish drainage proposals of the Govern- ment, would lead to a waste of British money, RS Mr. Parnell had warned them they would. Mr. Morley de- clared that as long a.s they had nothing to offer Ireland, and nothing to show Irishmen but the gaunt, grizzly, haggard figure of coercion, there was no chance of awakening the better mind of the country and of help- ing in its regeneration. TO present system would last until there was a general election, but no longer. He also insisted upon the claim of Scotland to manage her own affairs, seeing that the business was.not now satis- factorily dealt with by Parliament.

div.head: LORD GRANVILLE IN LIVERPOOL.
div.p: LORD GRANVILLE IN LIVERPOOL.

. lEarl Granville was on Saturday evening entertained at, a grand banquet by the Liverpool Reform Club, in their premises, Dale-street. Nearly 20Cl gentlemen were present. In reply to the toast of his health (proposed by the chairman, Mr. R. D. Holt), Earl GRANVILLE spoke briefly on the leading points of the Irish question as they seemed to exist at the present moment.. . As to the oft-repeated assertion that her Majesty's Government had an Irish policy, he said he should like to be authoritatively informed whether the policy of the Government was that of Sir Michael Hicks- Beach or that of Mr. Balfour; whether it was that of Lord Hartington or that of Mr. Chamberlain; whether it was that of the Newport speech of Lord Salisbury or that of his subsequent declaration of twenty years of resolute government. It was not be- pand the range of possibility that the Conservatives might offer a Home Rule Bill. Mr. Glads:.one happened to be the only statesman who up to the present time had brought in a well-defined bill, with clauses and pro- visions which should solve half the difficulty whenever the Home Rule question was brought up again. They had backed Home Rule against coercion, because coer- cion was one of the hideous examples of the rotten system which now existed, and their real determination was to obtain for the Irish people the adoption of the old Liberal principle that we could not govern a free people against their own will. . - Lord Honnovsn, in responding for the House of Lords, said he felt certain that if they bad in the House of Lords more men like the noble guest of that evening, they would have little to fear with regard to the Liberal party. In a very importaat department of their national affairs the House of Lords had shown very Radical tea- Jencies, and had shown a disposition to disturb its very foundation. The three chief coiner stones on which the great fabric of their land laws had rested for centuries were the law of primogeniture, the law of entail, and the law of aubinfeudation These three principles had never been touched till last year, and they had woven themselves into the very :•issue of their arrangements respecting land and pro- perty. These effects had not been fitted to the latter history of English society, and had produced mischief. He believed that if the bills passed into law they would prove beneficial to society. He feared that the gulf which separated the House from other classes of society was not narrowing, but increasing. Public discussion was tending more and more upon social questions, and he was not very sanguine of the future of the House of Lords. _ _

Mr. RALPH NEVILLE, responding for the House of Commons, said that if , in confidence placed at present by our countrymen n their representatives was to be maintained, we must, with all our efforts and at all hazards, maintain the pribciples which had guided our assembly and our representatives throughout the history of our country. Mr. T. P. O'Cowicon, M.P., also responded for the House of Commons; and the remaining toasts included "The Press," acknowledged by Mr. A. Ireland and Mr. E. Russell; and "The Health of the Chairman" (Mr. Holt), submitted by Lord Granville.

RAILWAY Accmarr.—Two light engines ran into a coal train at North End, Erith, on the South-Eastern Railway, on Thursday morning, owing to the signals being mis- taken. The rear part of the coal tram was wrecked, the guard's van being smashed and wedged firmly on the top of the foremost engine. Fortunately the guard was not in the brake or he must have been killed. The engine drivers were a good deal shaken, but were not otherwise injured. The damage to rolling stock is con: siderable.

div.head: ANOTHER MOONLIGHTING OUTRAGE.
div.p: ANOTHER MOONLIGHTING OUTRAGE.

On Sunday night a party of armed moonlighters attacked the house of a man named Farrell, who has been for some time in charge of a boycotted farm be- longing to Mr. Geoghegan, of Athenry. Several shots were fired into the house, and one struck Farrell, inflict- ing a dangerous wound in the thigh. The police have been investigating the outrage, but no arrest has yet been made. THE MURDER OF AN EX-CONSTABLE.

Dominick Long, a farmer, has been arrested and charged with being concerned in the murder of ex-Con- stable John Bruen, at Sooty, co. Sligo, on Saturday night, and the police are in pursuit of another suspected man. It appears that the crime arose out of a dispute, in which Bruen was charged with being a police spy. James Mc.Loug,iiiin was arrested at Londonderry, yesterday, on a charge of causing the death of ex-Con- stable Bruce, in county Sligo. The prisoner, who was en route for Chicago, admits he is the person wanted, but denies being guilty of the crime. THE ILL-TREATMENT OF MR. MANDEVILLE. . _ _ . .

Mr. William O'Brien writes pledging himself, in reply to Mr. Balfour, to substantiate every statement he has made in reference to Mr. Mandeville's case, with the ex- ception that he finds that the prisoner had a quilt as well as a sheet. As to Mr. Balfour's contention that the stripping of Mr. Mandeville was done without violence, Mr. O'Brien asks how a powerful man attacked in his bed, could be deprived of every shred of clothing "without violence?" The present question is not whether he was right or wrong, but whether, in matter of fact, he was stripped to the akin, and left to march up and down his cell in the depth of winter, with his arms and legs bare, and with nothing but a quilt and sheet thrown round him. This fact is established by Dr. Moore and Chief Warder Bartley; and the rest is, therefore, shabby quibbling. As to the question of evic- tions, Mr. O'Brien says Mr. Wyndham falsified his statement. He (Mr. O'Brien) did not say that tens of thousands of poor Irish families are now lying under sentence of eviction; but that there would be ten thousand evictions this winter. In reply to Mr. Wynd- ham's charge of exaggeration, Mr. O'Brien accepts his statement that there were only 3,270 eviction notices served during the Tune quarter, and says .the game thing is true of previous quarters since the passing of the Act of 1887; so that if notices have been accumu- lating at the rate of 3,000 per quarter, his own estimate of 10,000 unexpired notices was under the mark. As to whether my. Balfour treated Mr. Mandeville'4 fate with levity, and'his character with brutality, the public could judge from his words, and the laughter of his audience.
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

div.head: CONCERT .AT THE PUBLIC HALL,
div.p: CONCERT .AT THE PUBLIC HALL,
WARRINGTON.

Mr. H. T. Bywater, in Conjunction with Mr. H. 11. Pearson, gave a concert in the Public Hall, Warring- ton, on Wednesday evening, of an especially high- class character. The patrons were Messrs. T. Sutton (the Mayor), F. Monks, J. C. Parr, It. Francomb, and IP. Stubs' and there was a large and fashionable audience. The artistes were: —(soprano) Miss , Annie Marriott, (contralto) Madame Patey, (tenor) Mr. Sidney Tower, (bass) Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, (violin) Herr Poznanski, (violoncello) Mr. Edward Howell, and (pianoforte) Mr. Vv. Cook. Madame Patey was, of course, the "bright, particular star of the evening, and it is gratifying to be able to say that slie shines, if anything, with increased brilliance. She met with an enthusiastic recep- tion on her appearance, and the, enthusiasm was heightened during the evening, as the audience listened to her various songs: Her first contribu- tion was Handel's " Ombra mai fu," which enabled her to show to advantage her magnificent voice. Later on she gave "Our dear old home" in a very effective manner, and on being recalled she sub- stituted "Allan water." This favourite ballad was rendered by her with tenderness and power, and with fine dramatic effect. Watson's ballad of" The Quaker's daughter " was in an altogether different vein, but the humour of it was presented with so much piquancy and delicacy that it quite took the audience by storm. An encore being inevitable, Madame Patey next sang "Needles and pins," in a style which was irresistible in its vocalisation and refinkl comedy. Madame Patey, it should be added, also joined in the Spinning Quartet from " Marta," along with Mr. Tower, Mr. Pierpoint, and Miss Marriott. It lb. an admirable selection, and went so well as to necessitate repetition ; it would have been simply perfect if the English version had been sung. Miss Annie Marriott made an excellent impression as soprano. She has a voice of great sweetness and power' which she manages with no little skill, but the songs allotted ta her were none of them of a charac- ter to carry away an audience. Her, contribu- tions were—aria, "Roberto, o tu che adoro." song, "The Angel's message," and song, "Dear heart." It was explained that the tenor, lib% Sydney Tower, was suffering from a cold, but it was a pleasure, to find that it did not seriously interfere with his voice, which is of high quality, and great range. He sang "The Distant Shore," by Sullivan, "So like a dream," and the ever green "The Pilgrim of Love." He also joined Mr. Pierpoint in Safe's "Excelsior," but success with this duet was of a qualified kind. Mr. Bantock Pierpoint first appeared in Handel's "Revenge! Timotheus curs," which he sang with rousing. effect, his splendid voice doing justice to the noble music. Hewes no less successful, it should be added, in Blumenthal's song "Thy foe " ; but he look some liberties with "The heart bowed down," and cannot be said to have improved upon the original composer. Herr Poznanski showed himself to be a thorough master of the violin inthe solos that were entrusted to him—"Ungarischer," by Raft ; _ . .

and " Bohenuenne, by VieuxteTrips. His a'rpeggiO execution, after a recall, was something woaderful in its way, and it is a matter of course to say that it was highly appreciated. Mr. Edward Howell was equally captivating with the violoncello. His contributions were (a) andante, (Goltermann), (b) gavotte (Poffer) ; and, in the second part, "Caprice Hengroise " (Dunkler). The latter was admirably arranged for displaying the .capacity of the instrument, and the capacity, too, of the executant, besides being a charming piece of music. A high word of praise should be given to Mr. W. Cook for his taste and skill as ac,core- panist. which were observable throughout the pro- gramme, and especially so in the execution of the solo " Tarantelle." The concert opened with the allegro from trio in D minor, by Mr. W. Cook, Herr Poznanski, and Mr. E. Howell, and closed with the trio " Vieni al mar," by Miss Annie Marriott, Mr. Sidney Tower, and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint. As evidence of the keen appre- , ciationrof the merits of the vocalists and instrumen- talists, it should be stated that each artiste was recalled after every performance. The concert was in every respect a great success, and it is to be hoped that Mr. Pearson will be encouraged in giving another of a similar character before the winter is over.

The Blaick Mountain Expedition has resumed the burning of villages, the negetiations for peace having failed. Colonel Crookshank has died of his wounds.

A TELL-TALE BLOTTING PAD.—In the Divorce Division on Thursday, Mr. Justice Butt had before him the case of Harding v. Harding and Farquharson, the petition of the husband, a coffee planter of Ceylon, for a divorce by reason of his wife's adultery with Mr. Ronald James Farquharson another coffee planter. Mr. and Mrs. Harding lived happily together until the summer of 1887, when the husband's suspicions were aroused, and Far- quharson was forbidden the house. Ultimately, by Imeans of a blotting-pad the husband discovered that his Iwife was carrying on a clandestine correspondence. He held the blotting-pad, up to a looking-glass and saw the 'word "darling." Mrs. Harding ultimately admitted having been unfaithful. For the sake of the children and to avoid divorce he asked her to promise not to see Farquharson again, but she refused. The Judge granted a decree nisi with costs and custody of the children. The Tithes question is one which the farmers of Wales have taken up with characteristic spirit and determination; and signs are not wanting in this and other parts of England that those who have to pay this impost are disposed to resist it as something which they regard as vexatious and oppressive. The British farmer moves, however, very slowly; and, unfortunately for him, the ques- tion of the origin of tithes requires more historical research than he is,as a rule, disposed to give. It is a matter which has excited at various times a great deal of controversy; but now that the smoke of battle has cleted away, there are SOM6 things which are seen to stand out prominently. In the' first place it is necessary, in considering the sub- ject, to distinguish ,between tithes and endow- ments pure and simple. The clergy do not as a rule make this distinction in dealing with issues of this kind, and labour to show that it would be a monstrous injustice to touch any of the endow- ments of the Church. It would undoubtedly be wrongto deprive the Church of property left specifi- cally to the Church as we now understand it ; but tithes do not stand on this footing. Tithes are a tax upon property imposed by law ; and the law which leiries the impost can, if it should be thought fit, either abolish that tax, or so alter it as to require that the money received shall be applied to another and a better purpose. Our contention is that Parliament has the same title in law to deal with tithes as it haste deal with the income or any other tax. Those who are seeking infor- mation on this sqbject should make themselves acquainted with the" Key to the Tithe Question" by the Rev. W. M. Hawkins, of Hundon, Suffolk. The work is published by Messrs. John Haddon and Co., Fleet-street, London, and we can strongly recommend it as a handbook, after a careful Perusal of its pages. Mr. Hawkins shows from indisputable authority that tithes were originally voluntary offerings ; and if they had remained voluntary it is needless to say that they would not have been such a source of strife and bitterness as they prove to-day. But the clergy have always had an eye to the loaves and fishes; and they managed to persuade King Offa to give them a civil title to recover tithes. This was confirmed in 854 by what is known as the Charter of Ethelwulph, who declared that he had "taken the prudent and serviceable resolution of granting the tenth part of the lands throughout his whole Kingdom to the Church and members of religion, &c." We in these days may fairly ques- tion whether such a resolution was prudent and serviceable, seeing that it has resulted in the country being taxed every year to the tune of Fivz MILLIONS to the support of a State Church. But there is this to be said for the Saxon King, that in his time tithes were applied to a wiihr and nobler nse than they are put to to-day. They were the poors rate as well as the church rate of that early : period; but the Church during the last thousand years has drawn the whole tithe into its rapacious maw. It has gobbled up everything, left the poor to shift for themselves, and, like the daughter of the horse leech, it still cries—" Give, give, give." Can we wonder that inquiring men, who know these things and who feel the injustice 'of the tithe, should protest against it even to the resistance of the law ? In a recent debate on the Tithe rent Charge Bill, LORD BRABOURNE referred to the fact that, originally, tithes were applied to three purposes—the support of the clergy, the main- tenance of churches, and the relief of the poor; and he suggested—with justice as it seems to us—that one part only should go to the Church. Incidentally he referred to Porto GREGORY'S statement on the subject, upon which Lord SALISBURY said :—" If the present arrange- ment by which the clergy had the whole of the tithes could base itself upon a prescription stretch- ing back to the tiniz., of Pore GREGORY, there was no doubt that that would be as good a title by prescription RS could be wished." This was an adroit retort on the part of the PRIME MINISTER, but it was too clever by half. It is simply not true that Port GREGORY said anything about the clergy having a title to "the whole of the tithes." Quite the reverse; his statement on the subject is on record,and is as follows It is the custom of the Apostolic See to prescribe rules to bishops newly ordained that all emoluments which accrue are to be divided into four portions—one for the bishop and his family, because of hospitality and entertainment ; another for the clergy; a third for the poor ; and a fourth for the repair of the church," Ac. It will be seen from this extract that Lord SALISBURY is caught in his own net; he is wholly wrong about POPE GREGORY giving his sanction to the whole of the tithe going to the clergy; and as to the poor it is obvious that, going back to Saxon times, they had an equal title with the clergy to a share of tithes. The poor— not to put too fine a point on the matter—have I been robbed; • and the struggling farmer who is called upon to pay tithes and poor rates when he is farming at a loss feels that he is doubly robbed. He knows that if he were properly tithed he would not be called upon for more than a tenth of the natural produce of the soil, and, further, that that tenth would go in part to the relief of the

WE are nearing the time of the Municipal Elec- tions, and for once in a while in Warrington "the sound of battle hurtles in the air." There is' an end for the moment of those "arrangements" which were wholly satisfactory to selected candidates if they were not wholly satisfactory to the ratepayers. There has been now and again a skirmish byway of protest against the rule of compromise, but it has , been left to the Ratepayers' Association to break away from the traditions of the past. And by putting themselves in the field, they have brought others into it. "Independence" has become con- tagious, and it thus happens that there are preparations for a contest in every ward • ex- cept one. In Latchford ward, Mr. H. J. LONG- TON, solicitor, took the platform as a nominee of the Ratepayers' Association, in opposition to Mr. J. TAYLOR, publican, who has sat for the ward -for half a score of years. Both candi- dates are Conservatives, and we suppose it is quite consistent with Conservative principles that a true blues" of the old type should be very much shocked at Mr. LONGTON for venturing to inter- fere with the existing order of things. Do they not sing, or say, "As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be," and why should Mr. LONG- TON meddle' with the ever-during "arrange- ments P" But the electors of the ward take another view of the matter, and they are at any rate gratified to observe that Mr. TAYLOR was compelled, after many years, to put out an address and say something to them. He tells them that his interests are identical with theirs; but he will have a difficulty in persuading people who ,have cut their wisdom teeth that what is good for the publican is good for the public. Luckily for Mr. TAYLOR, MT. LONGTON was caught tripping in the matter of his nomination papers. If the Family Party could not hope to beat Mr. LoNGToN at the I poll, they have managed to bowl him out with technicality, and Latchford is again disfranchised. In South-West Ward, Mr. THOMAS JONES, con- fectioner, came forward as a candidate, on behalf of the Ratepayers' Association, on the formal retire- ment of Mr. EDWARD GREENALL, junr., who'is also interested in the drink tradk, As a Conservative, like the retiring councillor, it was thought Mr. JONES would prove acceptable; but he is being opposed, and singularly enough, by Mr. EDWARD GREENALL himself, for that gentleman,with marvell- ous inconsistency, has issued an address to the elec- tors conjointly with Mr. LEWIS VOISEY. The voters in this ward are, naturally enough, asking if Mr. GREENALL has behaved quite fairly in formally affirming that he was retiring from the Council, and then, when action is taken on the strength of his statement, stepping forward to claim the seat which he had surrendered. If Mr. JONES had been of another political faith, there might have been some excuse for thus eating one's own words. As it is there is none, so far as we can see ; for it is due to Mr. JONES to say that he has as respectable a trade and is as respectable a tradesman as Mr. EDWARD GREENALL. Let the latter ask himself if he has done the right thing in going back on his written word; or if he has a right to expect that conduct of this kind is calculated to secure the confidence , of the electors ? If he is a gentleman, he will retire from a contest in which even victory will be ' no credit to him.

In North-East Ward the " Richmonds " are all over the field. The Ratepayers' Association nom- inated Mr. F. DIXON, the retiring Councillor, and Mr. HENRY THORNTON ; but MT. S. BARLOW, who carlies the freest of free lances, put in an appearance; and then Mr. W. H. J. JENKINS came on the scene as an Independent— that is to say independent of the three Liberals who were struggling for two seats. As if to make confusion worse confounded, it transpired that a number of Liberals in the ward were anxious that Mr. Joseph Garner should be nominated, and, as Mr. Garner is well-known ix the ward and highly respected, this was no sooner suggested than done.. At this juncture a demand was made for a meeting of the Liberal electors of north-east ward with a view of taking a vote as to who should be the recognized candidates of the party. This meeting was hold on Monday evening, with the result that the choice fell upon Mr. Garner and Mr. Thornton, Mr. Dixon being one vote only behind Mr. Thornton. It should be stated that Mr. Barlow and Mr. Dixon still regard themselves as " in it ;" and it is matter of course to say that, altogether, there is "a pretty kettle of fish." The "independence " of Mr. Jenkins means, it is well understood, that he will have the Tory vote, and that he hopes to profit by the division amongst the Liberal candidates. It is said, too, that as solicitor to the Licensed Victuallers' Association he will have the support of "the trade " ; but that, so far as the interests of the public are concerned, is the strongest reason why he should not be returned. The paid agent of a body of this kind may preach "independence," but he is less likely than other men to practice it when the occasion is critical. In the North-West Ward, as in the North-East Ward, the duel is a three-cornered one. 3lr. Wm. PIERPOINT, the retiring councillor, and Mr. Taos. FLOOD, who is a working-man representative of working-men, are the selected candidates of the Ratepayers' Association and of the Liberal Asso- stion, and up to-last week-end -4t was thought their generally recognized claims would not be contested. Mr. JOHN HEDGCOCK .has, however, taken the field as the champion of himself and his friends. He occupies an anomalous position, for he is not only a Liberal, but a member of the Ratepayers' Association. Why he should oppose Liberals and members of tile Ratepayers' Associ- ation will be a matter for Mr. HEDOCOCK to explain —that is, if he can. It is not the fault of Mr. PIERPOINT or of Mr. FLOOD that the transcendent merits of Mr. HEDGCOCK have not been discovered by the associations with which he is connected; and it he has any regard for loyalty and consistency he will retire from an altogether false position. His " friends " may tickle his vanity and spend his money, but there is no prospect of them convert- ing him at the forthcoming election into a council- lor for North-West Ward.

The retiring councillors for the South-East Ward are Mr. W. BOLTON and Mr. T. HUTCHINSON. They are both Conservatives, and they are being opposed by Mr. WILLIAM DIGGLE. Mr. J. Mors- FIELD (junior) was also nominated, but technical objection was taken, on Thursday, to his nomina- tion paper, and it was declared to be invalid. It is left, therefore, to Mr. DIGGLE to do battle for those of the ratepayers who think they ought to be taken into account on the first of November *d if Mr. DIGGLE can, for once, be taken soriously Tie will cause Messrs. BOLTON and HUTCHINSON to look to their laurels. He is at any rate in the field; and it is for the electors to say if they will have Mr. DIGGLE to represent them. It is some- thing gained, looking at the prospect all round,

poor. Tithes as they are exacted to-day are a fraudulent tax upon the nation ; and if they are imposed they should be imposed not in the interest of the clergy alone,but for the benefit of the nation as a whole.
THE EXAMINER, SATTTRDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888.

Our correspondent "Home Rule" again favours us with a valuable article on the Irish question. It will be found on another page, and we commend it to the attention of those of our readers who can appreciate careful statement of facts and well- sustained argument.

The Dublin police have apprehended a man on suspicion of being the sham priest who recently left Liverpool whilst indebted to a money changer to the extent of f;500. He went about with a beauti- ful set of false teeth, and—oh, the difference!—he had only to take out his teeth to effect a disguise. But his weak point is that he is false as to principles as well as teeth.

The Black Mountain expedition is " progress- ing Col. A. Crookshank the commander of the fourth column has died of his wounds; and, as the natives wont give in, General McQueen, so the latest news says, has "burned two more of the enemy's villages." More of this, and we may drop the T' mountain," and describe it as the " black ' expedition.

Queen Nathalie is informed that she is divorced from the King of Servia ; but she does not sub- mit tamely to the injustice. She has telegraphed to the Metropolitan :—" Take note that I consider your decision null and void, and without legal value." The people of Servia are taking note, also, and it may be that, before long, the King will wish the Queen was by his side again.

'As soon as the November elections are over, people will begin to interest themselves about the County Council elections. There is not much likelihood of the Councils proving democratic bodies; for they are so hedged about that the big- wigs who can afford to pay travelling expenses, and are "not to half a day," have the running made easy for them. As soon as the County Councils get to work, it will be seen that the Act wants amending in the direction of really popular government.

A Widnes trademan was brought before the magistrates, on Thursday, for selling impure lard. The mixture," when analysed, was found to contain "25 per cent of cotton seed oil, and other fats other than lard." It was stated that it should have been sold as "lardine"—L brother we sup- pose, of " butterine," and "margarine "—but there was no "lardine" on the firkin, and defendant was fined ss. and costa. He got off easy, but it was a first offence. The poor we have always with us, and they are defrauded from the cradle to the grave.

The people of Tibet are being "looked up" by travellers in the East. They are said to have anticipated Darwin in the belief that man descen- ded (or is it ascended?) from a monkey. We hear but little now against the evolution theory. There is a change in opinion since Mr. Mortimer Collins crystalised the views of his day in the following epigram:— There was an ape in the days that were earlier; Centuries passed and his hairbecame curlier: Centuries more gave a thumb and a wrist, Then he was a man—and a Positivist.

The struggle for an. advance of wages amongst the miners grows keener every day. In some dis- tricts, employers have conceded the desired increase of ten per cent.; in others they have resisted, and the men are out on strike. The price of coal has advanced—in some cases—by leaps and bounds. The colliers get an advance of ten per cent., and the proprietors recoup themselves by an advance in the price of coal equal to fifty per cent. on wages! And then they have the audacity to throw the blame upon "working-men who are never satisfied."

The Master of the Warrington Workhouse has got the advance of salary he applied for, as it would seem the Committee that had the matter in hand were quite willing to allow their judg- ment to be sot aside Mr. Ward is an able officer; but we do not see that the ratepayers are under any obligation to subscribe to his theory that because the salary of the late master was £lBO he must have £lBO, although he engaged to do the work for £l2O. And what of Dr. Spinks ? As his application for an advance was not entertained, will he not be disposed to think the Board have mado flesh of one and fish of another?

The friends of iinsectarian education are accept- ing the challenge thrown out by the Royal Com- mission on Education. They are determined that the hands of the clock shall not be put back with- out a struggle. There is to be aipnference in Lon- don on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 20th and 21st; and the circular convening the meeting is most influentially signed. The whole object of the movement is 0 make a stand against the reactionary policy which the Tozies are promoting, and we have no doubt that when the masses see what it means they will declare against money being taken from the rates to be spent by persons who are not responsible to the ratepayers.

A CHALLENGE TO THE ATTORNEY GENERAL.— Mr. Carew, M.P., has written as follows to Sir Richard Webster, the Attorney-General, in refer- ence to his statement at the meeting at St. Helens, on Thursday week, that in Ireland "Cows, donkeys, and horses were steeped in parrafin, and burnt to death ";—"As the principal law officer of the Crown, I prestube you satisfied yourself before making this grave statement that it was well founded. I now challenge you to cite a single instance, giving date and locality, in which a cow, donkey, or horse, or any other animal, was steeped in parrafin and burnt to death in Ireland." ADVANCE or COLLIERS' WAGES.—A large and influential meeting of tlp coal owners of the West Lancashire district was held at the North Western Hotel, Liverpool, on Friday afternoon, presided over by Mr. Alfred Hewlett (Wigan Coal and Iron Co., Limited), to consider the notices issued by the miners for an advance of 10 percent. in their wages, and a recommendation of the Executive Committee of the West Lancashire Coal Association with refer- ence thereto. After a full discussion of the subject the following decision was arrived at :—That in anticipation of a further advance being obtained in the prices of coal, the masters assent to the colliers' request for an advance of 10 percent. in wages from the last making up day in the present month of October. s Fine BOOTS AND SHOES of every description go to Haynes', Horsemarket-at.. Warrington.—Advt. a THE MANX LINES.—The discontinuance of this rivalry between the Old and the New Manx lines of steamers is practically agreed upon. The share- holders of both undertakings met on Wednesday— one party in Douglas and the other in Liverpool— and resolutions to amalgamate on the terms set forth in a provisional agreement were unanimously adopted. During the short period that the compe- tition for the Isle of Man traffic has lasted it has been intensely keen; and for the New Company, according to the Chairman, decisive. It is antici- pated that the shareholders of the New line, who are to take £50,000 in shares of the Old Company and the remainder in cash, will come out with 20s. in the pound. STOVES in great variety at Garland's, 51, Bridge-st.,Warring- ton.—Advt. ODDFELLOWS DINNER. About 60 members of the Loyal Viaduct Lodge, of the Ancient Order of Oddfellows sat down to their annual dinner at the Wellington Hotel, Earlesto wn, on Sat- urday evening. An excellent repast was provided by Mr. Thorpe, and at the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by P.P.G.M. James Dolan, and the vice-chair by Bro. Wm. Sutton, N.G. The usual toasts were duly honoured, and it was shown that the lodge had made great progress during the past few years. At present they had 254 members with a capital of £1,707. The procerdings were interspersed with songs, recitations, &c., by Bros. G. and R. Wright, Sephton, Mandsley, Sutton, Kellett, Bro. James Lachland accompanying on the pianoforte. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.—OR Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, David Johnson, a sailor, was charged with having assaulted P.C. Taylor. . On datur- day night the constable had a woman in custody on a charge of drunkenness and a great crowd assembled. The prisoner attempted to incite the woman to resist- ance, and then took a a runningkick " at the constable, striking him on the leg.—The prisoner accused the police- men of not treating the woman properly, one constable having hold of her feet and the other had hold of his head. He denied having committed an assault.—He was ordered to pay 10s., and costs 9s. Bd., or go to gaol for 14 days. A DRUNKEN ROBBER AT Rnecomi.l--Janns Edward Clayford and George Reid, young men, were brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday charged with stealing three cabbages and a cauliflower, the property of Richard Cawley, landlord of the Crown Vaults, Heath- rd. It appeared that the prisoners were in the Vaults on Saturday afternoon, and shortly after their departure the vegetables were; missed. A stone mason named George Dyson, who lives in Jackson's-lane, afterwards saw Clayford allow a cabbage to fall to the ground and Read went to the Union Vaults and left a cabbage until he called for it.—Read informed the magistrates that he found one cabbage in Heath-rd., and Clayford gave him the other.—Clayford said he was drunk and his memory "clear went from hun."—Clayford was fined 10s. and Read was discharged. ASSAULT ON A COUNTY COURT BAILIFF.—John Newell, carpenter, of Waterloo-road, was summoned before the Rundorn magistrates on Monday charged with assaulting Alfred F. W. Torrie, a county court bailiff.—The complainant stated that on the afternoon of the 6th inst., he went to the defendant's house to levy an execution,but he could not get into the house. Aftert wards he met the defendant in the street, and after bidding him " good afternoon " said " Here's a writ for you." The defendant said he did net want it, and struck complainant twice on the face with his fist, and threw the writ to the ground.—lhe defendant alleged that the complainant seized held of him by the dollar, and he merely pushed him aside with his arm. He called two witnesses in support of this statement, and Mr. R. Reynolds said there was no doubt an assault committed, but it was not a very bad one. A fine of 6d., and costs 12s. 6d. was imposed.—The defendant said if he had known of this he would have committed an assault. A VIOLENT MENDICANT.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, James Cook was charged with begging in Albert-road on Saturday, and he was further charged with resisting and assaulting P.C. Almond while in the execution of his duty.—P.C. Almond stated that on Saturday night he was on duty in Albert-road, when he saw the prisoner go into the Bradley Hotel and speak to three men. Witness went in afterwards, and was told that Cook had been begging for his night's lodgings. Prisoner went into another room, when witness heard hits ask again for some money. When witness got him out Cook said he would go without him getting hold, and when he was loosed he attempted to get away. Almond followed and put the "snaps" on,when Cook kicked him several times on the knee. The assistance of several civilians had to be.talled.—Prisoner : I was very much aggravated when the policeman turned my wrist, so I struck him.—For begging, Cook was sent to gaol for seven days, and for the assault he was fined 10s. and costs, or fourteen days, one term to follow the other. RUNCORN WATER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Thomas Atherton of Lacy-street, was charged with having wasted the water of the Whines Local Board on the 19th July. Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Board, prosecuted. Inspector Barrow,' in making his usual rounds, at 2 a.m., discovered a con- siderable waste of water, and traced a flow of water to the defendant's house. The defendant afterwards admitted that he had left the tap open, and expressed sorrow for his action.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed..—Thomas Robinson. of Manchester. was charged with having unlawfully used the water of the Local Board. Mr. Allen said the defendant was a brick- layer and was employed in pointing several houses. He took water from a tao in the yard of one of the houses, and although he was a stranger to the town, he ought to have known that the water did not belong to him,' and that the occupier of the cottage had no right to give him water for the purpose he required it for. Had the defendant applied to the Local Board in the usual way the cost to him would have been 2i.—The* defendant pleaded guilty, and was fined 7s. 6d. and costs. OUTRAGE-AT HALE.—At Widnes Petty Sessions OR Thursday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, James Worrall, of Speke ; William Taylor, of Hale Cliffe. Bale: Henry Taylor, of Oglet, Hale; and ,Tames Whyke, of Hale- road, Spekt, were brought up on remand charged with having caused grevious bodily harm to Thomas Burke, a dock-labourer of Garston. On Sunday the 14th inst., Burke spent the evening with some friends at the Cock and Trumpet at Hale, and when he left at half-past nine 'he was merry. He had walked a considerable way 'towards Ciarston when he was attacked from behind by ; the prisoner Taylor, who felled him to the ground and then kicked him, inflicting serious wounds on his head and bruising his body. After his assailants had gone. Burke again start ail towards home when Woman and Whyke sprang fronra dark gateway, and knocked him downaffith their fists and kicked him. They ran i away upon Constables Walker and Clark putting n an appearance, and these officers having dressed Burke's wounds took him home. Next day he was seen by Dr. Hutchinson, who stated that for several days the man was in a dangerous condition.—The prisoners were com- mitted to the Assizes for trial. Mr. J. W. Knowles appeared for the prisoners Taylor and VVhyke. WasLayAN Fortzum MtssioNs.—The annual missionary meeting was held in the Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnek on Wednesday evening; there was a very fair attenditice. Mr. T. Bd. The amount collected in the Widnes circuit was £169 35., being an increase on the previous year of £45 19s. Id. (Applause.) The Chairman said the report was a very encouraging one, and he hoped that the labourers would still go on prose- cuting their good design, as by God's help he was sure they would prosper in it, and he also thanked God that he had given him such a love for mission work.—Mr. Sowerbutts spoke of the mission work which was going on in India—in the province of Mysore—and of the many people, both natives and settlers, who had been 'brought to Christ.—The Rev. T.
