AN EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL TEAM ''ON STRIKE." —An extraordinary scene was witnessed on the ground of the Earlestown Club ou Saturday, when the strong Reserve team of that club, who were down to play the Chester second team, decided to go "on strike," and they refused to fulfil the club's engagement. The visitors arrived in due time, but the Earlestown Reserve refused, in a body, to play them, on the ground that the Committee had not provided them with suitable boots and uniform. Persuasion failed to remedy the grievaißle, and only two of the team could be prevailed upon to play. A" scratch" eleven was accordingly selected and a game was played with the result that Chester won by four goals to one. The Earlestown Reserve team were on the ground during the course of the game. The Committee decided at their meeting on Tuesday evening to comply with the wishes of the team, and the matter has been amicably settled on that understanding. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Thursday after- noon. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Weir. Bran- dreth, Wallington, Heywood, T. Lewis, H. Linaker (clerk), H. Linaker, jun. (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances). BYE-Laws WANTED TOR APPLETON. The following letter to the Clerk was read from Messrs. Hugh Daihy- shire and Thomas Hall, overseers of the township of Appletos, viz. :—"lt is the wish of some of our repre- sentative ratepayers that you ask the Rural Sanitary Authority to put in force in the township of Appleton building bye-laws, and the overseers have been asked by Mr. R. Davies to write you re this matter. It is cer- tainly needed since a cheap, low-rented property tends to increase pauperism, and a high death-rate with its consequent sickness. In the event of bye-laws being in force, and the overseers advised of plans passed. it will facilitate our knowing what and where property is being erected, since at the present time the overseers have to -go looking around everywhere to find new erections; these are springing up so fast that if it continues we shall require to make a supplemental list every month, if we must keep pace."—After a short conversation Mr. BRAN- DRETK moved that the application be taken into consideration at the next meeting of the Authority, and that in the meantime the Clerk send to the overseers of Appleton a copy of the bye-laws in force at Frodsham. —Mr. Asacei seconded this proposal, which was agreed to. INSPECTOR'S REPORT.—Mr. Farrington reported that nuisances existed at Appleton, but arrangements were being made' for their abatement. On his application certificates of occupation were granted for two huts at

Acton Grange, erected by Mr. Walker; for eight houses at Stockton Heath, belonging to Mr. William Arnold; five houses, at same place, belonging to Mr. C. W. Devonport ; and for two houses, at Weston, belonging to Mr. W. Mort. The water supply of these houses was satisfactory. This was all the business.

div.head: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY SOCIETY. ANNUAL CELEBRATION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: WESLEYAN MISSIONARY SOCIETY. ANNUAL CELEBRATION AT RUNCORN.

The snipe services in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Wesleyan Home and Foreign Missionary Society were held on Sunday last. At St. Paul's chapel, the services were conducted by the Rev. James Finch, e Stockport, who preached an appropriate sermon, morning and evening, to a. good congregation. At Camden School chapel the Rev. J. Shipham preached in the morning, and in the evening Mr. Hayes was the preacher. Special music was rendered at each chapel. On Monday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in St. Paul's chapel, and there was a good congregation. The Sunday school scholars occupied seats in the gallery, and under the leadership ef Mr. J. Birkett, jun., assisted with the vocal exercises. Mr. Edward Hutchinson,J.P.,of Liverpool,occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. James Finch, G. Sawday (Missionary from Tumkar) W. Berson (superintendent minister), J. Judson, Messrs. John Si rnpson, T. Simister,B. Kniveton, P.Speakman ,Raw- linson' J. R. Frith, E. Taylor, R. Norman, F. J. Norman Mr. T. Simister read the annual report. The generai summary showed that there were 336 stations or circuits, chapels or preaching places 1338, missionaries, and assistant missionaries, including supernumaries 333,10tker paid agents 2,000, unpaid agents local preachers and Sabbath school teachers 3,859, full credit church members 33,325, on trial for church membership- -4,674, and scholars 59,388. The income of the parent society from all sources for the past year was £131,867 2s. 6d., and the expenditure £137,967 10s. 3d., leaving a deficiency of £6,100 7s. 9d. This,added to the deficiency of the previous year, left the total debt of the society at £16,869 7s. Bd. From the Runcorn branch the follow- ing amounts had been received for 1888 :-Collected by Mrs. Soulby, £8 18s. ; Miss Speakman £6 9s. 6d.; Mrs. F. J Norman £5 75.; Miss Norman £lO 35.; and Miss Simister £ll 9s. 6d. In Camden schools there had been collected in the boys classes, £6 Os. 3d.; girls classes, £4 3s. 9d.; collected by boys with books, £4 16s. 5d.; girls with books £l3 Os. sd; total of Camden school £2B Os. 10d., being an increase of £l4 Bs. 10d. on the previous year. At Brunswick Sun- day school there had been. collected in girls' classes, £3 18s. sd. • in boys' classes, £4 16s. 5d.; collected by boys with books, kl 9 10s. 2d. ;by girls with books £2.5 13s. lid.; collected in the school on the previous day, £9 14s. 9d. ; total for Brunswick school, £63 13s. Bd.; a decrease of £lO on the previous year, a state of things which he (Mr. Simister) hoped would be remedied in another year. The collection at Camden school was £1 is. The collection in the chapel on the previous day amounted to £l2 95., an increase of £1 us. The total amount (exclusive of the collection to be made that even- ing) contributed to the society by the Runcorn branch was £147 Ds. 6d., being an increase of £9 15s, 6d. (Ap- plause.) The Chairman, who received a most coklial recep- tion, delivered a brief adplrees- . He said ' there never was a time in the,history of the Society, when it needed more consideralton than it did at the present time. The debt that now existed was causing great anxiety to the Committee in London, who said that unless the income of the Society was raised to the expenditure they would have to withdraw some of the ministers of Christ from the Foreign Stations. They had sent these men out to different parts of the world to preach the doctrine of Christ-Should not they stand by the Mission- ary Society and support them and keep them in a posi- tion to labour for the cause of Christ? (Applause). He urged upon those present to give methodically to the Society, and during his remarks he gave some interest- ing reminiscences of Runcorn and the Wesleyan Chapel there 40 years ago-The Rev. J. Finch then delivered a. speech in whichhe related various incidents of msssionary zeal'. In parts of the habitable world, he said, the most degraded had been elevated by the force of Christianity and had been made good citizens of the state below, and of the everlasting state above; and he trusted that they were not to have any miserable retrenchment,. or restriction of the area or zeal of missionary enter- prise. They all intended to do their best to reduce the missionary debt, and he was delighted to inform them that the chairma,n of that evening had given £5OO for that special urpose. (Applause.)-The Rev. G. Sawday delivered an interesting address upon mission- ary work in India. It was common, he said, for the. people of India tote spoken of as niggers, but the people of India were worthy of their glorious land, and the whole of them should be bowed down at the feet of Jesus. (Applause.) The wealth of India was greater than the imagination of speculators had ever dreamed of, and the whole of that wealth would be brought to the feet of Jesus. (Applause.) The great difficulty in the way of the missionary, was the idolatry of the country, which was supported by the most pro- found philosophy. In India there were about 250 millions of people, and they had 3,300,000 gods and goddesses. Mr. Sawday exhibited a number of Hindoo gods, and narrated 'he traditions connected with them, and he declared that the missionaries were determined not to give way until this idolatry was destroyed for ever and ever. (Applause) Caste prejudices were dis- appearing before western civilization and Christianity. The speaker disputed Canon Taylor's statement that missionary enterprise was a failure, quoting facts and figures toeshow that Christianity was making rapid strides in India. Christianity pervaded India. India had given up her fairest sons and daughters tei Christianity. (Applause).-Mr. J. R. Frith moved that a vote of thanks be given to the deputation-Mr. Finch and Mr. Sawday. The motion was seconded by Mr. F. J. Norman and enthusiastically carried.-On the proposi- tion of Mr. B. Kniveton, seconded by the Rev. J. Judson, the Committtee were thanked for their past services, and were re-appointed.-The Chairman was cordially thanked for his presence on the motion of Mr. Simpson, seconded by Mr. Rawlinson, supported by Mr. Sirhister, each of whom were associated with Mr. Hutchinson at school over 40 years ago.-Mr. Berson announced that last year the collection at the public meeting was £33 3s. 7d.; and that night the collection amounted to £5B 12s. ld., an increase due in a great degree to the large heartedness of the Chairman. (Applause.) The services of the choir and scholars having been acknow- ledged en the motion of Mr. P. Speakman, the meeting concluded.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock, and Mr. H. Gaskell jun. ScnooL Boma, CasEs.—Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted a number of persons for not sending their children regularly to school. And the usual penalty of ss. was imposed in each case. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Mary Connor, of Travis-st... was fined ss. and costs for being drunk.—Marl Jane Riley, Water-st., Catherine Hynes, Marsh-st. ; Margaret Redman and Bryan Redman of Bedford-st., were each bound over to beof good behaviour for having committed breathes of the peace. Rummel Tim PoLtes.—Annie Gallagher, of Caroline- st.. was charged with resisting P.C. Porte, in the execution of his duty, and Mary Jane Rawlinson, of 14 Suttons Lane was charged with resisting P.C. Ratcliffe. On Saturday night Rawlinson's brother was drunk, and acting like a madman. The constable took him into custody, and the defendants resisted the officers to such an extent that Uri prisoner was with difficulty taken tothe police-station.—Each defendant was fined ss. and costs 7s. ed. HIGHWAY OFFEN&S.—Michael McLoughlin, ef Derby- road, was fiaed ss. and casts for riding on his limy without reins. John Bing, of St. Helens, was summoned for being asleep whilst in charge of two horses. He was fined 10s. and costs. CHIMNEYS ON FlRl4.—Samuel Pinches, Warrington-road, and Catherine Molloy, of Orford-street, were each fined is. and costs for allowing the chitnney of their dwellings to be on fire. Don AT LARGE.—Th•mas Brady, of Frederick-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large. ASSAULT ON THE Police .*.John Smith of Irwell-lane, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Gregory, on the previoes night. The prisoner was apprehended on the former charge and then became very violent, and struck Gregory several times in the chest. The efforts of three constables were required to convey him to the police station. The prisoner, who conducted himself very noisily in Court was fined 78. 6d. and costs for being drunk and 20s. and costs for the assault. POLES AT VARIANCE.—Martin StaShish, Of Hope-street, was fined ss. and kosts 13s. for assaulting Sylvester Iloustre, a Pole.

SIIDDBN DEATH or A CHILD.-311r. 11. C. Yates. coroner, held an inquest at the Red Lion, Latch ford. on Monday, touching the death of Margaret Duffy, aged 8, the daughter of a fish-hawker, living in Princess-st. It appeared that the child was taken. ill on Thursday morning, and in the afternoon Dr. Cannell was sent for. He was unable to leave home, but prescribed on description of the symptoms. On reaching home, however, the mother found her child dead. It transpired that deceased had eaten a large number of apples. A verdict of "death from natural causes" was returned.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bey/ sev-street, Warrington, not later than .ten o'clock on Weduescay morning
(RUGBY.)
FlatroN T. GLOBE RECEBATION.—PIayed at Halton on Saturday. Globe, 1 goal, 2 minors; Halton, 1 try, 11 minors. SUTTON RECREATION. —This match

WIDNES 3RD V. was played at Widnes on Saturday, and resulted in a -very easy win for Widnes by 5 tries and 4 minors to Sutton nothing. WIDNES HALTON VIEW WANDERERS V. RUNCORN TRANI Betirms.—This match was played on Saturday at Runcorn, and resulted as follows :—Halton View, two goals, three fulmars, to oneminor. GANDY'S WALK T. SANKEY EXCELSIORS.—This match was played at Sankey, on Saturday, and after a rough game, victory rested with the visitors. Result: Gandy's Walk, 1 try 3 minors; Sankey, 2 minors. WIDNRS A V. WIGAN A.—These two teams met 011 Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and the game was easily won by the latter. The result was—Wigan, 2 goals and one minor, to one try and 3 minors. Tuarro Hesen arn v. Dirros RECREATION.—The former team paid a visit to Ditton on Saturday. The home team won a hard-fought game by one goal, two tries and eight minors, to one try and three minors. MOSS BANK V. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S (Second Teams). —These teams metatMoss Bank on Saturday. Time was called with the result a draw—Moss Bank one try, War- rington St. Paul's one try and five minors. ORFORD RANGERS V. WARRINGTON JUNIORS.—ThiSI match was played on the ground of the farmer, on Satur- day, and owing to the visitors leaving the field, the Rangers claimed the victory by 1 goal and 2 minors to nil. ORFORD RANGERS V. WARRINGTON JUNIOR.S.—This match was played on the Rangers' ground on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the home team by 1 goal 2 minors to nil. Nuttall scored the try, the same player kicking a neat goal. MERSEY MISSION v. Winftes POST OFFCE.—Played on the ground of thelatter. Jones ran in a grand try from half way, from which Hough landed a splendid goal. Time was called, leaving the visitors winners by a goal and five minors to 2 minors. HALTON JOCKEYS T. TIMMLNS'S WHITE STAR—This match was played on the ground of the former, and re suited in a victory for the home team by one try and six minors to nil. The try was obtained by Fowler. The Jockeys also got two tries which were disputed. PARR V. LATCHFORD TRITE BLUES.—This match was played on Saturday at Latchford. When the whistle sounded the score was Latchford, four minors; Parr, nil. For Parr, Pickering and Little played a good game, while the forwards worked well to a man. Latchford backs did some good work. Sr. HELENS "A" TEAM V. FRODSHAM (First).—This match was played at St. Helens on Saturday. e game ended in a win for St. Helens by 1 try and 2 minors, to 3 minors. The three-quarters on each side plaited well, and were about equally matched. The home forwards played a rattlinggame and out-played their opponents. LYMM V. W. GLEAVE'S TEAM (WARRINGTON).—Amatch was played on Saturday, between the above teams, at Lymm, in beautiful weather, under the Rugby rules. A very pleasant game ended in a win for the home team, who played a good game all through, E. Jackson drop- ping the goal. Score: Lynam 1 goal, 3 tries, 8 minors; Warrington,l minor. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH V. RUNCORN FREE WAN- DERERS.—This match was played on the ground of the former, and after a good but one-sided game ended in a win for the Church by three goals, six tries to nil. The following scored :—Dunbavand, three tries; Clarke, two tries ; Hosker, two tries; Speakman, one try; Pea- rtnek, one try; Ward and Hosker kicked the goals. SANKEY T. WYCLIFFS.—This match was played at Sankey on Saturday. Soon after the start Sankey were forced to concede a minor. From the drop out Sankey soon worked their way to the visitor' line, Noon getting over, but the point was disputed afMr a goal had been kicked. Soon after Pemberton got over, no gaol result- ing. The drop put brought no relief, Sankey rushing over, Wycliffe having the best of a scramble. The home team not to be denied, scored several minors, and then Wood scored a try, no goal again resulting. The home forwards came again, Webster saving. Score at half- time Sankey, 2 tries 4 minors to Wycliffe 1 minor. The visitors kicked off, and following well up prevented a return. Soon after Sankey scored 4 minors in quick succession and then Noon scored a try,. no goal again. This brought no side, leavine Sankey winners by 3 tries and 8 minors to 1 minor. All the home team played well, Webster, Scotts and Teare for the visitors. Rl:meow; v. BROUGHTON RANGERS (" A" Tzaars.)— Played at Runcorn, on Saturday, before 1,000 spectators. Bowyer started from centre on behalf of the home team, Mclnnes returning. Woods and Whinyates carried play into the Rangers quarters, where Hood came to the rescue, Williamson, Robinson' and Kiffard working the ball back to centre. Shaw, Gatley, and Bowyer now got away with a grand dribble to the Rangers' line, the ball going into touch. From the line-out Woods and Lunt took the ball over the line, when the latter lost possession, Horrocks just getting up in the nick of time and saving grandly. Soon after the drop-out Booth put in a neat run and kicked to the visitors' 25. Spence, Hodgson, and Mclnnes returned and placed the home line in danger, Abrams clearing in grand style. Some severe scrimmaging was now indulged in on the home line, Booth being compelled to save. After the kick-out Evans got in a nice run, and passed to Lunt, who trans- ferred to Whinyates, and a series of scrimmages took place in clese proximity to the Rangers' uprights, Lunt missing ar good opportunity of scoring, Horrocks relieving his side by', conceding a minor, an operation which they had very quickly again to resort to. Half-' time was now called, the game standing in favour of the home team. The second half was also evenly contested, the final result being :—Runcorn, 6 minors; Rangers, 4 minors. Teams :—Rangers: Horrocks, back ; Mclnnes, Hodgson, and Hood, three-quarter backs; Marsh and Spence half backs ; Squires, Robinson, Williamson, Hall, Kiffard, Shore, Pickard, Fitton, and Orom, forwards. Runcorn : Booth, back; Lunt, Woods, and Whinyates, three-quarter backs; Evans and Abrams, half-backs; Gatley, Shaw, Rigby, Barker, Bowyer, Hailwood, Lee, Tipper, and Dutton, forwards, WIDNES v. WIGAN.—A very good match was decided at the Lower House-lane ground, Widnes, on Saturday, between these teams. Much interest was evinced during the game, the proceedings being witnessed by about 3,000 spectators. The visitors succeeded in putting their best team into the field, whereas Plumpton for Widnes had again absented himself from the lines of his men. For a considerable time the contention appeared very even, until at length the invaders registered two minors. Next Atkinson added a try, but failed in attempting to add the major point. The play continued to go on in an excellent manner until half time, when, after another minor had been ceded, the score stood— Wigan, one try and three minors to nil. Through the change of ends the homesters naturally expected to make an altera,tien for the better in their scoring posi- tion ; but this they did not achieve. They played with great determination, although they were considerably disabled by one of their men (Wright) being compelled ' to retire from the ground. The visitors secured two more minors to their name, and Slavin managed a fine try, but the place was again a failure. The Wigan terri- tory was visitedseveral times by the Widnesians,and some good result was expected, but they were eventually beaten away, and had to retire with the result standing —Wigan, 2 tries and 8 minors to Widnes nil. Teams: —Wigan: Bulloeh, back; Slevin (captain), Seddon, , and Baldwin, three-quarter backs; Hunter and Halli- well, half backs; Atkinson, Wardle, Lowe, Halton, Hartle,s, Dempsey, Swift, Telford, and Bibby, forwards. Widnes: S. Bingham, bask; Clark, Parkinson, and Hartles, three-quarter backs; Wilkinson -and Farrell, half backs; Smith, Kiddie, Barber, Williams, Gordon, tiewitt, Gandy, Wright, and Johnson, forwards. WARRINGTON V. OLDHAM (" A" TEAMS.)—This match was contested on Saturday at Wilderspool before a good muster of spectators in splendid weather. Both teams were strong, the hope team having the assistance of Mr. Riley, of the " Current Cash" Company. Adamson (the home captain) having won the toss Oldham kicked off, Lawless returning into touch. From the line-out Harrop broke away, and the forwards aiding his efforts carried play to the Warrington line. Jolley eventually relieved, but Cawley was allowed a free kick for off-side tackling; nothing, however, came of it, and a scrimmagewas formed in the centre. Bibby next gave Appleton a chance, but owing to the ball touching the referee an almost certain try was spoiled, a scrimmage being formed near the Oldham posts. After good passing by Lawless and Bate to paniels, this player ran to the line, where J. Bate tried hard to score, the ball going touch in goal. From the drop-out the visiting forwards dribbled the oval down the field, Jolley stopping a dangerous rush. Riley and Holmes were next prominent, and Lawless kicking across, Daniels picked up smartly and out-running his opponents gained a splendid try, the kick at goal by Bate being charged down. Lloyd spoiled the drop-out, but the Oldham forwards by good passing carried play to the Warrington qucter-flag. Hayes, Unsworth, and Adamson removed the pressure, and Lawless gaining possession eluded his opponenc,s, and gained a grand try, Isherwood failing at the place. The score at half-time was—Warrington, two tries and two minors to nil. After the interval Isherwood re-started, the ball eventually going into touch in the visitors' quarters. Adamson and Riley broke away from the line-out, and Kershaw kicking to Appleton, this player took a flying kick, and Unsworth, following well up, got over, but the point was disallowed. Good passing by Riley, Lloyd, and Bibby enabled Daniels to run to the line, causing Lowe to save. The Oldham front rank removed the pressure, but Bate ran the leather back again' Adamson forcing the visitors to concede a minor. After the drop-out, Riley, Hayes, and Lloyd came through the scrimmage, and Bibby gaining possession ran to the line, where he lost the ball, but Daniels completed the try, Isherwood failing to improve the point by a mere .` shade. Holmes was next prominent with a grand run, and finished by passing to Bate, who kicked, and Daniels following up gained his third try, the point not being improved. Bate returned the drop-out, and Oldham were again pressed, Lloyd getting in at the corner flag, but the claim was disallowed. From the scrimmage

Bate secured and passed to Lawless, who in turn threw to Daniels, this player forcing Oldham to touch down. Donahue, Riley, and Unsworth dribbled the ball af' er the drop-out, but the Oldham forwards came to the rescue and retaliated. The game was brought to a conclusion by a spirited run '.y Daniels, who had played in a ster- ling manner all through, the score being—Warrington, 4 tries, 4 minors; Oldham, nil. Teams :—Warrington : Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Bibby, and Appleton; half-backs, Bate and Lawless; forwards, Adamson, (captain), Holmes, Haves, Isherwood, Donohue, Unsworth, F. Bate, Riley and Lloyd. Oldham: Full back, Lowe; three-quarter backs, Taylor, Cowley, and Kershaw; half-backs, Hague and Harrop (captain) ; forwards, Jowles, Gardener, Newton, Wade, Chapman, Nuttal, Grimshm. Scr?gg, and Gies. Referee, Mr. Slack, Southport Olympic. Rl:acorns v. Beoutorrox RANGERS.—On Saturday the Runcorn team journeyed to Broughton to play the seventh fixture on their card of events, which was with the Broughton Rangers. The weather was beautifully fine, and the game was of a very pleasant character throughout. The visitors won the toss, and shortly after half-past three Tune kicked off for the home team, and the scene of hostilities was confined principally to the Rangers' quarters, the ball being returned by Brazendale. The Rartors pressed somewhat severely, but Riley and CromptoM who were watching very closely the progress of affairs, came to thebrescue, and relieved the pressure. Crompton kicked to Boyle, the Rangers' full back, but the latter mulled by stumbling over the ball, thus permitting Runcorn to get in, and the first try was obtained by Hampson. Crompton essayed to kick I at goal, and, although the place was an easy one, he failed to convert the try. This failure excited the I Rangers to enthusiasm' and they played with incresed, vigour, and evinced a determination to make matters even ; but the visitors were equally determined to pre- vent this being carried into effect, Dayies making a splendid run to the Rangers' line. no, Robertson, Moxon, and Skidmore dribbled 'the ball in the direction of the visitors' goal. the effort being a most commendable one ; but Riley, who was on the alert, relieved, and the defence was a grand piece of play, se much so that the home team found that their opponents had not lost one whit of their well-known prestige. Cromp- ton made a shot at goal, and a minor was scored for Runcorn. The remainder of the game ia the first half was of an easy nature, and the Rangers showed their intention to do their level best to equalize as far as practicable, the state of affairs, and they very nearly carried their intentions into effect. At the time the whistle was sounded, the scores were as follows :—Runcom,l try and 1 minor; Rangers, nil. W. Hughes subsequently restarted the ball on behalf of the wearers of the myrtle green. and as there was no return a scrimmage resulted, and Wood made a capital run to the Runcorn 25; a grand pass was made from Robertson to Cooper, and the play on behalf of Broughton was far superior to that which was manifested in the first half. Riley proved equal to the occasion, however, and tackled Cooper in grand style, thus averting what was appar- ently a dangerous preject. McGowan succeeded in getting in, but the sphere was ruled back, and Robert- son, who attempted a shot at goal, registered the first and only minor for his team. After the drop-out, Brazendale, who essayed a long kick, made it compul- sory for the home team to save; but at this point it was seen that the latter had decidedly the best of the play, and if they did not add to their score it was not owing to any want of energy on their part, but rather to the combined game for which the Runcornians have gained an envied name. Crompton, who has been dea- -1 dribed as "irrepressible," owing to his recent goal- kicking propensities, and especially to his almost unprecedented success as a scorer of major points, made another attack, and narrowly escaped a drop at goal. A I Minor, however, resulted. Within a very short time of the call of time, McGowan put in a splendid, run to the I visitors' goajghle, and almost immediately afterwards the game terminated with score as follows: Runcorn, 1 try and 3 minors; Rangers, 1 minor. Crompton, Davies, Brazendale, Riley, W. Hughes, Wood, and Hampson played a meritorious game, and to them the result may be credited, although as a whole the team gave a thorough example of the merits of combination. Teams: —Broughton Rangers: Boyle, back; McGowan, Robert- son, and Cooper, three-quarter backs; Edge and Wood, half backs; Atkinson, Tune, Moxon' Birch, Jackson, Skinmore, Higginbotham, Powell, and Squires, forwards. Runcorn: Brazendale. backs •W. A. Riley, Crompton, and Davies, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and Hol- lingworth, half backs; Faulkner, Hughes, Wainwright, Hancock, P. Riley, Hampson, Gayter, Andrews, and Dolan, forwards. WARRINGTON v. OLDHAM.

The first match of the old-time fixtnre took place on Saturday, when the Warriegtonians journeyed to Clarkesfield, Oldham. Previous games at Oldham have, with one exception, always resulted in a draw, and special efforts were made by the " wirepullers "to break this record, they placing their strongest possible fifteen in the field. It was pleasing to note that Jolley made his reappearance in the team after an absence of a, month through indisposition. A large crowd assembled to witness the" tussle,l and I Armstrong started from midfield with a strong sun at his back. Exchange kicking was first witnessed between Jolley, Barlow, Massey, and Moseley, the oval finally resting at neutral ground. Evans foiled Moseley, in an endeavour to get away, but a strong rush by the Oldham forwards compelled Massey to adopt saving tatics. Evans dropped out, and again splendid exchanges were witnessed by Barlow, Barnes, Greaves, and Massey, the latter putting in a grand punt to the Oldham quarter- flag. Mills and Moseley, by neat passing, gained ground, and a good dribble by Beetham was promptly stopped by Povey. Moseley passed well to Barlow, the latter getting past all opposition with the exception of Massey, but the tackling of the latter was superb. Directly after a second minor accrued to the home team. Moseley met the drop out with a grand return, and after Thomas had ineffectually* tried to force an opening, a good run by Moseley resulted in Lees scoring a somewhat shady try, as many expressed the opinion that the oval had been in touch. No goal resulted from Beetham's kick. Not to be denied, the Warringtonians worked with a will, and Nevins was applauded for a dashing run, gain- ing a lot of ground with his feigningto pass. Antrobus ran round the pack, and wound up with a good pass to Jolley, the ball gravitating into touch at the Oldham quarter flag. From the line out the visitors swept down on the Oldham goal, and Broadbent saved just in the nick of time. Bandies mute his mark from the drop out, and again the Oldham men were placed on defensive. Barnes put in trickey work, and after Barlow had got in a good kick to Massey to his own line, the Warringtonian rounded his opponents, winding up this brilliant piece of work by a smart kick to the Oldham line. Loud cheers greeted this last effort. Evans was the next to show with a well- executed run, getting over, but the place was too diffi- cult to allow Barnes to augment the score. The drop out again feund Warrington on the aggressive, chiefly by the aid of Antrobus and Massey, and it was only Broad- bent's safe play that prevented the Warringtonians from not adding to their score. Broadbent found relief by con- ceding a minor. Antrebus had a free kick awarded him and the game was on the Oldham line when the whistle sounded halftime, both sides having one try two minors to their credit. On resuming hostilities it was apparent that no liberties were to be taken by either side, the play somewhat deteriorating and not being so dciting as in the first half. For a time the game rested in midfield, until an extra effort by Evans nearly had the desired effect. By dint of hard _work W. Dillon got over, but through some informality only a minor was allowed. Oldham responded with a similar point, whilst a few minutes later Massey had to kick dead. A drop at I goal by Beetham went wide, and a combined dribble by Ashton, Littlewood, and Povey, placed the game at-the Oldham quarter flag. Speakman wasrepeatedly cheered fortis smart saving. A pass to Barlow was intercepted, but nothing came of it, and, although Turner made a desperate effort, he failed to cross the line by about a yard. A wild pass served as a relief to the home team, • and although Greaves, Barnes; Nevins, and Barlow . strove hard for their respective sides, no addition was made to the score, the result being a draw, Oldham hav- ing 1 try 5 minors to their credit, whilst Warrington had • 1 try and 4 minors. To speak of the game itself, it was most evenly con- tested, and the Oldham team must be complimented en L the improvement that has been made in their ranks. . They played Warrington a sterling game, although their ; tackling was at times too severe. On behalf of Warring- ; ton,Massey made his debut at full back. Never was such L an exhibition witnessed at Clarkesfield as displayed by L this player on Saturday. The cheers which greeted ; his performance speak for the form he showed, and it ' only remains to be said that if he takes kindly to this , his new position, higher honours are certainly in store for him. Evans played fairly well at centre, whilst L what work Barnes had to do was accomplished in a ; finished style. Jolley will improve with time -whilst Antrobus put in some tricky work, and Speakman had the unthankful task of repeatedly saving the strong : rushes of the Oldham forwards. Of the forwards W. L Dillon, Nevins, Turner, and Ashton were the best. ; Thomas, Beetham, and Broadbent were for choice in the • Oldham ranks. Teams :—Warrington: Massey, back; Barnes, Evans; I and Jolley, three-quarters • Antrobus and Speakman; half backs; W. Dillon (captain), Ashton, Fair. Turner, E. Dillon, Povey, Littlewood, Bandies, Nevins, and , Creaglian, forwards. Oldham: Broadbent, back; ' Greaves, Moseley, and Barlow, three-quarters; Thomas L and Mills (captain), half backs; Mallilew, Armstrong, • Lees. Ingham, Beetham Blomley, Mayers,- Whitehead, , and Woolstencroft, forwards. Referee, Mr. Dewhurst.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888.

NORTHWICH DIVISION AND THE COITNTY COUNCIL. The formation of the County Councils in January .of next year will mark an important era in the government of the people by the people. Though the change is not so Radical as was desired, and expected, it is regarded by earnest politicians as the first step towards greater things, and much interest is evinced in the manner in which it is proposed to provide the representation. The magistrates in Quarter Sessions assembled have mapped out the County of Cheshire into electoral districts, and it is instructive to notice the way in which the Northwich Parliamentary Division, of which Run- corn forms so important a part,' has been divided. There are ten electoral districts in which voters in ,the Northwich Division are inter- ested, and when the time of election draws nigh, their distribution and influence will be a very important point for the consideration of both parties, 'who will probably have the choice of the candidates. In the ten districts there are no less than 105 townships having a total population according to the last census, 76,672. Of these, 43 townships are in the Northwich division, with a population of 57,607; 43 in the Knutsford Division, with a population of 13,455; 16 in the Eddisbnry Division, with a population of 4,352; one in Macclesfied Division, population 113; one in Crewe Division, population 549; and one in Altrivacham Division, population 496. Fifty nine townships are in the_ Northwich Union, 30 in the Runcorn Union, and 16 in the Congleton Union. It will thus be seen that • three fourths of the population that will send Hon. members to the County Council resides within the boundaries of the Northwich Parliamentary Division and,the question arises is this population so distributed that its well- known Liberal proclivities can be exerted with success- ful effect in each district. Further details will give an answer to this question. The town of Runcorn will have the honour of sending two members to the Council, one for Runcorn North, and a second for Run- corn South.; the total population according to last cen- ' Sus being 15,120, there can be no doubt of the prepon- derance of Liberal opinion in this 'own. Winsford dis- trict comprises 3 townships in Northwich Division, population 11,154, and 2 in the Eddisbury Division, population' 862 ; total population 12,016. In Northwich there:are 5 townships, all in that parliamentary division, and containing a population of 8,143. In Witton there are three townships in the Northwich Division, and one in the Knutsford Division, the population in the latter , township being 777; total population B,622.—Davenham and Church Hulme district consists of 28 townships, I with a population of 5,816. There are 4 townships in , Northwich Division, population 857; 23 in the Knuts- ford Division,population 4,846; and one in theMacclesfield Division, population 113. In Weaverham Electoral District there are 9 townships in Northwich Division, population 5069; and 8 townships in Eddisbury Division, population 2784; total population 7852. Daresbtiry District comprises 10 townships from the Northwich Division, and 6 townships from Knutsford Division, the population in the respective divisions being 4625 and 1542; total 6167. Appleton District includes townships from three divisions :—Northwich, population 532; Knutsford 11, population 6012,; Altrincham 1, popula- tion 496; total 7040. Middlewich is thus constituted:— Northwich Division 7 townships, population 4255 ; Eddisbury Division,6, population 706; Knutsford Division, 2, population 278; Crewe, 1, population 549; total 9295. A perusal of the above facts will reveal that in eight of the electoral districts, voters of the Northwich Parliamentary Division vastly preponderate, and it may be concluded will have a corresponding influence upon the result of the elections. The figures quoted and the further details given below were submitted by Mr. W. Handley to the Sxecutive Council a few days ago: Parity. Poor Law Electoral Division. Division. Union. It was more, it was untruthful, and while I might say in retort that the writer knew nothing of her subject, I shalt be more to the point in saying that ancient writers, as modern writers, lay it at the door of all who pass idle and luxurious lives. Rad I space I would like to make some remarks on the letter of A. T. T. on boarding-house life. I think the comparison I could make betwixt American boarding-house life and English home life would be sufficiently trenchant to prove that Amerida has at the core of her life's system one of the foulest and most insidious life-eating ulcers that ever a nation was prostrated with. In conelusion, allow me to urge that the qaestion of free trade vs. protection be discussed without the everlasting dragging in of "It's English, ye know." Recognize principle if ye can for once, oh, ye Americans. HARRY WHITHATC 13, Valparaiso-street, S. E.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. Greening, W. Houghton, Kilsball, Voisey, Heaton, T. Jones. Blackburst, Harrison, Isherwood, Darbyshire, Owen, Grange, J. Houghton, Humphries, Hibbert, Ratcliffe, Clarke, Eckersley, Balharry, Strange, Swinton ;J. C. Sutton (clerk); S. Sutton (assistant clerk) ; C. H. Ward (workhouse master) ; and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate schools.)

div.head: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

The Padgate SchoolS-Goni-inctie-e7recommended that thd salary of Mrs. Fairhurst, porteress at the schools, be increased by the sum of 2s. per week, instead of Is. 6d. per week as previously proposed. Mr. Tickle, foster father Of No. 2 home had applied for an increase of salary, but the Committee could not recommend an increase at present. The minutes were passed. _ _
GIFTS. The Workhouse Masker, in his journal, reported that the ladies from Trinity Church had brought and dis- tributed b. large quantity of fruit to the inmates of the hospital and school.
SCHOOL FEES.
The School rees Committee recommended that fees be allowed in 69 cases, 52 of which were old and 17 new cases.—The Chairman was glad to see that the new cases were so comparatively few in number. •

A RESIGNATION. The CLERK read the resignation of Miss Harper, nurse at the Workhouse, who asked for a testimonial from the Board.—Mr. GREENING proposed that the testimonial be granted.—Mr. DARBTSHIRE seconded this proposal. He said the nurse had done her work in a very satisfactory manner so far as he was able to judge ; he was sorry that she was leaving. (Hear, hear.)—The proposal was i agreed to.

THE HOUSE COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that the application for an increase of salary from Dr. Spinks had been read, and a resolution passed that the same be not entertained. The application of Mr. and Mrs Ward, workhouse master and mistress, for an increase of salary was con- sidered, and it was unanimously resolved that Mr. Ward's salary be raised from £BO to £9O, and Mrs. Ward's from £4O to £5O, per annum.—The CLERK said that since the meeting of the House Committee another letter had been received from the Master on the subject of his salary as follows Warrington Union Workhouse, October 24th, 1888. To the Chairman and Members of the Board of Guardians. Dear Sir and Gentlemen,—After carefully considering the recommendation as communicated to me by the Visiting Committee on Friday, the 12th inst., I have come to the eonclusion that it is necessary, in my own interest, to write this letter. First, allow me to apologize to the Committee, and assure them .that I thank them for what they did, and I trust that nothing I may say in this will give any member the slightest offence. I feel assured that all acted in the kindest spirit, for what they considered the best, but I am afraid the desire to be unanimous in their recommendation overpowered all other wishes. I think it unfortunate I was not called into the room beforethey arrived at a final decision, as I could have placed my case • before them in its different bearings, and so have enabled them to con- cede to me what I consider a fair thing. As it is, I cannot help feeling that my work has not been appre- ciated to the extent I had hoped for. When I became a candidate for this appointment I was fully aware that you had been paying the sum of £lBO as salary, and had reduced it to £l2O. I have no doubt all the other candidates knew the same. As £lBO had been sanctioned by the Local Government Board, it was viewed to be quite certain that it was not too !Mich for the place. Therefore my impression was that the reduced salary was only temporary, to enable the Board to test the ability and fitness of the persons whom they might appoint, and that after proving themselves efficient, there would be a fair advance on the reduced amount until 04 old sum was reached, and until that sum is exceeded I do not see how a.nyonc cad reasonably call it increasing the salaries of the master and matron. There was one remark made by a Guardian from Earles- town to the effect that they must consider the rate- payers. lam afraid that he did not look upon the matter in its broadest sense. Beyond what I have pointed out, I should consider (if you will allow me respectfully to express my view) that inasmuch as the difference between a vote of £lO and £2O would be a very infinitesimal fraction in the £ on the ratable value of the Union, the difference is indeed too imperceptible to have possible place in the matter under consideration. On the other hand, where a man has to deal as I have, with some thousands of pounds, and a slip or two would make a difference of some hundreds, it is, I submit, better to pay a sum to secure the best ability obtainable In the interests of the ratepayers. After recensidering the matter, I trust you will be able to see your way to , advance our salaries at the present time from £BO to £lOO, and £4O to £5O respectively, and you may depend upon our united efforts being made to carry out the responsible duties of our office to everyone's satisfaction. The Guardians will see that I only ask for £lO in excess of the present proposed sum, and I would not have troubled your Board had I not felt that after your experience of me in the period I have been withyou, and after consideration of the merits of my application as set forth in my previous letter, you would grant me the sum asked for. I am, dear sir, and gentlemen, yours faith- fully, CHAS. HARRELL WARD, master of the Workhouse." The CHAIRMAN thought the best plan would be to con- cede the small additional increase asked for by the master. He thought they should be acting wisely in doing so, and, considering the way the master did 'his work, the amount asked for was not excessive.—Mr. GREENING, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the Committee thought it was not necessary that any increase of salary should be made to Dr. Spmks. The matter with regard to the salaries of Mr. and Mrs. Ward was pretty freely discussed, and there were some mem- bers on the Committee who thought the proposed in- crease was not enough but, in order that the recommen- dation should be unanimous, these gave way.—Mr. HHATON seconded the proposed adoption of the minutes. —Mr. BLACRIDIRST first suggested that the minute referr- ing to the master's and matron's salary should be referred back, but after an expression of opinion that this was not necessary, he moved that the master's salary be advanced from £BO to £lOO, instead of £9O as proposed by the Committee. He thought it was better to keep a good man when they had got one.—Mr. VOISET remarked that there was such athing as economi- sing on a false basis, and he seconded Mr. BLACK- RUST'S proposal. Mr. RATCLIFFE pointed out that while dealing with the matter they should bear in mind that since Mr. Ward came to the Workhouse there had been an assistant master appointed, who, taking things all round would, he reckoned, cost the Union £5O pir annum He thought an advance of £2O was quite tufficient for the present time.—Mr. HARRISON spoke in favour of Mr. Black- hurst's proposals. He did not think there was much in the argument about the assistant' master, because the late Mr. Mackie was assisted by an old inmate who unfortunately got 4im into trouble. The appointment of an assistant master had also been recommended by the poor-law inspector.—Mr. DARBYKIIRE said he should fetl pleased if Mr. Blackhurst's recommendation wgs carried out.—Mr. GREENING, speaking as chairman of the House Committee, said he did not think that the Committee would think the carrying of Mr. Blackhurst's proposal as a slight in the least.—Mr. Ilueron spoke in favour of the increase; and Mr. STRANGE expressed his opinion that Mr. Ward's salary ought to be advanced by £2O —Mr. Blackhurst's proposal was then put to the meeting and carried unaniniously.—Mr. RATCLIFFE thought that candidates for places under the Boaro ought in fugire to take the salaries offered in advertisements as definite.—The minutes of the House Committee, as amended, were then adopted.

div.head: APPOINT-MENT OF NURSE.
div.p: APPOINT-MENT OF NURSE.

In accordance with -previous -n—o-tle-e., Mr. GREENING moved that "Miss Daniels, of the Union Workhouse, Thirsk, Yorkshire, be appointed to the position of nurse in the female hospital at the Workhouse, at the annual salary of £25 with rations, furnished apartments, Sm., as determined at the last meeting."—This having been seconded by Mr. JONES, was agreed to.

div.head: VACANT RELIEVING OPFICERSRIP.
div.p: THE VACANT RELIEVING OPFICERSRIP.

The Board next_proceeded to the election of a relieving officer, inquiry officer, and collector for No. 2 or Newton district, from the following seelcted candidates : Wm. John Caldwell (23), Newton, temperory relieving officer; David Davies (40), Earlestown, iron moulder ; John Fair- dough, jun. (28), Burtonwood, farmer; J. H. Graham (35), Earlestown, railway clerk; E J. Mitchell (39), War- rington, club manager ; and N. B. Powlson (35), War- rington, bookeeper, The first voting resulted as follows :—Caldwell 18, Davies 4, Fairclough 9, Graham 11, Mitchell 14, Powlson 6. The three candidates who had received Atie smallest number of votes—Messrs. Davies, FaircloughTkaad Powl- son—were then thrown out of the contest,which now lay between Mr. Caldwell, who received 17 votes; Mr. Graham, who received 8 votes;, and Mr. Mitchell, who received 13 votes. Mr. Graham having,been disposed of, the final selection lay between Messrs. Caldwell and Mitchell, the latter receiving 4 votes, and the former 17. Mr. Caldwell was, therefore, elected.

A fire on Wednesday afternoon caused damage to the extent of £2,500 at the works of Messrs. Margerison and Co.. firelight manufacturers, at Preston. The mail steamer Calabar, which arrived inthe Mersey on Thursday, brings intelligence of fighting among the natives in the region of the upper reaches of the Gambia. H.M.S. Goshawk had been despatched up the river to assist in putting an end to the hostilities. •

THE CRISIS IN THE COAL THADE.—The strike which commenced on Tuesday at the Yorkshire collieries was considerably extended on Wednesday, when, their notices having expired, several thousand men left work. Although in some cases the masters have conceded the men's demand, the great majority of the owners remain firm in their resistance to it, and there is likely to be a prolonged struggle. In Yorkshire—the only country in which as yet the miners' strike has actual' assumed serious proportions—the men engaged at several large pits ceased working on Thursday. Although the majority of the owners shoVr no sign of yielding, the feeling among them as a body is not unanimous, and the colliers hope that the fast of the advance in wages having been granted in some cases will assist them in obtaining the concession all round.
TOBACCONISTS COMMENCING.—See Illustrated Guide, post free.—Tobacoonists's Outfitting Co., Beech-et., Loudon, E.O. —Advt.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

An inquest was held on Monday itt Manchester touch- ing the death of Jonathan Spearitt, lately living at Heaton-street, Union-street, Ardwick. On Saturday afternoon the deceased went to act as umpire at the , football match played under Rugby rules at Slade Lane, and one side being a member short he took part in the game. During the play he went off the field and had some brandy, and after that ha took no active part, but occasionally kicked the ball when it came near him. A few minutes before the game ended the deceased was found lying dead just outside the ropes. Mr. W. J. Heslop, surgeon, Stretford-road, made an eximination of the body. and said death was due to heart disease of an acute kind. The jury returned a verdict of death from naiural causes. The Cheshire team for the match Cheshirev. Westmor- land, which will be played at Runcorn on the 31st inst., is as follows :—J. Braz,endale (Runcorn), back; T. H. Davies (Runcorn), C. J. Luya, and W. H. Male (New Brighton), three-quarter backs; H. Hughes (Runcorn) and L. R. Paterson (Birkenhead Park), halfbacks; A. G. Wood, K. Monteath, N. Allardice, P. 11. Lockwood 1 (Birkenhead Park), W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, Or. T. Wainwright (Runcorn), R. F. Muir (New Brighton), and H..A. Howe (Sale), forwards. The "Colliers" visited Widnes on Saturday, and inflicted a severe defeat on the Chemicals. With the exception of their captain (Plumpton) Widnes had their full strength, but, according to impartial eye witnesses, were quite unable to cope with the smart tactics of Wigan. The absence of Pluippton had without question, a disorganising effect upon the back play of the home team, but there would seem to be a lack of combination all round, and if this want were supplied, we should have to oftener record the success of the Widnes Club. There is much good material to work upon, but an able tntor appears to be imperatively necessary. A' hard fought and even game took place at Manchester. between Broughton Rangers and Runcorn, but the Cheshire champions kept up their reputation for speed, staying power, and combination, and added their sixth victory to this season's record. So far only one match has been lost (Bradford) and, if present form is kept up, there appears to be no likelihood of another being "added to the list" for some ,time to come. In seven matches Runcorn have scored 12 goals, 7 tries, and 39 minors to their opponents 1 goal, 2 tries' and 12 minor points, and amongst the vanquished are four first-class clubs. ,

The St. Helens (Rugby) club met Morecambe, at St. Helens, on Saturday, and exceptional interest was mani- fested as the visitors sustained a defeat by the Recs. on the previous Saturday. The visitors were much the heavier lot and possessed =advantage in thescrimmages. but the home team were otherwise in splendid form, and their victory of two tries and one minor to four minors was well deserved.

The Recreation team had Radcliffe as their opponents. The home fifteen kept up their good form of the present season by sending them back defeated by one goal, one try and eleven minors, to one goal and one minor. The local Association Championship was played be- tween Whiston and St. Helens Association clubs. The match took place at Whiston. The play was verj fast, though, if anything, St. Helens had rather the(nest of the ghme. They were certainly unlucky in havi g two points credited against them, while one of the easiest possible chances of scoring was missed by the rash kick- ing of one of the St. Helens forwards. A hard-fought game resulted in a draw of three'goals each. ,The Earlestown first team, short of the brothers J. and W. Shaw, Sims, and Champion, journeyed to Chester on , Saturday and met the Chester Club. The home team were declared the winners, much to the dissatisfaction of the visitors—by three goals to two. The Haydock Club sustained a severe reverse at South- port. They met the High Park Club, and the latter won by five goals to one. A team representing Liverpool and District met the Renfrewshire County team at Liverpool on Saturday, and the result was a victory for Liverpool by four goals to two. The winning eleven included the brothers 3. and W. Shaw and T. Champion, of the Earlestown Club. The brothers Shaw were loudly cheered, while Cham- pion's defence in goal was very good.

div.head: AMERIOAN LETTER:BY MR. WHITHAM.
div.p: AMERIOAN LETTER:BY MR. WHITHAM.
The ftillewingisthe letter referred to by Mr. H. Whitham last week. We take it from the columns of the " San Francisco Morning Call :'— "IT'S ENGLISH, YE KNOW."

Sir,—A little while ago you kindly allowed me a little space in your paper to make a few remarks. Please grant this privilege once more. As a new arrival in your famous city, I,naturally look with some wonder at the various interesting phenomena I witness around me. Much that I see I admire, and I am serry to say very much more that I see sets my teeth on edge. The very, severe struggle now going on betwixt the two political parties occupies. of course, the first place in my attention. As a worker I am deeply interested in the question now being so earnestly debated on the different platforms as to whether or no protection or the modified free trade list of the Plesident, or, shall I say, the Mills Bill, shall or shall not be the American policy of the future. Working as I do among a goodly number of those whose votes count and whose opinions are of some importance, I natur- ally listen, and in a manner place myself at the feet of the Gamaliels around me, and what is the result? This: lam stricken with dismay to find that not one workman out of twenty believes in the honour and truth of any one of the leading poli- ticians of either party. Nay, they do more than, this—or shall I say worse than this ?—they enter into what they call the "fun of the thing," hoping, by and by, to participate in the profits which they assert will come before November goes out. I, in a manner, a looker-on, ask myself, often, to what will it all lead?. Can it by any possible turn of events work out for the good and welfare of this, the land of my adoption? There is but one answer: No! I listen to speakers, read the articles in "The Call," and" Chronicle," and note the pictures in the two leading protection papers. I am bound to confess the impression made on my mind is simply, one of disgust. So far as the pictures go, it seems to me that pure and unadulterated insult is intended, not only for England, but for all English- men who have made this country their honie. It

isn't "English, ye know," to in'sult the stranger within your gate. More than this, it is not good policy. For quite a number of years now, through- out urope, has the tidings been borne that in this vast continent there was room enough -for all. American gold has paid for thousands of articles in European newspapers depicting in the most glow- ing colors the benefits to be derived, both by artisan and agriculturist, in this vast spreading continent, but now the time seems to be changed. Instead of cordial welcome, insult is meted out ; especially is this so to Englishmen. Why is this so? Do Englishmen fail in their duty as citizens? Do the California police courts know more of the presence of Englishmen than of other nationalities? Why, your own columns testify, in the reeent sketch given of criminal records, that Englishmen head the list as moral and law-abiding citizens. What is the secret, then, of the animus shown towards us? Is it that English- men are at the head and front • of nearly all the industrial establishments of the country, while Other nationalities govern and control the mere distributing channels? Is the feeling, one bears and sees so much of, conveyed in the term "It's English, ve know," simply the outcome of more petty childish jealchisy ? I fear it is, and as such, believe me, it is an infallible sign of weakness, and the sooner it is got rid of the better for the nation. In the Woman's Column I always find interesting matter. Not always do I find it improvirg; A recent lady writer, denouncing the practice of ladies carrying pug dogs in their arms, must drag in the phrase "It's English,ye know, which no true

div.head: COST OF UNION OFFICIALS.
div.p: THE COST OF UNION OFFICIALS.

In answer to a question by Mr. W. Houghton, the CLFRK said that the salaries of Union Officials came to about 7-Bths of a penny in the £ on the rates; that was to say, that, if the poor-rate was 10d. or is in the £, 7-Bths IV a penny of the 10d, or is. would be absorbed in the payment of the salaries of Union Officials.

div.head: NOTICE OF QUESTION.
div.p: NOTICE OF QUESTION.

Mr. RATCLIFFE said that at the next meeting he would ask a question as to the number of paupers in the vari- ous townships of the Union as compared with the rate- able value of those townships. This was all the business of public interest.

THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS IN WARRINGTON. MEETING OF MR. LONGTON'S SUPPORTERS. On Tuesday evening a meeting of the supporters of Mr. H. J. Longton, cine of the candidates for Latch- ford ward, was held in the Wesleyan Mission-room, St. James-street, Latchford. Councillor W. Pier- point presided, and there was a fair attendance. i A NON-POLITICAL CONTEST. The CHAIR.MAN said it would bf necessity seem a rather singular proceeding that he, a pronounced Liberal, should be acting as chairman of a meeting called together for the purpose of furthering the candidature of a pronounced, active, and, he believed, a fairly intelli- gent member of the Conservative party. He should like to explain how that came about. They knaw that in Warrington there was a body called the Ratepayers' Association of which he happened to be a member, and of which Mr. Longton was also a member. That body was called into existence by some large ratepayers of the town who felt dissatisfied with the action of the Tow's Council in directions that were leading to a great expen- diture of money. Last November the Ratepayers' Associa- tion managed to introduce three of its members as representatives in the Council, and this year they decided again to ask gentlemen to allow themselves to be nominated for different wards of the town. The Association having come to that conclusion, he, as owing allegiance to it, and believing in the principles it was endeavouring to enunciate and forward, thought he was in his proper position in taking the chair at Mr. Long- ton's meeting. He understood that the action he was taking that night in occupying that platform would have the effect of creating opposition against himself in the north-west ward. He did not object to that opposition, but he did hope that those gentlemenwho took exception to his aspiring to the position of still representing the north-west ward would put somebody up who would advocate the Sanitary Committees' Scheme. He was willing to take that as a test question and to let the poll show whether the present policy of the Sanitary Com- mittee was one that met with the approval of the rate- payers or not (Hear, hear, and applause.) A POLITICAL ARRANGEMENT. Mr. Lorimar,' said that for the last ten years there had been an agreement between the two political parties whereby the Conservative Association was to nominate the representative for Latchford Ward. Mr. Taylor, therefore, as one of the members, had had no opposition in any shape or form; he could not have had any oppos. ition because no reasonable man would have dared to oppose him, because they knew they would have the United opposition of the Liberal and Conservative Associ- ation to contend against. The ratepayers of the ward had consequently had no voice as to their representation except through the ponservativo Association. Matters to-day were, however, somewhat different, as the two political parties had determined not to take any further part as political associations in these elections. HIGH RATES. He was in the field because those who had asked him to come forward were not satisfied with the rates of the borough. They were of opinion that the rates were too high, and they were also of opinion that some emphatic Protests should be sent from BS many wards as possible, and especially from Latchford ward, in order that the members of the Town Council might no longer be asleep, as it were, but respond to the feeling of the town with respdst to the rates. That was really and pre-eminently the position he took in that matter. He said the rates were too high, and he thought, every pcssible means should be taken to reduce them. The Sanitary Corn- mittie, in particular, had during the last few years been a rdost expensive Committee to the ratepayers. They had spent in round figures something like £20,000 on the machinery at Longford and on the works there, and they had raised the yearly expenditure of the borough by something like £4,000. He did not think the Sanitary Committee had acted like business men. They had, he thought, gone intoan experimental policyand linatpolicy had turned out a failure. (Hear, hear.) As an illustra- tion of the effects of high rates, Mr. Longtpn mentioned that two large firms were removing their business establishments from Manchester solely on account of the saving that would be effected in rates. (Hear, hear.) WHO MR. TAYLOIA REPRESENTS. If Mr. Taylor went into the Council the only Associ- ation he would represent would be the Licensed Vic- tuallers' Association. (Laughter.) That Association had already one representative from Latchford in Mr. Ashton, and, as he did not think beer was the principal industry in Latchford he thought the beer trade was already sufficiently represented. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Longton then spoke in favour of a reduction in the price of gas to consumers, and said that he got his figures as to the leakage given in his address from the yearly state- ment of the Corporation accounts. (Applause.) THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. Questions having been invited, Mr. J. WALKER asked Mr. Longton as to his views on the question of freeing the public library. In reply, Mr. LowoDox said he had not had time to go iwo the question as fully as he should like, but he could as a lawyer answer the question as regarded lending the books at a charge, that neither the Library Committee nor anybody else had any legal right or authority to make a charge in any shape or form. (Hear, hear.) The Corporation were restricted to a rate of a penny in the pound for the support of the library and that amount was taken already, but even if that were not so he was not going to stand in the way of the education of the peonle, and he believed that the free lending of books was a great boon. (Applause.) THE ENFORCEMENT OF THE LICENSING LAWS. Mr. J. WALKER asked if,as a member of the Town Council, Mr. Longton would be prepared to put what pressure he could on the Watch Committee to get them to carry out the law as it exists. A good many people were brought up and convicted of drunkenness and in nine cases out of ten somebody had been guilty besides the men picked up in the streets but they yen' very rarely saw the man who made others drunk brought before the magistrates, although the law said that should be done. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. LONGTON : I have very much pleasure in answering " Yes " to Mr. Walker's question. (Applause.) Mr. E. Twrss then moved a resolution that Mr. Long- ton was a fit and propoiterson to represent Latchford in the Town Council, and pledging. the meeting to use every, legitimate means to secure his return—This pro- posal was seconded by Mr. J. WALKER, and carried all but unanimously, only two hands being held up against it.=-A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Mr. Longton, and seconded by Councillor Dixon, brought the meeting to a close. .

div.p: MR. TAYLOR'S CANMDATURE.

_ A meeting of the supporters of Mr. Taylor, the retir- ing memlxr of the Town Council for Latchford, was convened for Thursday night, in St. James' schoolroom, Latchford, but owing to the disqualification of Mr. Longton, Mr. Taylor's opponent, the meeting was not proceeded with after this Circumstance' had been explained. At the time advertised for starting—eight o'clock—there was a fair attendance, Alderman Chandley took the chair, being supported on the platform by Councillors J. Taylor (candidate), and J. V. Taylor. MR. LONGTON'S DISQUALIFICATION. The CumnstiN said they only intended to keep the audience there a few moments to announce the fact that the qualification of Mr. Longton was erased, the des- cription in his nomination paper being wrong, and the Mayor that afternoon had found it invalid. Mr. Longton had described himself wrongfully, and net only so, but he (Alderman Chandley) had been told by the deputy-town clerk that the latter had told Mr. Longton thedescription he was giving of himself was informal and illegal, but the latter pooh-poohed this and said he knew better—the qualification was right and he should adhere to it. He had, therefore, only himself to blame for being thrown out of the contest (Hear, hear). They did, not wish to cast any reflection on Mr. Longton, who was a young man, and would perhaps know better another time., (Laughter).

Taylor. The temperance ques- tion has not been made a test question at this election, and there is no Liberal candidate in the field. If either of these circumstances had arisen I should have had no hesi4tion in offering to Mr. Taylor a strong, conscien- tious but not personal opposition. Another question of very greatimportance to the good government of the borough has, however, been prominently brought for- ,ward by Mr. H. J. Longton and that is the manner in Which the sanitary work of town has been conducted for years past. I looked upon Mr. Longton's candida- ture as an attack upon the general policy of the Sanitary Committee, a policy which, I venture to say, has on the whole met with a success unequalled in any borough in Lancashire, and, as a member of the Sanitary Com- mittee, I was not disposed to submit tamely to Mr. Longton's attack or to allow his fallacious assertions to go uncontradicted. This then is my excuse for ventur- mg into a contest which has come to so untimely an end."—A letter of apology for non-attendance was also read from Mr. William Tinsley.

LECTURE ON "LORD TENNYSON.° On Monday evening an excellent lecture on "Lord Tennyson" was given in the Bold-st. Wesleyan Schoolroom, Warrington, by the Rev. R. P. Downes, of London, editor of "Great Thoughts." Mr. W. Owen, All 1.8. A., presided, and briefly introduced the lecturer. TENNYSON'S PLACE AS A POET. The Rev. R. P. Downes said Lord Tennyson did not stand in the first 'rank of poets, in the rank of men like Shakespeare and Dante ; he could not be said to stand even in the rank of men like Wordsworth. He did not create for them a picture, but delicately described one already before them. He did not with one flash of splendid power, open up the infinite, but rather particularised the finite; he dealt in method and detail. His genius was microscopic rather than telescopic; subtle rather than sublime. Lord Tennyson must be carefully read if he is to be appreciated as he deserves. He possesses a keen mind, subtle, passionless, often remarkable rather for intensity of intellect than for intensity of feel- ing, watching his consciousness with minute attention to fix and condense and shape into forin the vague shadows of thought and feeling that flitted across it, and scrupulously careful in every touch and tint of his almost unrivalled pencil. (Applause.)

div.head: GREAT POETIC ARTIST,
div.p: A GREAT POETIC ARTIST,

Lord Tennyson was, perhaps, the noblest poetic artist the world had ever known, and in that judgment they did not except the great William Shakespeare himself, for the genius of that mighty master was so great that it seemed to shape his creations for him. They traced in him no labour of the sculptor's chisel ; he "toils not neither does he spin." He was' a king, the sceptre being natural to his hand and the purple his proper wear. (Applause.) With Tennyson it was not so. They knew his continual, careful, and delicate toil. "Come into the garden, Maud," one of the most charming of his songs, is said to have been written fifty times before it caught the perfect shape in which we now possess it. " Locksley Hall " cost him six weeks of arduous labour and the stanzas of." In Memoriarii "were repeated again and again to the chime of the silver sea before they pos- sessed the perfect music in which they are now uttered. He had been charged with a refinement that was exces- sive and one critic, whose impertinence surpasses his discrimination, calls him " Miss Tennyson. But there are many poems of Alfred Tennyson which declare that beneath the broad-cloth culture of the genpeman there sobs a soul passionate, swift, and proud, and that his keen blade can split a helmet as well as sever a silken thread. (Hear, hear.) PURITY OE TENNY9ON. They found also through all the exquisite poetry of ' Tennyson that he had not written a line which at death he might desire he had not written. It had evidently been his intention to oppose the modern fleshly school of Swinburn among poets and " Ouida " among novelists, a Woman whose novels he hoped were never found in the hands of any one in that school.

div.head: HIS MODERN SYMPATHIES-.
div.p: HIS MODERN SYMPATHIES-.

Tennyson was also memorable because of his keen sympathy with his own age. He did not sing of some far-back age in which we had never lived and with which we had no sympathy, but he addressed hirriself to the men of his own time, seeking to inspire them to worthier and nobler aims. We do not compare him with men like Shakespeare,to Dante and Milton,but what they did for the age in which they lived he is doing for this age of ours, and as the age in which those meif lived is embalmed in their poems, so in the fine amber of Tennyson's words, the history of this century will be embalmed for the study of after generations. They found also that\ he is in keen sympathy with modera science, but while he does not hesitate to light his thought at the, torch which science bears with an onward beckoning hand his soul continually rises against the materialistic assumptions of science. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The lecturer next gave a brief sketch of the poet's career, and also in the course of the lecture gave admirable recitations from the poems under his notice; that of the" Charge of the Light Brigade" being enthusiastically applauded. Tilt usual votes a thanks to the lecturer and chair- man brought the meeting to a close.

• 'NEW'BOOKS Szc • The Hansom Cab Publishing Company are fol- lowing up the success they obtained in issuing "The Mystery of a Hansom Cab" by the young Australian author, Mr. Fergus Hume. "Madame Midas " is the title of a new novel by the same clever writer. It is an altogether readable book, but it is not so absorbingly interesting as his first work. The various characters are distinctly drawn, but with an exaggerateß, Dickens-tendency to humorous exaggeration. The weakest part of the story is the end; it is not that there is a lack of graphic description ; but the surprises are strained, and of the sensational drama kind. Mr. Hume has, however, made his mark, and will Continue to be read. " His Last Passions," by Martius, is published by the same firm, and it is to be wished that they had some- thing better to publish. The story is not badly written quite the reverse of that; but it is• a story which is not worth- telling. It is at times too realistid; and cannot be said to be conducive to mental or moral health. The writer is capable of better things. Those who are interested in military matters will wel- come Mr. Arthur Law's sixpenny pamphlet on "The Less of the Empire, a revelation of the alarming condition of; our NationalDefenees." It gives a large number of facts which require to be duly considered, but the conclusions axe of an altogether alaiming kind. Mr. Law dock not take sufficiently into account the fact that England is surrounded by water and that that alone, in the way of defence, is worth a million of men to us. • "The Westminster Review" ought to be on the table of every club—especially every political club. It is becoming more and more a factor in determining opinion on all sorts of social and political questiens. "A Fore- cast " is given of the next general election in which the writer who, as it seerks to us, is too sanguine predicts a majotity of 64 for the Gladstonian Liberals. Amongst other topics ably dealt with are ;—The Scriptural doctrine concerning Marriage and Divorce; Causes of Popular Sympathy with Ireland; Poverty; The House of Lords; Pampered Sport and Pheasant Rearing; Elementary Education &c. ; and there is .the customary trenchant review of Home Affairs. . The great feature of Scribner's Magazine for this m i onth s aValuable paper on the "Temples of Egypt," by Mr. E. L. Wilson. The illustrations are from draw- ings by Mr J. D. Woodward, and it is due to say of them that they are the high-water mark of work of this class. They are numerous and obviously faithful. Mr. Lester Wallack contributes a first paper on "Memories of the last fifty years " ; and its interest is enhanced by portraits of eminent American actors, &c. The." Rail- road in its business relations" is also illustrated, the first portrait being that of George Stephenson. Photo- graphy has been laid i,nder contribution In "Behind the scenes in an opera house," while Mr. R. L. Stevenson photographs with his pen in "Contributions to the " History of life." "The plot of some of the most famous of old English plays "is a little work from the pen of Mr. Henry Grey, who has a special aptitude for tasks of this kind, as witness " Birds Eye View of English History" and "Key to the Waverley Novels." It may be mentioned that Shakespeare's plays are not included, as .they were epitomised by Charles Lamb. Accompanying each account. of plot, there is an index of the principal characters. The work is throughout well done. The publishers are Messrs Griffiths, Farren & Co., London. A new volume begins with the current issue .of the English Illustrated Magazine published by Messrs. Mac- Millen & Co. The magazine has been enlarged, and it is besides, altogether strong both in matter and illustration. The frontispiece is a really fine engraving of Gerard Dow's portrait of himself. Mr. A. C. Swinburne contributes a characteristicpoem. "John Hoppner and his time," is charmingly illustrated by portraits of charming women. " A Dead City," by Mr. James Haler is illustrated by Mr. , Walter Crane; and there .is also an illustrated paper on "The Motto D'Arthur," basides. continued stories, &c. The English Illustrated is unequalled as a sixpenny fine- art magazine. "'Hie Ladies' Treasury" for October has for frontis- piece,a very pretty picture with the title of the "Mussel Gatherers," and there is a brief paper on the subject. The " Short Biographies of same of the Armada men" are interesting, especially as they are illustrated. As ' usual, the contents are very varied, and there is a large space devoted to description, and illustration of the latest fashions.
