RUNCORN PUBLICANS IN COURT.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst, Henry Jackson, landlord of Wilson's Hotel, Bridge-st., was charged with having permitted drunkenness en his premises ; and also with serving drink to a drunken person.—David Jones. was charged with being drunk on licensed premises.—Mr. A. Pletcher, of Northwich, defended.—lnspector O'Donnell said that on Sunday night, the 14th inst, he visited the vaults I of the Wilson's Hotel, in copipany with, Constables Hulse and Brew. They ,found a man named .David 'Jones there •he was drunk. Asked where his beer was, Jones stepped to anothei part of the counter, and took up a pint mug, filled with ale, and said, "This is mine." He asked the girl in the bar if she had supplied Jones. and she replied "No." Mr. Jackson was then fetched in, and he said "Some of the girls" had supplied the man.—By Mr. Fletcher: When he told Jones he was drunk the latter said "You're a liar," and refused to give • his natne.—P.C. Hulse gave corroborative evidence.-15.C. Brew, was also I called, and deposed that the Inspector asked Jones , where his beer was, and he replied that he had none. ; Hulse then pointed out a pint cup of beer about two lyards away, and the girl said that belonged to a man who had just gone out. Jones then stepped up and said "this is my beer."—Mr. Fletcher_ asked the Bench whether a more trumpery case was ever brought into Court than the one now before:them ; whether they had ever had a case against's, licensed victualler in which there was so much ammus shown by the police—such' strain- ing and studying and desire to obtain a conyiction., The evidence of Constable Brew of what took place a,greed in almost every detail with the evidence of Mr. Jackson. Mr. Jackson was in another part of the house, and about 9.30 the servant girl came to him to say there were two men in the bar. Mr. Jackson directed her to serve the men, one of whom was named Ellis and the other Bayley, with beer. While these meu were in the bar Mr. Jackson went in, and a man, apparently .a Shiß Canal navvy, entered and was supplied with a pint of ale. He asked where the closet was, and Q,II being 'directed, left the place without drinking his beer. Wm. Jackson left the bar and there were then only. Ellis and Bayley in the room. In about ten minutes he received word that the police were there, and went into the bar. An altercation was then going on between the officers and Jones as to the condition of the latter. Constable Brew distinctly admitted that the police were told that Jones had not been supplied with beer ; and that the pint-of ale be- longed to a man who had lus: gone out. He (Mr. Fletcher) asked why Inspector O'Donnell kept back that evidence? If Inspector O'Donnell had no animus against the licensed victuallers, why did he keep back statements made when everything was fresh, and when there was no time to coin falsehoods, if he thought the defence did coin falsehoods? It was immaterial to the defence, Whether Jones was drunk or sober, because he was not supplied in the house. On the whole case there had been a straining to get a conviction against a man who was trying to conduct his house properly, and he hoped their Worships would say that Mr. Jackson left the court without an imputation upon his character.— He called Mr. Jackson who corroborated this statement and said the navvy who ordered the beer returned in a quarter of an hour and drank it. If Jones had asked for a glass of ale, he should have supplied him— James Ellis, uncle to the servant, also corroborated and said Jones was net drunk.—Emma Ellis said Jones was not supplied with beer, and was not drunk—Mr. Isaac Speakman, chemist, Bridge.st., said he saw Jones pass- ing along the street, and the constable asked him was Jones drunk. He replied "No" ; the man was capable of going home steady and, straight. He might have had some drink, but was no. drunk. He was a surly man, had an impediment in his speech, and a peculiar gait that might mislead people who did not know him.—The Bench fined Jones ss. and costs for being drunk, and dis- missed both charges against Mr. Jackson.

WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY. Sir.—The "unsatisfactory condition" of the Musical Society seems just now to be occupying the minds of some Warringtonians. Many suggestions have been put forward to improve matters, some of which are perhaps worthy of consideration • others, by far the largest pro- portion, are absurd; and based on a lamentable ignorance of the constitution of the Society and its management. When things are not quite what they might be, there are always many persons who are loud in the expression of their opinion, ready with their advice, and quite will- ing and anxious to effect a revolution in the existing state of things, until they become personally responsible and have everything before them, when, in nine cases out of ten, their voice is no more heard. Referring to the two letters in a recent issue, that by an" Old Subscriber" is written in a fair spirit, and in moderation, though in a few points he requires correc- tion ; but I should imagine" An Amateur is young and inexperienced, and wofully ignorant of the existing state of things as regards the Musical Society. "An old Subscriber "asks," Is the Committee truly re- presentative of a Musical Society ?" I say yes • but, for the moment, allow that it is not so ; what is the cause? Simply that the general meetings are rot representative. In other words, these meetings are generally poorly attended, in spite of all the notices sent out and the advertisements. The result is that the Committee and other officers are usually re-elected with slight altera- tions. If, therefore, the Committee are not represegta- tive, the blame can only rest with those who, having other views, will not come and put them forward at the proper time and place. As regards the conductor: Till within the last few weeks there has not to my knowledge been any expression of opinion as to whether he is acceptable to the sub- scribers or not. If he is not, I should suggest that those having this opinion attend the next meeting and raise the point. That Dr. Hiles is very popular, and much liked by the choir, is certain, nor can anyone justly deny his skill as a conductor and choir master. Certainly he has not been successful and popular with Warrington instrumentalists, but may not this have been due to mis- understanding arising from amateurs having a tendency to over-estimate their powers, and to take offence if, according to their views, sufficient trust is not placed in them. The 3rd question relates to members. I can only say that Dr. Hiles has always expressed his opinion as to the neeeesity of any new member passing a test and of his being satisfied as to his or her capabilities. To say that these tests are a farce is hardly fair to Dr. Hiles, and certainly the Committee have never empowered him to lower the test. Next, as to rehearsals. "An Old Subscriber's" suggestion as to weekly rehearsals is again a matter that could, I think, only be discussed at a general meeting. At regards Mr. Yeerman and the Orchestral Society, Dr. Hiles was in no way responsible for the collapse of that Society •, it ceased to e,xist solely because it proved impossible to get amateler instrumentalists together who would undergo the amount of work necessary to a successful performance. "An Old Subscriber" concludes by disparaging - the performances. I maintain that few choirs do better work. If it is the principals who are deficient, the only remedy is increased support. Turning to "An Amateur's" letter,as a member of the Committee I emphatically deny the statements contained in the first paragraph of his let er, That Dr. Hiles has _roadg suggestions, and that hiS suggestiona have been listened to arid dtgcussed by tht Committee, is true, but if" Amateur " knows, as he professes, any- thing about the working of such societies, he must also know that no conductor worthy of the name would act i unless this were the case. His remark as to the utility of a society like the Warrington Musical Society is to the point and true, and there may be something in what he says as to the time of rehearsals, but his insinuation that members of the choirs are driven away by Dr. Riles'] sarcastic remarks is not, nor is the inference which he draws in this paragraph of his letter. "An Amateur" next makes an unqualified and unjustifi- able attack on the President of the Musical Society. Perhaps" Amatuer " is not aware that the society was founded in 1834, nor of the fact that the president has rendered valuable service as assistant secretary, secre- tary, treasurer, and president, having been intimately connected with it from the first. If not, he may learn it now. Further, I maintain that he still takes an active interest in the society, and that if he does not work as formerly, his advice, based on the experience of more than half a century, is invaluable. As to Mr. Down I have no wish to disparage him or his work. I am not personally acquainted with him, and the only time I addressed him was when the Musical Society was endeavouring to form a band. Knowing how much he was interested in instrumental music, and that he was closely associated with Warrington amateurs, I asked him to use his influence with members of his band to induce some of them to join the Musical Society, but without success. "An Amateur" lays down rules very dogmatically for the proper working of the society. Since he has such knowledge, and can use it to such good purpose, let him prove his sincerity by supporting the society by taking a keen interest in it; let him get appointed to the committee, and then bring his theories to bear. The constitution of the Warrington Musical Society stamps it as a public society. Its objects have never been lost sight of, and it is much to be deplored that its work has been so much hindered by causes and events over which the officials of the society have had, :and could have had, no control. If all those who are dissatisfied with the existing state of things, and so ready to find fault, would be a little more charitable, or, betterA still, would support the society—attend all meeting C and bring their influence to bear in an effectual and legitimate way, it would be far better and more generous than trying to increase the existing difficulties, and, further, would be far more more likely to attain thedesired ends This letter is entirely unofficial and is not meant to challenge a correspondence, for whidlt I have neither time nor inclination. It would not have been written at all, had I not felt it incumbent upon me, seeing that I have been so intimately connected with the Musical Society, especially in connection with the instrumental part of the work, to ptt sitters in their true light.—l am Are., JOHN P. REYNOLDS. Beech House, Latchford, Warrington. Oct., 1888.

CRUELTY TO HORSES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, William White, greengrocer, Runcorn, was charged with hat ing, on the Ist inst., caused a horse to be cruelly illtreated by allowing it to be worked in an unfit state.—P.C. 17-7 proved that the defendant's boy was driving the horse, which had four wounds on different parts of the body.— Inspector Aplin. R.S.P.C.A. described the condition of the horse and said he told die defendant he ought to be ashamed to travel the horse a hundred yards. The defendant stated that he had the horse destroyed on the following day.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.— Thorrias:Holland, greengrocer, Warrington, was charged with causing a horse to be worked in an unfit state, and Wm. Barlow, his servant, was charged with cruelly illtreating the animal by "forking the same. Both defendants pleaded guilty.—P.C. Royle stated that on the afternoon of the 13th inst. he saw Barlow driving a mare attached to a lurry loaded with greengroceries. He found three wounds on the horse : one the size of the palm of his hand, was on its chine discharg- ing matter. The horse was so weak that it could scarcely walk along the road without the lurry.—lnspector Aplin said he saw the horse on the 14th inst. and advised Holland to have it destroyed. Holland said he would not have allowed the horse to have been worked had he known it was so bad.—Each defendant was filled 10s., and costs 10s. Bd.

SANKEY Smoot. BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the school, Great Sankey, on Thursday, when there were present: Messrs. 4. C. Ridgway (chairman), Grange, Hatton, and S. Sutton (clerk.) The Clerk reported that there was a balance in favour of the Board of .£llB 18s. Bd. Mr. Clarke, the head master, presented hiamonthly return which shewed that the number of scholars on the books at the end of September, was 240, number present 238, average 221.7, and the total receipts for the month £l5 14s. 3d.—The Clerk stated that he had received from the Education Department the schedules of the recent examinntion by Mr. Harrison, Her Majesty's Inspector, and, taking everything into consideration, the children had passed a very fair examination. It was decided to allow to Mr. Davies, the assistant master, who had passed 96 per cent. of his scholars, a bonus of .£lO. This was all the business of public interest.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY '4 ARIEL."

That the appeal of the Manchester Ship Canal Company against the increased assessment of their i property n the Runcorn Union will be heard at Chester on Friday next. That the Assessment Committee have retained Sir Richard Webster to appear on their behalf, but as that legal luminary is so busily engaged with " Pamellism and Crime" at the present time, it is extremely unlikely that he will attend the inquiry. That the question is asked "What will become of the heavy retaining fee paid to Sir Richard if he does not appear?" That the bazaar in aid of the Runcorn Catholic Church promises to be a most successful affair, and the friends at St. Edward's have the good wishes of other sects and parties. That religious bigotry and party passion dis- appears before the genial smile and outstretched hand of Dr. Gastildi, and that on Wednesday afternoon Mr. Brunner will receive a cordial welcome from an audience composed of Catholics, Churchmen, and Nonconformists. That it is hoped that the energetic priest will have the satisfaction of wiping off a good portion of the heavy debt on his church. That the public of Widnes do not seem very eager to invest in the Conservative Club Company, Limited. That the project has been launched for a period of two years, and .so far only 1,200 of the 2,500 shares issued have been taken dp. That perhaps this is the reason why the Company yesterday informed the spectators that contri- butions could be placed on the corner stone. That it is not a pleasant augury for' the Club that charity should be invoked before the Company have erected the structure.
SELLING ADULTERATED ADULTERATED LARD AT WIDNES.

Mr. Edward Johnson, of St. Helens, who carries on business at Widnes, St. Helens, and other towns, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thurs- day, to answer a charge of having sold impure lard.' —P.C. Thompson stated that on Friday the 14th September he visited the defendant's shop in Widnes-rd., and purchastd a pound of lard for which he paid 6d. The manager, Owen Monagan, said he would not sell it as pure lard. Mr. Johnson afterwards came into the shoo and made a similar statement. —Superinten- dent Johnston handed in, the analyst's certificate which stated that the lard was adulterated with 25 per cent, of cotton seed oil and fats other than lard. The superintendent added that the defendant called upon him, and he did not then dispute the ownership of the shop. He asked if the case could not be 'withdrawn and he was told "No."—The defendant contended that the shop was not his; it was carried on by his son Charles. In the second place, supposing the shop had been his, he should' not have known that ,he was doiag anything contrary to the law in selling that lard as a mixture. The lard was originally sent from America as pure, and Messrs. Polling and Stanley, the Liverpool agents, had sold it as pure lard , until a prosecution took place. The firkins were then branded as " lardine," and the agents told the retail dealers they were quite safe, and meeting the require- ments of the law in selling the mixture as lard.—P.C. Thompson recalled said the lard was not labelled lardine. —The Bench remarked that this was a clear case, but as Mr. Johnson had not been up for a similar offence, they would only impose a light fine of ss. and costs 225.

div.head: LORD CRANBORNE AT WIDSES CON-
div.p: LORD CRANBORNE AT WIDSES CON-
SERVATIVE CLUB.

Yesterday the ceremony of laying the corner stone of a new Conservative Club, which is in course of erection on land adjoining the Drill Hall, was performed by Lord Cranborne M.P. for the Darwen Division. The club will be in the Elizabethan style of architecture, and the plan shows a building with a frontage to Victoria-road of 58 feet and to Bold-st., of 72 feet, the height from the ground to the eaves being 25 feet, and to the ridge 38 feet. A large assembly room capable of seating about 300 persons will also provided and will be well adapted for meetings, banquets. balls, &c. It is expected that the Club will be ready for open- ing in about six months. Messrs. Frazer of War- rington are the architects, and Messrs. Sayce and Rand Jes are the contractors. —Amongst those present at thn &ropily yesterday, in addition to the central figure, were Major Cross, Captain Walker, ' Messrs. T. C. Edwards Moss, M.P. &c. Air. E. W. Parnell extended a hearty welcome to Lord Crad-, bourne, and he assured his lordship that the Conservatives of Widnes appreciated the honour he had conferred upon them in coming that day. (Applause.)—Lord Cranborne expressed th e pleasure he felt in taking so prominent and so useful a part in Conservative organisation of that district. Organise organise, organise—that was the watchword of the Unionist party at that moment. (Hear, hear.) Of course a political club was primarily interested in the work of organisation and electioneering, and the work of successfully returning his honourable friend Mr. goss, to the House of Commons at the next election. (Applause.) His lordship then pro- ceeded to refer to the advantages of a club, and in conclusion appealed to those present tck make that club a success.—Mr. Moss M.P. proposed a vote of thanks to Lord Cranbourne, and Major Cross secon- ded the proposition which was enthusiastically carried.—Lord Cranbrook responded and afterwards departed for Gateacre Grange where he was the guest of Sir A. B. Walker. We hold over our report of the meeting in the evening, which was held in the Drill Hall.

div.head: CONCERT AT WIDNES.
div.p: CONCERT AT WIDNES.

The annual concert in aid of the Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel was given in the Volunteer Hall, on Monday night. The artistes were Miss Fanny Bouffler, soprano; Miss Harriette Rutherford, contralto; Mr. Percy Whyte, tenor; Mr. George Platt, baritone; Mr. Frank Weston, solo violoncello; Mr. H. J. Nicole, buffo; Mr. E. J. Macready; Mr. Herbert Whittingham, accom- panist. There was a large and fashionable audience. Mr. W. E. Chopping, of Birmingham, presided, and was supported on the platform by the Rev. Mr. Graham and the Rev. Mr. Hughes. After the introductory addresses the programme was pro- ceeded with. The first item was the quartette "When hands meet," by Miss Hoak; Miss Ruther- ford, Mr. Macready, and Mr. George Platt. This was rendered in a faultless style, the voices being well balanced and modulated. Theyianoforte solo "Pasquinade," was given in a masterly manner, and was quite a treat. Mr. George Platt, was very happy in the song "The Yeoman's Wedding," and met with a hearty encore. Miss Rutherford was also re-called for her song "Oh, oh, hear the wind blow," and gave ." Home. sweet home." She possesses a voice of considerable regisi,er, which at times is suggestive of a mezzo-sopitno. Mr. Percy Whyte was very effective with the ballad "When other lips," the audience demanding a second appearance. Miss Boufffer quickly took the fancy of the audience in her song "Esmeralda," which she gave in fine style, having of course to respond to the applause when she gave "Sitting on the stile." Mr. Frank Weston also made his mark with his violoncello solo "Caprice bon gris," He also found it necessary to give a second "piece," The duet by Miss Bouffier and Miss Rutherford "In the Dusk of Twilight" was given with much sweet- ness. Mr.-Nicholls in his humorous sketch " A Lullaby" after reappearing brought the first part to an end. Durirg the interval a vote of thanks was passed to the chairman for presiding. In the second part the artistes sustained the success which they had scored in the first part and without exception. Mr. Wittingham deserves special praise for the valuable assistance which he rendered at the piano. Without specially commenting on the items of th second part the programme was as follows :—Trio "0 Memory," by Miss Bouffier, Miss Rutherford and Mr. E. J Macready ; song, "The Sailor's Graves," by Mr. Whyte; song, "Dolly's Revenge," by Miss Bouffier ; song, "Out on the 'Deep," by Mr. George Platt; song, "Ora pro Noble," by Miss Rutherford, violoncello solo by Mr. Frank Weston; duet, " Excelsior " by Mr. Whyte and Mr. Geo. Platt; Buffo song, "The Merry Grey Fat Man" by Mr. Nicholls. Finale "Sleep :Gentle Lady" by Miss Boater, Miss Rutherford, Mr. Macready and Mr. Platt. The promoters of the concert are to be congratulated on the result of their efforts.

INSTITUTION OF THE REV. TILE HON. R. POWYS, LL.B.—The Archbishop of Canterbury has instituted the Rev. the Hon. Edward Victor R. Powys, LL.B., of Trinity College, Cambridge, to the Vicarage of liernsing, near Sevenoaks, on the presentation of Lord Sackville. The benefice was vacated by the cession of the Rev. G. Bridges Lewis, and is only of the net annual value of £9O, with a residence, the population numbering nearly 500. Mr. Powys, who was recently offered, but declined. the Rectory of Warrington, is a brother of Lord Lilford, ;of Bank Hall, Bretherton, near Preston.
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

At the first named of these sub-sections, a number of men have been withdrawn from their work between Tom Payne's and Twenty Step Bridges, and are employed on the left of the Northwich-rd., between Stockton Heath and Latchford. Looking from St. Thomas's church-yard, at present the appearance of a landscape seems to give to strangers the idea that an earthquake has occurred there, and leads to many strange comments on the work from passers by. At Walton, steam navvies are cutting through the earth at a rapid rate, and at Morley common, where rock instead of soft earth has to be removed, progress is steady. A VISIT FROM THE FIRST LORD OF THE TREASURY.

Mr. W. H. Smith, M.P., after inspecting the Ship Canal works between Barton and Salford on Wednesday, was entertained at luncheon by the mayor of Salford (Mr. Alderman Dickens) at the Salford Town Hall. , Responding to the toast of his health, the right hon. gentleman expressed his admiration of the enterprise played by the promo teifi of the ship canal, and his confident belief that thafr great waterway when com- pleted would conduce to ?the prosperity of this district and of the country at large. Mr. Alderman M'Kerrow responded to the toast of "The Borough of Salford," and took occasion to referto the report on the amalga- mation of the borough with Manchester, whicn, he said, was deserving of senous and unprejudiced consideration at the hands of the Town Council. Sir. J. C. Lee, in acknowledging a vote of thanks for his courtesy as a ship canal director, predicted that the undertaking would be completed and the canal in use in three and a quarter years from the present time.

div.head: THE/EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888.
div.p: THE/EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 27, 1888.

EXPLORATIONS IN PALESTINE. On Thursday evening an interesting lecture wasj delivered in St. John's Presbyterian Church. Winwick-et.. Warrington, by Mr. George St. Clair, F.G.S., in aid of the Palestine exploration fund. The lecture was entitled—" Jerusalem, from Nehemiah to Titus." The chair was occupied by the Mayor (Aldeanan T. Sutton) and there was a good attend- ance. In introducing Mr. St. Clair the Chairman said that a lecture in regard to the ancient city of Jerusalem could not fail to be both interesting and instructive. Mr. St. Clair, in the course of his remarks, said that they were able now, in a [peat measure, to restore the Jerusalem of ancient times, and to see the city as it was in the days of David, of Nehemiah, and of Christ. What had already been attained by the work of the Society indicated what further import- ant discoveries awaited them if the work of excavation was continued. Jerusalem. though so small a city, was the most interesting one on earth, and to understand its history in detail a correct map of the whole city was required. The city was surveyed in 1864, at the\expense of Lady Burdett Coutts, who desired to see if the inhabi- tants were supplied with pure water, a boon which was refused after the survey owing to the action of Certain wicked old Turks, who had an interest in the bad water. The survey, however, resulted in the production of an excellent map of Jerusalem. In order to understand Bible history, they required a map of the city as it was in ancient days. The lecturer spoke at some length on the dis- coveries made by the Exploration Society, illus- trating his discourse by means of plans and maps. Important discoveries, it may be mentioned, were made last year. Amongst these was the discovery by Herr Schick of the Byzantine Pavement, which, in th'e opinion of many, is thought to be the pave- ment made by Constantine in front of his group of churches. The Phoenician inscriptions found in Palestine have proved of inestimable value to the Bible student. The Society states that all over the country there are ruins, mounds, and ancient sites where excavations would lay bare treasures of antiquity. A collection was taken up in aid of the fund.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT RINGSLEY.-011 Friday evening, a special thanksgiving service for the ingathering of the harvest was held at the Parish Church. The decorations were of the usual kind. The anthem "I will give thanks" (Barnby) was well I rendered by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. T. G. Cole. Mr. C. Hibbert, of Frodsham, presided at the organ. An appropriate address was delivered by the Rev. E. P. Alexander, M.A., vicar of Alvanley, at the conclusion of which-a collection was made in aid of defraying church expenses. RE-OPENING OF THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL, HELSBY.—This chapel, which has been closed for a short time on account of necessary repairs, for painting, ventilating, and decorating, was re-opened on Sunday, when the Rev. J. Judson, of Halton, preached, in the afternoon from the text Matt. xiii. 3-8, and in the evening from Joshua xxii. 20. Special hymns, harvest and others, were sung by the choir, assisted by Messrs Guest Bros., Mr. G. S Guest, and other friends. Each service was well attended. The collections, which amounted to £l3 2s. ed., will go towards defraying the costs already incurred for the repairs.

div.head: NAVVIES' RESORT AT RUNCORN. A PUBLICAN FINED.
div.p: THE NAVVIES' RESORT AT RUNCORN. A PUBLICAN FINED.

Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Major Ilazlehurst, Runcorn Petty Sessions. on Monday, Robert Morgan, landlord of the Wheatsheaf Inn, Bridge- street, was charged with permitting drunkenness on his premises, further'with supplying drink to four drunken persons. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defence.—lnspector O'Donnell deposed that about ten o'clock on Saturday night. he visited the Wheatsheaf Inn, in company with Sergeant Woolley. In the taproom there were 10 or 12 navvies, and four of them were drunk. On the table was a pint mug, with some beer in it. a glass of beer, and a quart can filled with beer. Two men named Davies and Collins claimed to have paid for the quart of ale, and both men were drunk. A man in another nart of the room then said" That is say beer; lam sober enough and I paid for it: Davies then proceeded to divide the beer amongst his drunken companions. The four drunken men were James Davies, John Collins, Henry Renshaw, and Rutter.—By Mr. Linaker: There was no quarrelling or disagreement going on, but the men were rather noisy.—Mr. Linaker: You object strongly to the drink trade? do nothing of the. kind; Ido my duty.—Have you never said outside this court, some- thing to that effect? No sir, not at all.—Mr. Linaker: I will not go into the box against you myself.—ln answer to further questions the Inspector said he had been in Runcorn five months, and was in New Ferry two years. He had been in the Cheshire constabulary 17 years. He-had no instructions from the Chief Constable to go into the public-houses.—Mr. Linaker: All this harrassing of publicans emanates from yourself then ! The Inspector said he was simply doing his duty. He visited houses weekly, and eftener.—Mr. Linaker: But the town was kept in good order long before you came here ?—The Inspector: I don't dispute that in any way; I did not come to reform it,—Mr. Linaker: I say you have harassed the trade of Runcorn and respectable .houses at night.—The Inspector: I take all nOtISAS in town.—Sergeant Woolley gave con- firmatory evidence. The men were "stagger- ing drunk." He visited the house a isecend time, and the defendant asked "What is amiss ?" Wit- ness replied "The men are drunk." "Then," retorted the landlord "if I can't fill drink as long as the men cati stand up to drink it, I will shut thehouse up." The defendant then ordered the men out and closed the house.—P.o 's Bowen, Dale, Taylor, and Hulse also stated that the men were very drunk, and the latter stated that Collins, who was a man who never wore a hat, called into the Navigation Inn, and the landlord refused to supply him.—Mr. Linaker, in addressing the Bench for the defence,saidwith reference to the Inspector of Police now stationed in Runcorn there had never, sines he remembered Runcorn, been such a stirring up amongst public-houses. There were complaints, not only amongst the publicans,but strong complaints,which he could prove in evidence, about the inspector going three or four nights in a week into every room in houses where respectable tradesmen went to spend an hour or two and who did not like to be under the sur- veillance of a man like that.--Superintendent Holling- worth objected that this was not the time nor the place to make a complaint about an officer.—Mr. Reynolds said he did not see what it had to do with the case.— Mr. Linaker said he thought the inspector was led away by over-zeal in visiting public-houses, and was led away by his opinions, he would not say to commit per- jury, but to put things in a stronger light than he otherwise would do. There were now living in lod- gings in Runcorn a large number of navvies who worked on the Ship Canal, and surely it was not too much, after a lahorious week, that these men should spend three or four hours in a public-house treating each other, and enjoying themselves in their own rather rough way, if they conducted themselves properly. Surely these men were not to be hounded out of society by a staff of police-officers.—He called the defendant, who stated that he had been a foreman on the Ship Canal, and his house was the resort for navvies. When the Inspector called there were eight men in the house. Henshaw had three pints of ale about seven o'clock, and returned at a quarter to ten for a parcel he had left. He did not apply for any drink. He stood on oneleg to show the police he was not drunk.' Rutter was on the " road ' and he gave him a pint of ale and some bread and cheese. He had no more in the house. Davies was looking for lodgings and never had any drink in the house. Between five and seven o'clock Collins paid for two or three half gallons of ale for the company. He came back about a quarter to ten and asked to have a quart of ale on strap, but he refused. None of the men were drunk; they were all sober. He asked Sergeant Woolley if he should supply the men with beer and the Sergeant replied" Na." He (witness) then said he would shut up the house and take the men down to the Town Hall, and see the Superintendent. He did so, but the Superintendent was not in. The men did not stagger down the street. He never used the wprds attributed to him by the Sergeant.,;— William Wright, carter to Mr. Moore, deposed that the men in the house were sober' and that there was no disturbance taking place.—Peter Crompton, furnaceman at Messrs. Wigg Bros.and Steele, said he had lived in Runcorn all his life, and had never been under the supervision of the police. The men in the house were not drunk. He paid for the quart of ale in the can, and Davies had no right to divide it.—Mr. Harry Wright, clerk to Mr. Linaker, deposed that he had declined to give evidence unless summoned. He was in Bridge-street at the time the public-house was closed up, and saw the men turned out. They were not drunk ;it was not true that they staggered. The men walked steadily and straight. William Brimelow, pork butcher, Regent-street gave similar testimony.—Jane Parry, Blantyre-street, said Davis lodged at her house on the night in question.—He arrived at the house at 10.45 and was quite sober.— Samuel Brown, labourer at Norton Town, also gave evidence that the men were sober.—The Bench con- sidered that drunkenness had been permitted on the premises, and imposed a fine of 20s.,and costs 205.; total £2. Mr. Linaker gave notice of appeal.

WARRINGTON BLUR COAT CHARITY SCHOOL.— Canon Barker, who has recently made his annual inspection of the above school reports as follows : "I may say that in my opinon the school is keeping up its reputation in every way; excellent work has been done in the past, and the children look well and happy." lIAuvEST SERVICES AT La..TolFoun.—The anni- versary services and harvest home in connection with the Latchford Weelevan Methodist Sunday school were held on Sunday, in the Temperance Hall. In the morning Mr. J. B. Isaac save an in- teresting address. The Rev. J. Tonga preached an excellent sermon to a crowded congregation in the afternoon, and Mr. S. G. Prout, of North Devon, was the evening preacher, the room again being crowded. Special hymns were sung by the children an an anthem, "Cry out and shout thou inhabit- ant of Zion," was creditably rendered by the choir. The room was neatly decorated, and liberal collec- tions in aid of the school funds were taken.

div.head: SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST WAR-
div.p: SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS AGAINST WAR-
RINGTON MEN.

At the Borough Police Court,yesterday morning two men named William Putman, Wellington-st., and Thomas Whitehead, I ..:Idgewater-st., who are both in the employ of Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, millers, as carters, were brought up in custody on, remand on a charge of having felonicusly assaulted Annie Foden (14), the daughter of James Foden, of Macclesfield, on the 23rd inst. Mr. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk) appeared for the prosecution. Mr. A. Browne appeared for prisoner Eastham. and Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins for prisoner Whitehead The case for the prosecutionwas to the effect that the girl, who is a silk piecer, left home on Tuesday morning for the purpose of finding work. She walked to Knutsford, where a woman gave her some tea and a bun. She told this woman that she had Mends working in Manchester, and would go to Warrington and try to get forward to Manches- ter. The woman who had befriended her said that some Warrington carters would give her a lift, and later in the day she left Knutsford with the prisoners, In one of their carts. it was alleged that on the journey one of the prisoners Whitehead, feloniously assaulted the girl twice, and that when the men got to the stables with their horses the other prisoner committed an assault upon. They afterwards left her in the street, and, she told a policeman what had happened.—Complainant, in her evidence, bore out the statement of the pr3secu- ting solicitor, and Dr. S. Smith spoke to the injuries that had been received by Foden. After several witnessesliad been called, the magistrates committed prisoners to take their trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. At the Borough Court, on Wednesday, a respect- able looking man, named Chatles McCollom, was committed for trial on a charge of having attemp- ted to criminally assault a girl named Letitia Smith, (17) a domestic servant. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the prosecution, and said that the offence was alleged to have been committed on the 22nd Oct., in a warehouse occupied by McCollom, who is a joiner, in the neighbourhood of Friars- green. It was alleged that he was walking with the complainant and forced her to go into the warehouse, where he endeavoured to assault her. The defence, which was conducted by Mr. A. Browne, was that the complainant was a consent- ing party. At the Occasional Court, yesterday, before Mr. P. Stubbs, Wm. Roberts, a Ship Canal labourer, was charred with having committed an outrage upon a girl named Eliza Ward, at Walton. Prisoner was remanded in custody, for a week, when it is expec- ted another charge will be preferred against him.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council will be held on Tuesday evening next, at the Town Hall, for the purpose of winding up the business of the municipal year. 'r THZ FOLIOS OF LATC6FORD.—The Watch Committee will recommend "that for the better watching of the outlaying portions of the Latchford side of the Boroqgh, the force be augmented by the appointment of addi- tional constables, not exceeding six in number, and that the Chief Constable be instructed to report to the Committee when, in his judgment, the appointments should be made." Tart RscaNrr FALALITY AT HOWLET.—The paving and Sewering Committee, having considered thc verdict and presentment returned by a jury respecting the drowning of a boy on the 7th October,in Howley Brook, and which brook the jury urged the Corpor- ation to have covered over from the river to Mae "Mount," the Committee will recommend that notice be given to the owners of the property adjoin- ing the brook (which the Corporation is informed is a private watercourse) requiring them to fence off the said brook. It has been further resolved that, in order to prevent the backing up of tidal waters in the brook, a penstock be constructed at the river end of the brook.

THE GRAMMER SCHOOL REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNORS.— Mr. Edward Milner having resigned his appointment as one of the Representative Governors under the scheme for the administration of the Warrington Grammer School Foundation, the General Purposes Committee recommend that Mr. Alderman Webster, the chairman of the School Attendance Committee, be appointed a Representative Governor in his stead. VOTES OF THANES.—The minutes of each of the Com- mittees contain resolutions acknowledging the services of their chairman and vice-chairman during the past year, and at the Council meeting the following resolution will be proposed by Alderman Hohnes, viz.:—" That the best thanks of this Council be presented to Thomas Hindmarsh Sutton, Esq., Alderman of this Borough, for tho satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate of this Borough during his year of office, and for the unvarying courtesy and impartiality displayed by him when presiding over the deliberations of the Couimil and in his intercourse With its members." The annual report of the Chief Constable on the police establishment and the state of crime will also be in the hands of the members of the Council.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

VotuNTEEns.—On Sunday the H (Lymm) company of Volunteers assembled at the Cross for church parade. After going through a few movements, under the com- mand of Captain Jones. the company marched to Lymm Parish Church, where the Rev. E. Lomax preached.

MrruALIMPROVEMENTSOCIETT.—The subrject appointed for Monday night's meeting was "Readings from Miscellaneous Authors, with criticisms," but as there was such a scanty attendance, it was decided to adjourn I the meeting until the following week. The limited atten- dance w.s believed to be due to the other attractions in the village. Lraus GOOD TEMPLARS.—On Tuesday evening, the r Tower of Refuge Lodge held their weekly meeting in the Congregational Schoolroom. The ledge was visited by a deputation from the Purity Lodge, Altrincham, consisting of the Rev. A. Kirkland and Bro. Perrin, who each gave an interesting address, and also by several brethren from Latchfo,rd. BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The weekly meeting was held on Wednesday. Readings were given by Messrs. Griffiths, G. Clarice, Hurstfield, and G. Diamond. An impromptu speech on " Sympathy " was introduced by Mr. G. Clarke, and discussed. A recita- tion was given by Mr. W. Gould, "Paddy's version of Excelsior," and the adjourned discussion on "The Life and Times of Cromwell" was continued. LECTURE.—On Monday evening a lecturewas delivered in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Rash Green, by the Rev. Principal Macpherson to a crowded audience. The Rev. G. E. Young presided. Principal Macpherson based his discourse upon St. Mark xiv. : 'Christ's last day in the temple." The lecture throughout was of a most interest- ing character, and was much appreciated by the audience. The usual votes of thanks terminated the meeting. ST. PETER'S CHURCH, 91JORTRINGTON.—The harvest services at this church were continued on Sunday, when Holy Communion was celebrated at 9 a.m. At the morning service the preacher was the Rev. G. W. Guest, rector of Lymm. In the afternoon a sacred oratorio was rendered, entitled "Christ and His Soldiers." At the evening service, the pulpit was °Coupled by the Rev,

Kenneth L. Jones, rector of St. Bride's, Stretford. Good congregations assembled at each service, and the offer- tories were devoted to the day schools of the parish. Ir No RElNS.—Samuel Rutter, teamsman, Lymm, was charged at the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, with riding without reins at Timperlev. P. C. Carter proved the case. The aunt of the defend- ant, who appeared, stated that the defendant, who was employed by Mr. Peters, had been working for three nights dunng the week. The Chairman said that the defendant was not charged with being asleep while in charge of a cart, and for the offence of riding without reins he would be fined Is., slid 10s. id. costs.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Walter Calvert Is in custody, at Worksop, on the charge of attempting to murder his brother James by shooting him in the head on Thursday night. SHOCKING SIIICIDE.—The body of Mrs. Morrice, the wife of the vicar of River, near Dover, was found dead on the railway on Friday Morning, her head being smashed. The case appeared to be one of suicide. STEAMERS IN COLLISION.—The City of Dublin Com- pany's cargo steamer Dublin and the Tedcastle Line steamer Longford were in collision off Great Orme's Head on Friday morning. The former sank, the crew es- • caping. The Longford sustained severe damage. MERTHYR TYDVIL ELECTION.—The polling at Merthyr Tydvil was opened on Friday morning in dull weather. The candidates were Mr. F. Foulkes Griffiths (Glad- stonian), and Mr. Pritchard Morgan (Independent Liberal). A later telegram says the polling passed off without serious dis urbance, although in some districts ' bands and choirs paraded the streets. TEE COAL TRADE.—The adjourned conference between the colliery proprietors and the miners' representatives of the Oldham and Ashton district was resumed at the Queen's Hotel, Manchester, on Friday. After a somewhat prolonged conferconce, the masters agreed to give the 10 per cent, asked for. Between 3,000 and 4,000 colliers were represented at the meeting. TILE PARNELL COMMISSION.—The Parnell Commission continued its sittings on Friday, when, on the application of the Attorney-General, it was decided that in future the Court should sit on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thurs- days, and Fridays. The Attorney-General, after calling for the production of certain American documents men- tioned in Mr. Lewis's affidavit, resumed his speech, and the Commission adjourned until Tuesday next.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY.—The sugar market is gener- ally dull; beetroot quoted 13s 144 October, 12s 100 Novem- ber-December. Coffee market firm for most qualities. Tea: only 280 packages Indian and Ceylon advertised for sal,. to-day. Rice without change. Cotton market steady. Jute active at full values. Tallow unaltered. Rape oil, 29s 6d; linseed oil, 19s 6d. Turpentine, 33s 9d, Petroleum: American, 6d; Russian, sid spot.

- - LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. Beef is very firmly held. Pork rules steady at recent rates. For bacon there is a better demand from the country, and values have a harden- ing tendency. Hams and shoulders are steady at unchanged rates. Cheese and butter close without special feature. Cable adyices from America quote a decline of 5 to 10 cents per 100 lbs. in the value of bogs, and Is 94 per cwt. on lard. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

BRICK-STREET SUNDAY ScuooL.—The first meet- ing of a Band of Hope in connection with this Sunday School was held on Tuesday night. The attendance was large, and an address upon " Intem- perance " was given by Mr. William Wright. A miscellaneous entertainment of songs and recita- tions was successfully given.

cATROLIC BALL.---Tie annual Catholic ball was held in the Public Hall on Monday evening. It was preceded by a tea, to which a large number sat down. When dancing commenced, the hall was well filled, and tho enjoyment waskept up until the early hours of the following morning; The proceeds are in aid of the Catholic schools of the town. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT HOLY TRINITY.—The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with Holy Trinity church were continued on Sunday, the preacher in the morning being the Rev. Canon Dodd, M.A., vicar of Stretton and in the evening the Rev. Frederick %Barker, Ma., vicar of Grassen- dale. There was a scholars' service in the after- noon, when an address was delivered by the Rev. W. L. Warne. The collections for the day, which were in aid of the day schools, amounted to nearly £25. The decorations were pretty and effective. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—On Sun- day evening the Rev John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Bewsey-street, preached an interesting sermon that was especially addressed to young men. The subject of the dis- course was "Follow Me," and the preacher urged Christ's claim for immediate, obedient, and devoted discipleship. At the conclusion of the seas-ice a collection was made in aid of the Lancashire Inde- pendent College, an institution formed for the purpose of training young men for the Christian ministry.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A BARBER.—On Mon- day, at the Borough Police Court, Peter Green, a barber, who lives in Winwick-at., appeared to answer a summons charging him with having assaulted a girl named Mary Bennett, daughter of Reuben Bennett, of Winwick-st., on the 17th inst. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the prosecution, stated that the case was a serious one, and alleged that the defendant called the girl into his shop and indecently assaulted her. Bennett gave evidence to that effect and, after other witnesses had been heard, Mr. Davies,for the defence,contended that no act of indecency had been committed by his client. After hearing• evidence, the Bench dealt with the case as one of common assault, and imposed a fine of ss. and costs. AN OVER-SCRTJPULOUS SHOP-REEPER.—At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Margaret Gill, shop-keeper, High Leigh, sued John Earl, of Crowley, for the sum of 12s. On the plaintiff being requested to take thejoath, preliminary to stating her case, she declined, in an emphatic manner, stating that the defendant's wife, who appeared for him, was "going to swear false," and she (plaintiff) was not going to swear against her. His Honour pointed out that if the plaintiff refused to be sworn, her case:would have to be struck out. The Registrar: If yon tell the truth you need not fear that the oath will do harm to you.—Plaintiff, how- ever, refused presistently to be sworn, and left the court, the case being struck out,

HARVEST SERVICE AT Sr. ANNE'S CHURCH.—A service of thanksgiving for the ingathering of the harvest was held at St. Anne's Church, •Winwick- road, on Thursday evening, when there was a good congregation. The following laidies assisted with the decorations :—Pulpit, chancel, and alter, Miss Ashbrook ; chancel screens, Miss E. Jefferson; lectern and litany stool, Miss Baird and Miss James; choir-Stalls, Miss Downie; font, Miss James, Miss Skelland, and Miss Murray. The vicar (the Rev. J. G. Richards) read the prayers, and the lessons were read by the Rev. J. Philips of Orford, who was also the preacher. In the course of his sermon, Mr. Philips said that agriculturists had suffered greatly this year from the bad harvest, and drew the deduction that God might in that way be punish- ing the guilt of the nation—the drunkenness, immorality and crime that so widely prevailed. The collection was in aid of Church expenses. Dur- ing the service, the choir sang an anthem. Mr. Percy Randall presided at the organ. AN UNFORTUNATE MARRIAGE.—At the Borough Police Court, on Mnnday morning, a case came before the magistrates in which a pensioner named Healey was charged with having left his wife and five children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. B. Shearer, enquiry officer, said that prisoner's wife and children were admitted to the Workhouse on the 9th inst. It ovs the

second time that prisoner had been charged with desertion.—When called upon for his defence prisoner said that his Wife "would drink as much money as a coiner could make in a week." She spent his earnings in drink, and he and the children had to starve. On one occasion he gave her .£'2, 10s., and when he came home in the evening she had_spent nearly all of it for drink, and there was no food in the house.—The Chief Constable : She is a woman who is given to drink. At times she gets seriously drunk, and recklessly spends his money.—The Mayor: It seems a hard ease.—Alderman Harrison: You should take some sensible steps to keep her out of mischief.—After some consideration the magistrates adjourned the case for a month to see what arrangement prisoner could make. They advised him to keep the four eldest children, and, in the event of his wife refusing to behave properly, to pay for her maintenance in the Workhouse. TRAVELS IN THE SOUTH OF IRELAND.—Last even- ing week, at a meeting of the Wesleyan Improve- ment Society, a paper was read by Mr. Arthur Bennett, entitled "Two nights in Trappist Monaster- ies." The Rev. W. Brookes occupied the chair. The essayist gave an interesting description of recents travels in the South of Ireland, confining his atten- tion more particularly to two nights spent in Trappist Monasteries. The Trappists, as an order, he said, give themselves up to the meditation of Divine things and to the tending of the poor. At the first of the monasteries he visited, S. Joseph's, Tipperary, the secular work was done wholly by lay-brethren, who did the baking, gardening, wash- ing. &c., of the establishment. Theywere distin- guished from the monks proper by a brown instead of a white garb. Only the prior read the news- papers; and all retired each evening at eight o'clock, rising the following morning at two o'clock for early prayers. Mount Melon, on the banks of Black- water, the Rhine of Ireland, was next visited. There they had a fine library, and one of the works which caught the eye of the visitor was the famous " Leban Jesu," by Strauss. John Stuart Mill was also well represented. In the chapel a lamp was kept continually burning. The essayist spoke highly of the hospitality shown to him by the reverend fathers. In the discussion which ensued the Chair- man and Messrs. C. Plinston J. E. Richardson, W. H. Butler, S. B. Stringer, and J. Neil took part.

ST. MART'S ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.—On Sun- day solemn exposition of the Blessed Sacrament took place at Buttermarket-st. Church. At eleven o'clock High Mass was celebrated by the Superior of St. Mary's (Father Sumners), 0.5.8., the sermon being preached by Father Flanigan, 0.5.8. After the Mass, the monstrance, or relinquary, which con- tains the Sacred Host, was placed in exposition upon the marble throne of the high altar, and re- mained all through the afternoon exposed. sur- rounded with flowers and lighted candles. Many persons visited the church during the day, and in the evening the building was crowded to witness the solemn procession of the Blessed Sacrament round the interior. Shortly after half-past six he usual devotion of the Rosary recited by priest and people commenced, English hymns being sung at intervals. During the offertory the choir sang a selection from the great masters, and a few minutes , past seven the procession of children filed into the ' church through the long corridor on the south side of the building. When the children had arrived in the church, the procession of the officiating priests entered, cross bearer, acolytes, torch bearers, and incense bearers walking first, followed by Father Browne, 50.5.8.. a 4 sub-deacon, Father Flanigan, 0.5.8., as deacon, the Superior of St. Mary's, Father Sumner, as officiating priest, walking last. The priests walked first to the high altar, when the Sacred Host was taken from the throne, and placed in tlie hands of the officiating priest, the procession then starting on its way down the middle aisle. The cross bearer. with the large processional cross, walked first, followed by many children dressed in white, with bouquets or baskets of flowers in their hands. Beautiful banners were carried, and the streamers of the banners were held by children of tender age. At the end of the procession came the acolytes with lighted torches, and the incense bearers ; and the three priests in vestments of gold colour walked under the canopy of white satin, the brass poles of the canopy being held by four non-commissioned officers from Orford Barracks. During the procession round the church the choir sang the "Gloria," Mr. Richard Eccles conducting. The Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament was after- wards given at the high altar by Father. F. W. Sumner, assisted by Father Flanigan and Father Browne.—Cort.
Croos,

WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1888. PTHE BURGESSES OF NORTH-WEST WARD. I,lntas AND tatr..teriantrx,—ln response tothe requisition of a largeirody of the electors of the North-West Ward, sad of the Ratepayers' Association, we beg to offer ourselves as Can- didates `for your suffrages at the forthcoming Municipal Election. At the eleventh hour, a contest has been provoked by one'tf our friends who thinks he has a better claim to your support than we have; but that is a matter which we must leave onu, as Electors, to determine. Weere of opinion that Warrington 'occupies an rtneaviable position in the matter of its high rates, -and that, with a view to encouraging the Trade of the Town, a resolute endeavour I should be made to effect a substantial reduction atthe earliest I postrole opportunity. -We pledge 'ourselves, if returned as your Representatives, to do our hest to lessen this burden upon the Ratepayers. We regard the working of the Sanitary Department of the 'Corporatiom as of vital importance to the well-being of the community, and shall pay especial attention to secure greater efficiency and more economical administratioir. The Question of Open Spaces and Recreation Grounds, in Cue densely-populated parts of the Town, shall at all times have our earnest consideration. We shall aid the movement for making the Library really !Free to the Inhabitants, for we believe this can be done with- 4iut adding to the rates, and that Warrington ought in this respect to be placed on a level with all the towns by which It is surrounded. We have good reason fp suppose that, before long, the Gas Committee will be in a position to effect a Reduction in the price of Gas; and we promise you that we shall direct our efforts to secure, as speedily as possible, this boon to the Inhabitants. - Our views on these and •other matters will be explained at a Public Meeting of the Electors, which Will be held in Wycliffe Hall, on Monday everring,and we need hardly add that we shall have pleasure in answering, as fax as we may be able, any questions which may be put to us. We are, Ladies and Gentlemen, Tour obedient Servants, WILLIAM PIERPOINT. THOMAS FLOOD. Warrington, October'24th, 1888.

TO THE SURGESSES •OP THE NORTH-EAST WARD.. LADIES END' GWITLEMEN,—Atthe urgent request of many of my Fellow 'Ratepayers of this Ward, I have contented to become a Candidate to represent you in the Town Council. Having resided in the Ward upwards of Fifty Years, lam known to most•of you, and should you de me the honour of Electing me as one of your Representatives, nothing shall be wanting on my part to serve you faithfully and to the best of my ability. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOSEPH` GARNER.

rrO THE 'BURGESSES ••OF THE NORTH-EAST. WARD. , LADIES AND GENTLEMEaq,—HaNing received a unanimous invitation from the Ratepayers'vlssociation to become aDandi- ' date for the representation of your Ward in the Town Council, ,Inive much pleastwe in ,placing my services at your disposal. As a Member of the Ratepayers' Association, I shell con- sider it ray.ditty, at all times, to devote my best attention to your interests, by proposing and.supporting a policy of economy combined with efficiency. I know, and regret to know, that complaints are very numerous about the serious nuisance caused by the Inter- cepting Depnt in Lythgoe's-lane, and if elected I will endea- vour, by all the means at my command, to influence the Council to make a most searching inquiry with the view of having theevil remedied. The rates of the Borough are excessively high, standing, as they do, seeond in height on the lit of Lancashire towns. Considering the increasing growth of Warrington, we have a right to expect and demand a substantial reduction. I am of opinion that the price cnarged for gas is exorbi- tant. This has the effect of preventing many of the working class from becoming consumers, thus placing them at a great disadvantage. If the price of gas were lowered, the consump- tion—and as a natural consequence the profits to the Borough —would begreatly increased and the inhabitants benefited. These and other kindred matters shall, if I am elected, receive at all times my best attention. Soliciting your interest and votes. I am, your obedient servant, HENRY THORNTON. Wartington, October 19th, 1888.

'lO THE !BURGESSES OF TH4 NORTH-EAST WARD. LADIS9 and GENTLEMEN,—Myterm of office in the Town Councitexpires at the end of this -month, and I offer myself for re-election. My vliews on the working of the •Zanitary Committee and the Gas Committee have been so often expressed during the past seven or eight years, that I do not think it necessary in this address to do more than in this.way refer to them. Ifithe votes that I have recorded,in the past meet with your approval, I hope you will show the same by giving your suffrages in my favours and placir,g sine as a Candidate of the Ratepayers' Association, at the head of the poll. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, FRANCIS DIXON, Warrington, Octcber 18th. 1888.

WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. 1888. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE NORTH-EAST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLENEN.—At thosolicitation of a large and influential body of Ratepayers I hawe -been duly nominated., and am now, a Candidate for your -.suffrages in this most important Ward. I have Already had some experience in the Council in regard to municipal matters. I am an old resident in the immediatewicinity of Tour Ward. and a larger ratepayer in it than any of my opponents. I was born in it, and now pass through it daily and know its "ins and cute," and its requirements and interests, as well asanost men among you. My sole object shall. be, without dictation or cliquism, to ensure the thoroughly good and Economical Government of my native town; and, if returned as your , represen.ative, I will do my utmost to secure your approbation. Ladies and Gentlemen, in conclusion I may say that I shall not canvass nor ask for a vote frornany one of you. I think, in these days of enlightenment s.nd intelligence, to do se would be absurd and degrading. I am free and indepen- dent of any Association. lam acting purely and simply for your and my :interests. I appeal to you directly, without fear or favour, believing that I tan unearth and fathom certain irregularities which exist in our local Government, and which should be immediately rectified. The result would be a reduction of rates and an advantage to all concerned. I hope shortly to have a few opportunities of addressing you, of which due notice shall be given. I have the honour to be' Ladies and Gentlemen, Your most faithful Servant, SAMUEL BARLOW. The Polley, Warrington, October 18th, 1888.

MUNICAPAL ELECTION, WARRINGTON, 1888 TO THE BUROBSSES OF THE NORTH !' -WES WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I ;13ave been honoured by a request from a most,infuential and numerous body of Rate- payers of this Wardto allow myself to be put in nomination for your suffrages, and to represent your interest :in the Town Council, which distinguishedgavour, after due delibera- tion, I have decided to aceept. In soliciting your vote and interest, Ido so, not as the nominee of any political party, or any local association, but as a thoroughly independent eandidate, only anxious to serve the general interests of all classe% of the community; in makers relating tea wise, efficient; and economical govern- ment of my native borough. As an employer of labour, and a considerable ratepayer and property owner, lam personally desirous of lessening the burden of taxation, which at thepresent moment is excessive, Mid. in my opinion, unnecessary. All other -questions affecting the well-being of our town, which may from time to time demand attention, would, I trust, so have my consideration and votes as to secure your confidence and approval. Ladies and Gentlemen, I leave the issue in your hands, and in doing so, ask you to return me as one of your representa- tives, and it shall be my Elarnestendeavour faithfully to dis- charge the high trust committed to my care. Believe me, Ladies and Gentlemen, to remain, Yours obediently, JOHN HEDGCOCK. Ivy Lodge, 2, Froghall-lane.

TO THE BURGESSES ON THE NORTH-EAST WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMENo—A requisition, numerously and influentially signed, asking me to stand as a Candidate to represent you in the Town Council, has been laid before me. After careful consideration. I have decided on seeking your suffrages. No word of reproach as to the Gentlemen who are my opponents will fall from my lips. If you think they are better qualified for the position than myself, by all means support them; if not, I shall esteem It an honour to represent you. You are the judges I Should you think fit te elect me, my desire is to enter the Council unfettered by political or other bias. My endeavour would be to secure Economy and Efficiency in the administration of municipal affairs. The efforts which are being made by all creeds to improve the educational and social status of the community will receive my heartiest support, and, so far as I can afford, my practical sympathy. The interests of 'the industrial classes in a community like ours demand our earnest attention. To those interests it will be my highest plemure to apply myself; at the same time the interests of the Capitalist and the Dreployer of Labour are also entitled to our watchful care and considemtion. If you elect me to represent your interests in the Council of ourgood old Town, I can only hope that my efforts may tend to promote Economy, Efficiency, and Prosperity. Soliciting your vote and interest, I rentain. your obedient Servant, W. H. J. JENKINS. Bank Chambers, 1, Winwick-street, Warrington, 17th October, 1888. . _

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.—WARRINGTON, 1888. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-WEST • WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—At the solicitation of an infirm- dial section of your number, we have expressed our readiness to become candidates for Me two vacancies it is your privi- lege to fill up in the Town Council. Opposedta us is one gentleman who is the nominee of the local Ratepayers' Associaticn,lllee help of which lattcrin its present constituted form, we, common with the large majority cf you, think we can very sensibly dispense with. The opinion in the ward is general, too, that we have plenty of good siren amongst ourselves, able and willing to take the position of your representatives in the Town Council, with- out calling in assistance of doubtful value from helpers out- :side. 1 One of us has had the -honour of already representing you in Use Council, and he hopes you will confer upon him the privilege of re-election. The other of us, if elected bythe favour of your votes, will appear there for the fititt time. But ones- , tione of any moment, ,whether now pending in the Council Chamber or done with, that have from time to time had con- sideration there, have had his observant attention, .and he will not be unprepared, if elected, to take part in all important questions that have to come under discussion. We ask you to do us the favour of electing us, 'but hesitate to make you any specific promises of what you may expect from us if you send us to the Council. You have many good and able men in the Council, aftstithe desire of 'the whole its members is we are all ready to believe, to do the best • they can for their townsmen as a body. If we promise you, as we do, that we will apply all our ability, and -endeavour to side with the ablest and best intentioned amongst them, you will, we trust, consider this promise a sufficient pledge for the confidence we venture to hope you will extend :to us. We have the bottom-to be, Your obedient Servants, • EDWARD GREBNALL, JUN, LEWIS VOWEL Wmauxorox,,l9th October, 1888.

• 'iFO THE BURGESSES OF THE LATCHFORD WARD. Ladies and Gentlemen,—l have had the bonourtottepresent your interests for the above Ward in the Town -Council for about -ten years, and‘am now a member of no less than six Committees, but ant -certainly not a member of the Sanitary Committee, and therefore have not voted for all the "extra- vagances and expensive experiments of the Longford Depart- ment, and in that way helped to spend thousands of pounds of your money," which have been spent by that department, as alleged by my opponent, Mr. H. J. Longton. Without following Mr. Longton's address, and dealing separately with the theories and allegations he sets forth in proof of my unfitness to continue as your representative in our local parliament, and of his pre-eminently high qualifica- tions for that honourable position, I will content myself by eaying, that in all I have done as a member of ;the Council, I have been influenced only by a desire to do my duty conscien- tiously in all that concerns your interests and my own, for they are Identical. If I .vote in favour of extravagant and unnecessary expenditure, as alleged, do I not punish myself as well as,you ? Have I not to bear my share af it? Apply- ing the principles of common sense, is it at all likely that I akeuld be a party to such on insane policy? I feel sure you will not be misled by such false statements as have been put forth to defeat my re-election. I therefore beg with great respect to solicit a renewal of your confidence on-the Ist of November next, assuring you that in • the event of your so honouring, me, I will spare no effort to show you how jealously I shall watch the expenditure, and how earnestly I shall render/11 the assistance I San to secure the efficient and economical government of the town in all its departments. If, on the other hand, you should beef opinion that Mr. Longton could move diligently and ably represent you than :Leonid, I shall cheerfully accept your decision, and retire, gratefully acknowledglng your kindness for past favours. I have the honour to renmin, • Ladies and Gentlemen, your faithful servant, JOSSYII TAYLOR. Laws:Foam, 17th =October, 1888.

BOROUGH OP ST. HELENS. ToTHE BURGESSES (IF PARR WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The period for which you did me the honour to re-elect me, unopposed, in 1885, as one of your reprerentatives, expires at the end of this Municipal year, and I again— with sincerest thanks for the past marks of your confidence—seek your suffrages. As you are doubtless aware, the work of your Council will be somewhat changed, and conaidembly increased by the new County Government Act, which, as you are also aware, was a pressing reason for the enlargement of your Council next year. Owing to the action and representations of your Represen- tatives, in common with those of other Boroughs, St. Helens now ranks as a County Council, and secures all the benefits of its own estate as hitherto administered. In consideration of the value of that estate, the unusually large area of our Borough, and the rapid increase of our popu- lation, there could be no question as to our right rank as a County Council. If in continuance of your kindness, and the confidence you have reposed in me, you should see fit to re-elect me, I can only say that you may rely upon my doing my utmost for the interests of Parr Ward and a the Borough. I have the honour to be. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, EDW. JOHNSON.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. TO THE BURGESSES OF PARR WARD. 1 LADIES and GENTLE-ME:I.—I feel honoured by the trust you have reposed in me by re-electing me as one of your ward representatives. I will endearour to show that your confidence has not been misplaced. I have the honour to be, Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, EDWARD JOHNSON. Greenbank Alkali Works, Oct. 25th, 1888.

I have thclionour to remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JOHN LOWE. Elton Head, Sutton, October 17, 1888.

BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS. MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, ter NOVEMBER, 1888. rro THE BURGESSES OF THE ECCLESTON wABD. LADIES AND GEINMEMEN,—The term for which, in 1885, you, for the third time, elected me ,to represent you in the ‘Clouncil Chainbenis about to expire, and I beg to again offer my services to you. In the past I'have always endeavoured, by a careful and 'close attention to the business ef the Councih to secure, with 'economy, the welfare of the Borough at large, and at the same time to see that your interests were not neglected. Among the many important questions that have arisen, I may mention the most recent—that of the increase in the number of theanembers of the Council—a measure to which I gave my support. as it seems to me that the property and interests of the Borough have of late years so much increased in value and importance as to require greater attention at the hands of the Burgesses' Representadves. If you againAmnour me with year confidence, I shall do my utmost to continue to faithfully fulfil the duties of so reopen- 'able an office. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, W. H.
